docs.title: RedGem 3D Engine
docs.text:
RedGem is a 3D game engine with its own editor. You build levels in the editor (or in Blender), write the gameplay in Ruby, press Play, and export a standalone game.

This manual is for people making games with it.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
1. Install the editor.
  2. Follow Your first game: about fifteen minutes from an empty folder to a playable game.
  3. Keep Behaviours and the API reference open while you write scripts.
  4. The command line reads and changes scenes as text, plays a game with no window, takes pictures of it and looks it over: handy in scripts and with coding assistants (see Making games with an AI assistant).

docs.title: How a game is organized
docs.text:
A game is a folder:

Path What it is scene.glb The main level: objects, meshes, lights, cameras scenes/*.glb More levels scripts/*.rb Ruby behaviours and scene scripts models/*.glb Models you can drop into a level sounds/ .wav, .ogg, .mp3 or .flac files images/ Pictures for menus and the HUD (.png, .jpg) locales/ The texts players read, one translation file per language: en.json, pt.json... (see Texts in several languages) game.json The game's id, title and window size

The editor reads and writes these files directly. There is no project database and no import step: what you see in the folder is the game.

docs.title: Making games with an AI assistant
docs.text:
For an MCP client, the stdio server exposes the same developer commands through eight tools, with a read-only mode, an allow list and cursor-based process events.

A coding assistant that works in a terminal (one that reads files and runs commands) can make a RedGem game with you: write behaviours, place objects in a level, play the game and read what went wrong. RedGem gives it what it needs in text, so it does not have to guess an API it has never seen, open a binary scene file or look at a window.

docs.title: What a new game comes with
docs.text:
redgem new (and the project hub) writes two files into every new game:

  • AGENTS.md: the guide to the game, in the file most assistants look for: its layout, the commands below with examples, how to run its tests, its conventions (one behaviour per file, named after its class) and the 25 calls games make most, each with a line of Ruby. Under 120 lines, so it costs little to read at the start of every session. The calls are taken from the same reference redgem api prints, so they are the engine's real ones.
  • CLAUDE.md: one line that points at AGENTS.md, for the assistant that reads that file instead.

Edit AGENTS.md as the game grows: what an assistant should know about your game (its rules, its scenes, what not to touch) belongs there.

docs.title: The commands it uses
docs.text:
Every one answers in a few lines and ends; each says more with --help. See The command line for all of them.

Need Command What is in a level redgem scene list . (a line per object: #5 Player pos=0,1.1,0 scripts=Player tag=player) One object in full redgem scene get . Player Move, tune, attach redgem scene set . Coin1 position=1,2,3 prop.speed=2 script+=Spinner Add or remove redgem scene add . Coin6 --from Coin1 position=4,1,0, redgem scene remove . Coin6 Is the game in order redgem check . (and --run-tests to run its tests) Does it play redgem run . --seconds 5: each script error once, with its file and line What it looks like redgem shot . shot.png --at 2: a small picture of that moment What a class can do redgem api, redgem api Transform, redgem api --search raycast

Scenes are changed through the same code the editor saves them with, so an edit made from the command line is saved exactly as the editor would save it. Objects are named by a short id (#12), a path or a name; a name several objects share is refused with each of them listed.

The common errors come with what to do about them: a mistyped method of one of the engine's classes is answered with the names near it, a class no script defines with the file it is looked for in, a scene the game lacks with the scenes it has.

$ redgem run . --frames 30
error: scripts/goal.rb:3: Goal#start on 'Goal' (behaviour disabled): undefined method 'positon=' for Transform (NoMethodError) -> did you mean: position=, position (redgem api Transform)
ran main for 30 frames (0.5 s): 1 errors, 0 warnings

docs.title: A good loop
docs.text:
1. Ask for one thing at a time: "a coin that spins and adds to the score".
  2. The assistant writes the behaviour in scripts/, attaches it with redgem scene set, then runs redgem check . and redgem run . and fixes what they report.
  3. When it matters how it looks, redgem shot takes a picture to look at.
  4. A system test in tests/ (see Testing your game) keeps it working: redgem check . --run-tests.
  5. Open the editor (redgem .) to see and play it yourself.

docs.title: Keeping it cheap
docs.text:
What an assistant reads, it pays for. RedGem's answers are short on purpose; a few habits keep them so:

  • List a level with --depth 0 or --limit 20 first, then get the objects that matter.
  • Ask redgem api <Class> or redgem api --search <word> instead of reading the whole reference.
  • Prefer redgem run (text) to redgem shot (a picture) to find out whether something works; a picture is for how it looks. Shots are 512x288 unless asked otherwise.
  • redgem check lists a screenful of problems; fix those before asking for --all.

docs.title: The manual for assistants
docs.text: The manual's site has llms.txt, an index of its pages with a line about each, and llms-full.txt, every page in one file to search. The docs build writes both (tools/docs/llms_txt.py). The API reference is also data: redgem api --json, and docs/scripting/api.json in the repository, which tests keep in step with the engine.

docs.title: Repeating a headless session
docs.text:
redgem run uses fixed steps of 1/60 s and a random seed of 0. Use --seed N to repeat another Ruby and particle random stream, including random values read while scripts first load. A seed is a whole number from 0 to 2147483647. Scatter requests keep their own explicit seeds. Network traffic, web responses and scripts that read external clocks or files are outside this replay.

Keyboard input comes from a JSON file. Each event replaces the whole set of held keys before its zero-based frame; keys remain held until the next event. An empty list releases them:

[
  {"frame": 0, "keys": ["w"]},
  {"frame": 30, "keys": ["w", "space"]},
  {"frame": 31, "keys": ["w"]},
  {"frame": 120, "keys": []}
]

redgem run my-game --seed 42 --frames 180 --input input.json \
  --assert "Scene.find('Player').transform.position.y > -10" \
  --print "Scene.find('Player').transform.position" --every 60

--assert evaluates a Ruby expression after every frame and fails the run at its first false or nil result. --until stops successfully when its expression becomes true; reaching the frame limit or quitting without satisfying it fails. Both expressions use ordinary Ruby truthiness (0 is true). --print evaluates an expression every --every frames (60 by default) and on the last frame, showing its Ruby inspect value with a one-based frame number. Values and total output are capped; increase --every to keep a longer run concise.

Expressions run in the game's interpreter with its script timeout, and can call game APIs. Use them to read state: a mutation or a call to rand changes the session too. The order is input, game frame, assertion, periodic print, stop condition. On an early stop, a final print runs after the stop condition. A syntax error, exception or timeout in any expression fails the run with its frame and option. The command exits 0 on success, 1 for a failed run, and 2 for invalid options or an invalid input file. Input currently covers keyboard state only.

docs.title: Object identities
docs.text:
An object's #id identifies that object across saves, renames and changes to its parent. Removing another object does not renumber it. Objects made, duplicated, pasted or imported in the editor get new identities; undo and redo restore the same identities with the objects.

A scene that has never been saved by the editor starts with numeric identities (#0, #1, and so on). Its next save persists them in the scene. New objects use compact hexadecimal identities. Always take an identity from redgem scene list or the result of scene add, and pass it back unchanged; it is not an array index. Names and hierarchy paths remain valid selectors too.

The file keeps identities in the private REDGEM_object_id glTF extension, with an id string on each node. It is listed in extensionsUsed so other glTF tools can ignore it. The engine repairs invalid or duplicate identities with a warning. An external exporter that drops this extension creates a scene without those persistent identities; list its objects again before editing it. Identical names in different scenes do not identify the same object.

Before editing a scene, keep a copy of its .glb. Afterwards, use redgem scene diff . --against /path/to/before.glb to inspect the changes by persistent identity. It reports object additions, removals and changed fields without writing either file. --scene chooses another scene and --limit caps the details; see the command line.

docs.title: The command line
docs.text:
For an MCP client, redgem mcp <game> --read-only exposes scene and API inspection over stdio. See MCP tools for editing, headless runs, process events and permission options.

Besides opening the editor (redgem my_game), playing (redgem my_game --play), making a game (redgem new) and building one (redgem build), redgem has tools that answer in a few lines of text and end: they read and change a scene, play the game with no window, take a picture of it, look it over, and say what the scripting API has. They are made for scripts, terminals and coding assistants: what they say is short, and every problem they report says where it is and what to do instead.

Each one says more with --help. They end with exit code 0 when everything went well, 1 when something is wrong with the game, and 2 when the command line was not understood.

docs.title: redgem scene: read and change a scene
docs.text:
A scene.glb is a binary file. redgem scene shows it as text, one line per object, and changes it through the same code the editor saves with, so a scene changed here is saved exactly as the editor would save it.

$ redgem scene list games/platformer
scene main: 27 objects (#id name, then what differs from the defaults)
#0 Ground pos=0,-0.5,-4 scale=14,1,14 collider=box
#4 MovingPlatform pos=0,1.5,-25 scale=3,0.5,3 scripts=Mover axis=x body=kinematic distance=2.5 speed=1.2
#5 Player pos=0,1.1,0 scripts=Player body=character jump_speed=9 speed=6 tag=player
  #6 Visor pos=0,0.45,-0.35 scale=0.5,0.2,0.12
#7 Coin1 pos=0,1,-4 scripts=Coin tag=coin trigger=true
#24 Camera pos=0,6,9 rot=-28.6,0,0 camera scripts=CameraFollow distance=9 height=5 target=Player
#25 Sun pos=5,12,5 rot=-44.8,24.4,0 light=sun
...

A line says only what differs from an object's defaults: its position (pos, meters), rotation (rot, degrees about X, Y and Z), scale when it is not 1, the mesh it shows when it is named otherwise than the object, its light or camera, the classes of its scripts, and its custom properties. Children are indented under their parent. --depth 0 lists the top objects alone; --limit N stops after N lines (200 unless said; --limit 0 lists all).

Naming an object. #12 is a persistent object identity, independent of its place in the scene file. A path (Player/Visor) or a name works too when only one object has it; a name several objects share is refused, with each of them listed by id and path. Identities survive saves, renames and reparenting. New objects get hexadecimal identities: take them from scene list or scene add and pass them back unchanged.

Command What it does redgem scene list <game> every object, a line each redgem scene get <game> <object> everything about one object: its path, parent, placement, mesh and materials, light, camera, scripts, properties and children redgem scene set <game> <object> key=value... changes the object and saves the scene redgem scene add <game> <name> [--from <object>] [--parent <object>] [key=value...] adds an empty object, or a copy of another (with its children), and saves redgem scene remove <game> <object> removes the object and its children, and saves redgem scene diff <game> --against <before.glb> compares the current scene with an earlier save, without changing either file

Every command takes --scene <name> for another scene than scene.glb: --scene level2 is scenes/level2.glb.

For diff, save a copy of the scene before editing, then pass that file to --against. Objects are matched by their persistent identities: a rename or a reordered node array does not create a new object. The summary counts added, removed and changed objects; details show the fields that changed, including placement, hierarchy, properties, materials, image bytes, geometry, cameras, lights, skin bindings and animation keys. Geometry and binary assets show content fingerprints. Unused assets and glTF data the engine does not load are outside this comparison. Re-encoding an image changes its fingerprint even if it looks identical.

--limit N bounds the detail lines (50 by default, 0 for all); the summary always counts every object. Numeric object and material fields tolerate float differences up to 0.00001; custom properties and fingerprinted asset values are compared exactly. Use an earlier save of the same scene: independently exported scenes without persistent identities cannot reliably identify the same objects.

What set (and add) take:

Word Effect position=x,y,z (or pos=) where it is, in its parent's space rotation=x,y,z (or rot=) its rotation, in degrees scale=2 or scale=1,2,1 its size name=Gate a new name parent=Level moves it under another object, keeping where it is in the world; parent= moves it to the top prop.speed=2.5 a custom property: true/false, a number, or a text (prop.label="Big coin"); prop.speed= removes it. A text that reads as a number is given in quotes that reach redgem: prop.code='"12"' (a list shows it as code="12") script+=Door, script-=Door, script=Door,Sound attaches a behaviour, takes one off, or sets the list (Door is scripts/door.rb) 
$ redgem scene set games/my_game Coin1 position=1,2,3 script+=Spinner
#7 Coin1 pos=1,2,3 scripts=Coin,Spinner tag=coin trigger=true
note: scripts/spinner.rb does not exist yet; it must define class Spinner
$ redgem scene add games/my_game Coin6 --from Coin5 position=3,3,-31
#27 Coin6 pos=3,3,-31 mesh=Coin5 scripts=Coin tag=coin trigger=true

A copy made with --from of a prefab = true template is an object of the scene, not another template. Names are made unique as the editor makes them (Wall, then Wall.001), by add and by name= alike; a name that starts with # or holds a / is refused, since it would read as an id or a path.

The words of a list line are what set takes back: pos=, rot=, scripts=Coin,Spin (the list of scripts), and a property as speed=6 as well as prop.speed=6. A key that is a typo of one of set's (positon=) is refused rather than made a property; prop. makes any key a property. mesh=, light= and camera say what an object is: they are taken back as they are, and not changed.

docs.title: redgem run: play with no window
docs.text:
$ redgem run games/my_game --seconds 3
error: scripts/coin.rb:12: Coin#update on 'Coin1' (behaviour disabled): undefined method 'spin' (NoMethodError)
ran main for 180 frames (3 s): 1 errors, 0 warnings

It plays the game with no window and no sound for a while (5 seconds unless --seconds N or --frames N says otherwise), each frame one fixed step of 1/60 s with nothing pressed, so the same run gives the same answer every time. It says each warning and error once (with how many times it came), led by the place in the game's scripts it points at, then one line of summary, and ends with an error when a script failed. --scene level2 starts on another scene. What the game saves goes to a folder of the run's own, deleted afterwards: a run never touches your progress.

docs.title: redgem shot: a picture of a moment
docs.text:
$ redgem shot games/my_game shot.png --at 2
saved shot.png (512x288, scene main at 2 s)

It plays the game to that moment (1 second unless --at says otherwise; --frames N counts fixed steps instead; at most an hour of the game, as for run) the way run does, draws every frame off screen, and saves the picture of the one asked for. Small unless asked otherwise: --size 1280x720 for more. --camera Name shows the game through the camera of that object instead of the scene's first camera; --scene starts on another scene. It needs a graphics card: it opens a hidden window to draw with. The same moment gives the same picture.

docs.title: redgem check: look a game over
docs.text:
$ redgem check games/my_game
error scripts/coin.rb:5: syntax error, unexpected end of file, expecting "'end'" (SyntaxError)
error scene main #20 Goal: scripts/goal_post.rb is not there; did you mean goal.rb?
error scripts/door.rb does not define class Door (attached in scene main #8 Door)
check: 3 errors, 0 warnings (12 scripts, 2 scenes)

Without playing the game it checks that every script compiles, every scene reads (with what the loader warns of), every script a scene attaches is there and defines the class its name says, and every sky_image is in images/. It lists a screenful of problems (--all lists every one).

--run-tests then runs the game's own tests (tests/*_test.rb, see Testing your game) with redgem-test, system tests with no window, and adds a line per failure with the first error it said:

$ redgem check games/my_game --run-tests
FAIL tests/score_test.rb: FAIL ScoreTest#test_a_coin_is_worth_ten: RedGemTest::Failure: expected 10, got 1
tests: 3 passed, 1 failed
check: 0 errors, 0 warnings (12 scripts, 2 scenes)

docs.title: redgem api: the scripting API
docs.text:
$ redgem api Transform
Transform: Where an object is, how it is turned and how big it is.
  position                        its position in the world (Vector3)
  position = vector               moves it; a physics object is teleported
  rotate(degrees)                 turns it by those Euler degrees
  ...

redgem api alone lists the classes, a line each; redgem api <Class> the methods of one; redgem api --search <word> the methods that have to do with a word (at most 20). --json says the same as data, for tools. It is the API reference, which --markdown writes, and which is made from docs/scripting/api.json.

Errors that run and shot report come with a hint when they are common ones: a mistyped method of one of the engine's classes gets the names near it, a class no script defines the file it is looked for in, a scene the game lacks the scenes it has.

docs.title: Working on the engine
docs.text: For people changing RedGem itself. To make games with it, the rest of this manual is enough.

docs.title: Demos
docs.text:
Demos: games/city (a crossroad with Ruby-driven traffic: lights, braking, spinning wheels; Kenney CC0 models), games/platformer (WASD/arrows, Space jumps: grab 5 coins, reach the flag) and games/driving (W/S throttle, A/D steer, Space hand brake, R reset: drive laps).

Showcase (games/showcase, not committed: it is built from downloaded assets). A street at dusk with a drivable car, traffic that keeps its distance and overtakes, parked cars, shop fronts and cafe tables, a crowd on the sidewalks, potholes and falling leaves, made to push the renderer. Blender only builds the scene; everything that happens in it is set up in games/showcase/scripts/main_scene.rb:

python3 -I tools/assets/fetch_showcase.py      # street: Poly Haven and ambientCG (CC0)
python3 -I tools/assets/fetch_ad_assets.py     # car and people: BlenderKit (see showcase/CREDITS.md)
SHOWCASE_RENDER=0 BLENDER_MEMORY_MAX=8500M tools/blender/run.sh build_showcase.py showcase
./build/src/redgem games/showcase           # then Play: WASD drives, Space brakes

The export needs about 7 GB of memory (close the editor first); without SHOWCASE_RENDER=0 it also renders showcase/renders/ad.png with Cycles, which needs an NVIDIA RTX card. games/city is rebuilt with tools/assets/fetch_kenney.sh and tools/blender/run.sh build_city.py games/city.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
cd build && ctest --output-on-failure        # everything
ctest -L system                              # only the system tests

Tests are run by a program of their own, redgem-test, built beside redgem (see Libraries and programs). A system test is a Ruby file run against a game: redgem-test <game_dir> <file.rb> [--screenshots <dir>] [--headless] [--work <dir>] [--after <test.rb>] (--headless runs without a window, --work gives the run a folder of its own for its save file and notes, --after goes on from an earlier test's run in that folder as if the game were started again; redgem-test --help lists every option).

The engine knows nothing of tests. Neither redgem nor redgem-player, which is what every built game ships as, has test code in it: what tests are written with (TestInput, SystemTest, RedGemTest, the runners and their command line) lives in src/testing and ruby/testing, a library that only redgem-test links. The engine gives it nothing but general options (EngineOptions: a fixed step per frame, an input fed by code, a save file, who shows the game) and the window a game is shown in tells whoever asks when a frame is drawn; the pictures a test takes (t.screenshot) are written by the test tool from there. Keep it that way: the app.ships_no_test_code test looks into the built redgem-player and redgem and fails when test code got in.

  • C++ unit + integration (doctest): math, extras parser, glTF loading from Blender fixtures, scene hierarchy, physics world, Ruby VM, and an engine nobody shows running the sandbox fixture game (and one shown by a presenter that records what it is handed).
  • Tests of the test tool (tests/testing/, doctest): its command line, its save file, what it adds to a game's Ruby, and whole runs of passing and failing tests.
  • Ruby tests run inside the engine's mruby: redgem-test --ruby tests/ruby/vector3_test.rb.
  • Editor system test (tests/editor_system/) opens the editor window on a copy of the platformer, picks, edits, plays, stops, undoes and saves.
  • System tests (tests/system/<game>/*_test.rb, run against games/<game>) open the real game window and drive it frame by frame with simulated input:
SystemTest.define do |t|
  t.hold(:w, frames: 60)
  t.wait_until(frames: 30) { Scene.find("Coin1").nil? }
  t.assert("score counts the coin") { GameManager.instance.coins == 1 }
  t.screenshot("collect_coin_after")        # saved to build/screenshots/<game>/
end

A template is tested as the game it makes: tests/system_templates/<template>/*_test.rb run against a game created from it by redgem new. Every template needs at least one.

What a game keeps between runs is tested by starting it again: tests/system_restarts/<game>/<name>_restarted_test.rb plays games/<game> after tests/system/<game>/<name>_test.rb did, on copies of the save, display settings and bindings that run left. The first run is a ctest fixture of the second (redgem-test --work <dir>, then --work <dir> --after <first_test.rb>), so asking for the second runs the first once before it.

Test fixtures are regenerated with tools/blender/run.sh build_test_fixtures.py tests/fixtures.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
Every pull request runs these workflows (.github/workflows/), side by side:

  • Linux (linux.yml): the build, every test (the system tests in windows drawn by Mesa's software renderer on a virtual display) and every linter.
  • Windows (windows.yml): the build with llvm-mingw and the tests that open no window.
  • macOS (macos.yml): the build and the tests that open no window on Apple Silicon and Intel, and the editor system test.
  • Android (android.yml): the player built for arm64-v8a and x86_64 by tools/android/build_runtime.sh, with the NDK tools/android/fetch_toolchain.sh pins (kept between runs). Nothing runs on Android there: it catches code that only breaks that build.

  • Sanitizers (sanitizers.yml): the tests that open no window (unit and integration, the testing library, Ruby, the command lines of the relay and the server) in a build with AddressSanitizer, LeakSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and in one with ThreadSanitizer, stopping at the first finding; and a build with coverage, whose report of src/ is the run's coverage artifact. The system tests are not run there: drawn by a software renderer, they would take hours with sanitizers on.

  • Fuzzing (fuzz.yml): the fuzz targets below, a minute each on a pull request, ten minutes each every night.

Every workflow builds with -DREDGEM_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS=ON: a compiler warning in src/ or tests/ fails it (the dependencies keep theirs). Build the same way before pushing to see them first. A sanitized build is made and tested the same way as CI does:

cmake -S . -B build-asan -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo -DREDGEM_SANITIZERS=address,undefined
cmake --build build-asan
tools/sanitizers/run_tests.sh build-asan address     # thread: -DREDGEM_SANITIZERS=thread

A finding in the engine's code is fixed. One inside a library the engine is built from goes into the suppression file of its sanitizer (tools/sanitizers/*.supp), with a line saying why.

Every archive cmake/Dependencies.cmake fetches is pinned by its SHA-256, as is the Android NDK (tools/android/fetch_toolchain.sh); a dependency fetched from git is pinned by its tag or commit. THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md is generated: after adding or updating a dependency, run python3 -I tools/licenses/collect_notices.py (after a build) and commit what it writes. The test tools.license_notices_are_up_to_date fails when it is stale.

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text:
The parsers of what comes from outside have fuzz targets in tests/fuzz/ (fuzz_<target>.cpp): gltf (the glTF loader), image_header (PNG, JPEG, WebP and Radiance headers, Radiance and small WebP pictures decoded), wire (MessagePack messages and the frames they travel in), http_response (answers of web servers, in pieces) and json_scanner (the custom properties of a scene's objects). With clang, libFuzzer makes up inputs for them:

cmake -S . -B build-fuzz -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo -DREDGEM_FUZZ=ON -DREDGEM_SANITIZERS=address,undefined
cmake --build build-fuzz --target redgem_fuzz_targets
tests/fuzz/run_fuzzers.sh build-fuzz 60 fuzz-work      # seconds each; what it finds is in fuzz-work/findings

Each target's seeds are in tests/fuzz/corpus/<target>/, and every build replays them (redgem_fuzz_<target>_replay, the ctest test fuzz.<target>). When a target finds an input that crashes it, fix the code and add the input to the target's corpus: its replay keeps it tested. A new parser of untrusted input gets a target of its own (redgem_add_fuzz_target in tests/fuzz/CMakeLists.txt).

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
src/core      what everything shares: math, logging, the fixed timestep clock, files, the platform
              layer (the only place, with the sockets of src/net, that asks which system this is),
              the words of a command line, embedding files in the binary, the game folder's layout
              (config.hpp)
src/scene     scene graph (objects, transforms, copies), particles, the custom properties scenes
              carry (props.hpp); in folders of their own: gltf/ (the loader: meshes, skeletons,
              animations, Blender extras), animation/ (clips and their playback), shapes/
              (primitives and terrain)
src/physics   PhysicsWorld interface + Jolt implementation
src/input     keys, axes/actions, keyboard, mouse, gamepad and scripted input sources; a touch
              screen's on-screen controls (touch_input_source.hpp), which only the program for
              a touch screen puts in front of the others
src/net       message framing and wire format, the host/guest session and its connection approval;
              socket/ (the only place with OS socket calls, what the systems spell differently being
              in socket_native), discovery/ (games on the local network), rooms/ (the relay and the
              entry point of its program, relay_main.cpp, and what a dedicated server's rooms share
              with it: codes, the lobby, guessers kept out), http/ (the games' web requests:
              HTTP/1.1 over Mbed TLS, one thread per request)
src/audio     sound effects and music (raylib, or silence when there is no audio device)
src/storage   what a game keeps between runs (the save store)
src/render    the window (window.hpp: the only place that opens one, with its graphics card, frame
              pace and pointer), the renderer that draws in it and owns what is on the card (HDR,
              shadows, reflections, post-processing), shaders, environment, culling, mesh
              conversion, what differs per graphics API (gpu_profile.hpp), the font texts are
              drawn with
src/script    mruby VM, behaviour host, native bindings
src/app       what plays a game: the engine loop, which draws nothing and hands each frame
              (FrameView) to a presenter (presenter.hpp); the presenter that shows a game in a
              window of its own and the painter every drawing presenter shares; game.json, the
              game beside a built executable, where saves go, user settings, the entry points of
              the player (player_main.cpp; on Android, android/android_main.cpp)
src/editor    editor: session (play mode), camera, picking, the app and its panels; document/ (the
              scene document: undo, save, the glb it edits, importing models), scripts/ (the script
              tabs), ui/ (ImGui panels and theme)
src/project   the tools around a game: new games from templates, builds (desktop, and Android in
              android/), recent games and the project hub, the command line, the entry point of
              redgem (main.cpp)
src/testing   what runs tests, apart from the engine: TestInput, the pictures a test takes of the
              game (TestScreen), the system test and Ruby test runners, the audio tests listen
              with, redgem-test and its command line
ruby/engine   Ruby prelude embedded in the runtime (Behaviour, Vector3, UI, Network...)
ruby/testing  the Ruby tests are written with (assertions, test cases, the system test DSL),
              embedded in redgem-test only
templates     the new-game templates: each folder is a whole game (scene, scripts, sounds) and a
              template.json about it, embedded in redgem as it is; a new game is a copy of one.
              A template is edited like any game: redgem templates/platformer
locales      the texts users read, one translation file per language (see Texts users read)
assets/editor fonts of the editor (Inter, JetBrains Mono; SIL Open Font License, see the license files)
games         demo games: scene.glb, scripts and the .blend each scene was built from
showcase      renders of the showcase scene and the credits of its assets
tools/blender scene builders (run with tools/blender/run.sh), walk_rig.py
tools/assets  downloaders of the free assets the demos use
tests         unit, integration, Ruby and system tests, with their fixtures
cmake         dependencies (pinned versions) and file embedding

The folders of src are layers, in the order above: each includes only itself and what is below it (core; then scene, net, input, audio, physics, storage; then render and script; then app; then server, editor, project; testing sees everything and nothing sees it). Each layer keeps its own numbers in a <layer>_config.hpp next to its code.

docs.title: Objects, and keeping hold of one
docs.text:
A scene object's ObjectId is a slot. The loaded scene's objects keep their slots (an id below the node count is that node); the slot of an object made while the game runs (Scene::clone, Scene.spawn) holds a new object once it is destroyed. Every object also gets an ObjectSerial no other object ever had, in any scene.

  • What keeps an object past the step it was handed it (a skin's bones, a vehicle's wheels, a character's own clip, a behaviour, a Ruby GameObject or Transform) keeps an ObjectHandle and asks Scene::resolve for it each time: that finds the object while it is alive, and nothing afterwards, whoever sits in its slot.
  • Only a registry the engine updates in the very step an object is destroyed may key by bare id: the physics bodies (Engine::process_destroyed removes them) and the scene's own hierarchy and copies.
  • Destruction is two steps: request_destroy marks an object and what is under it, its on_destroy runs with everything still there, then the batch is torn down children first.

docs.title: Libraries and programs
docs.text:
The folders are built into a few static libraries, one on top of the other, and each program links only the ones it is made of (src/CMakeLists.txt):

redgem_core     src/core                                           links nothing of the engine's
redgem_net      src/net                                            redgem_core, the JSON library,
                                                                   Mbed TLS
redgem_runtime  scene, physics, audio, input, storage, render,     redgem_net, raylib, Jolt, mruby,
                script, app, and the Ruby prelude                  cgltf, the JSON library
redgem_game_server src/server (without server_main.cpp)            redgem_runtime
redgem_editor   src/editor                                         redgem_runtime, Dear ImGui
redgem_project  src/project (without main.cpp), the templates      redgem_editor
                and the licenses
redgem_testing  src/testing, ruby/testing                          redgem_runtime

redgem-player   src/app/player_main.cpp    redgem_runtime   what players receive: plays the game in
                                                            the game/ folder beside it, nothing else
redgem          src/project/main.cpp       redgem_project   the editor, the project hub, the command
                                                            line (new, build, --play)
redgem-relay    src/net/rooms/relay_main.cpp     redgem_net       the meeting point for games over the
                                                            internet: no window, for servers
redgem-server   src/server/server_main.cpp redgem_game_server
                                                            a game run on a server for players to
                                                            join, in rooms: no window, no display
redgem-test     src/testing/main.cpp       redgem_testing   runs a game's tests
libredgem.so    src/app/android/android_main.cpp   redgem_runtime   the player on Android, loaded by the app

A built game is a copy of the player, never of the program that builds it: redgem build and the editor's Build take redgem-player from beside redgem, or runtimes/<system>/ there for another system (tools/windows/build_runtime.sh, tools/android/build_runtime.sh build those). cmake --install build --component redgem --prefix <folder> puts the five programs in <folder>/bin and the players for other systems in <folder>/bin/runtimes, where the same lookups find them.

Keep what players receive small: nothing the player links may include editor/ or project/ (the include directions below say so, and linking proves it). The tests app.player_ships_no_tools, app.relay_ships_no_game and app.server_ships_no_tools look into the built programs (tests/ships_no_tools.sh) for texts only the tools, or only a game, have.

A program opens one window, through Window, and makes what draws in it afterwards (a Renderer, the editor's ui::Interface): the project hub, the editor and a played game each do. The engine never does: it is given a Presenter. WindowPresenter shows a game in its own window (redgem-player, redgem --play, redgem-test), the editor's Scene view is another (EditorApp::GameView), and without one nobody shows the game (NullPresenter: tests, servers). What a game can show is a field of FrameView, drawn in FramePainter: added there, it reaches every presenter. tests/include_directions.sh holds the table and fails the test suite on an include that goes up.

docs.title: Texts users read
docs.text:
What a user of RedGem reads is not written in the code: it is in translation files, one per language, under locales/<part>/<language>.json, and the code names it by a key (tr("editor.menu.file"), see src/core/translations.hpp). Today there is English (en.json) alone; a translation is another file beside it, with the same keys.

  • Into a translation file: everything a user reads in a window or at a terminal. The editor and the project hub (menus, buttons, panels, tooltips, dialogs, hints, the status bar, the inspector's labels), the help, usage and errors of the command lines of redgem, redgem-server, redgem-relay and redgem-test that are about what the user typed, and the texts the engine shows players (the labels of GameMenu).
  • In English in the code: the log, and the messages of errors that are for whoever works on the engine or a game (a broken file, a failed call). Those are searched for, quoted in bug reports and read next to the code; they stay in one language, as the code does.

Each part is the texts of one library, built into it (redgem_embed_texts in src/CMakeLists.txt), so that a program carries only what it shows: core (what a command line says of an option it cannot read), game (the runtime: what players read), editor, project (the hub and redgem's command line), server, relay and testing (the command lines of the other programs). A program adds its parts and picks the language as it starts: the one in the user's settings ("language" in settings.json), else the system's; a key a translation lacks is shown in English.

A key is the part's name, then where the text is, then what it is: editor.menu.file. The first word says which file it is in. A text with values in it names them, Created {game}, and the code fills them in: tr("project.cli.created", {{"game", name}}). A long text (a command's usage) may be a list of lines. tests/unit/translation_keys_test.cpp fails when the code shows a key English has no text for, when an English text is shown nowhere, or when a translation has a key English lacks; keys are written whole in the code, as string literals, for it to find them.

A game's texts are not the engine's: they are in the game's own locales/<language>.json, and its scripts show them with I18n.t("hud.coins") (see Texts in several languages), behind which are the engine's game part (the prelude's I18n.t calls, in ruby/engine/), so a game's files may translate those too. The same test checks the games and templates of this repository: every key their scripts show has a text in their locales/en.json or the game part, and every text of theirs is shown.

docs.title: Not there yet
docs.text:
• Blend trees and animation events. Characters copied with Duplicate in the editor keep the pose they were copied in.
  • Spot light cones, and camera clip planes from the scene (the engine uses fixed ones).
  • Reusing data when the same model is imported twice, and dropping the data of deleted imports from scene.glb (each import appends its meshes and textures).
  • Mirrored objects (negative scale) are drawn inside out.
  • More vehicle options from Blender properties (drive layout, engine torque); hot reload of scripts while playing.

docs.title: Reading the process event history
docs.text:
The native tooling API can read logs without replacing the console sink. Include core/event_journal.hpp, take log::event_cursor() before an operation, then read log::events_since(cursor, limit, minimum_level). Pass the returned cursor to the next read, including when the level filter matched nothing. Read another page while more is true.

The process retains 512 messages, each limited to 2 KiB plus a truncation marker, and returns at most 128 messages per page. Text keeps whole UTF-8 characters and removes terminal control characters while retaining line breaks. dropped counts messages overwritten since the supplied cursor. cursor_ahead reports a cursor beyond this process's latest event; reset the reader to the returned cursor. Cursors belong to the process that issued them and do not survive a restart. Writes and reads are synchronized; installing a custom log sink does not disable this history.

docs.title: Dedicated server
docs.text:
With a dedicated server nobody has to host: the game runs on a machine on the internet, with no window and no player, and everyone joins it, phones included. A small rented Linux server (a VPS) is enough. It needs no display and no graphics card.

The server is a program of its own, redgem-server. One server holds several rooms. Each room is a match of its own, with the whole game running in it. Players join by the server's address and get the first room with a free place, or a new room when every room is full. A friend can follow them into the same room with its code (Network.room). A room closes when its match ends: the game calls Game.quit, or everyone left. The next players get a new room, with a new game.

Nobody runs a server for you: each game runs its own, on a machine its players can reach, as below. The same goes for a relay.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./build/src/redgem-server games/platformer      # listens on port 7777
./build/src/redgem-server games/platformer --port 9000 --max-players 4 --rooms 16 --data /srv/platformer
Option Default What it is --port 7777 The TCP port players connect to (0 picks a free one) --max-players 8 Players in one room, up to 15 --rooms 8 Rooms open at once, up to 64 --threads The machine's cores Threads the rooms run on, up to 64: each room has one of its own while there are no more rooms than threads --per-address 24 Machines one address may connect, up to 1024: raise it when many players share one address (a campus, some mobile networks) --data <game>-data beside the game's folder Where the game's Save is kept (save.sqlite3), for every room and every run

It writes what happens to its output (rooms opened and closed, how many players) and stops cleanly on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM: every room is closed and its players are told.

A room is light (a platformer room takes 1 to 2 MB of memory and a few percent of one core), but every room runs the whole game, so --rooms is what sizes the machine. Each room runs on a thread of its own, so the rooms use all the machine's cores, and a room loading a level (when its first player arrives, or when its game loads another) holds up no other room. Players connect and are placed in rooms on the server's main thread meanwhile. With more rooms open than --threads, the rooms share the threads there are: a level loading in one then holds up the others on its thread for that moment.

docs.title: Run it with Docker
docs.text:
Dockerfile.server builds an image holding the server and one game, nothing else:

docker build -f Dockerfile.server --build-arg GAME=games/platformer -t my-game-server .
docker run -d --restart unless-stopped -p 7777:7777 -v my-game-data:/data my-game-server --rooms 4

GAME is the game's folder, relative to the repository. docker compose up server does the same for the platformer (GAME=path/to/game docker compose up server for another). The container runs as an unprivileged user and writes only to /data, where the game's saves are kept (a volume, so that they outlive the container).

docs.title: Put it on the internet
docs.text:
1. Rent any small Linux server with a public address, and install Docker on it (or build RedGem there, see Install).
  2. Copy the repository and your game there, then build and run the image as above.
  3. Open the port: allow TCP 7777 in the server's firewall and in the provider's control panel.
  4. Point the game at it. In the platformer demo, set SERVER in scripts/main_scene.rb; in a game made from the platformer template, set SERVER in scripts/online.rb:
SERVER = "play.example.com".freeze      # or "203.0.113.7", or "play.example.com:9000"

The game's menus then offer Play online. In your own game, it is one line:

Network.join("play.example.com")                  # any room with a free place
Network.join("play.example.com", room: "K7QM3P")  # the room a friend is in

docs.title: Make the game work on a server
docs.text:
The server runs the same scripts as the players, with Network.server? true. It has no player of its own, so whatever a script does for "my player" is skipped there:

Network.on_connect do
  spawn_my_hero unless Network.server?                # the server plays nobody
  Network.players.each { |peer| show_hero_of(peer) }  # the others who play, never the server
end

Network.host? is true on the server: it hosts the game and owns the level's own objects, so what the host decides (scores, a door opening, the end of a match) is decided there. Menus never open on a server. Call Game.quit on the server when a match is over to give its room to the next players.

Save on the server is the server's own: a SQLite database in its data folder (--data), shared by all its rooms and kept across restarts. Each key is a row of its own, written as soon as it changes, in a transaction (a crash keeps every change made before it, never half of one), and only what a script asks for is read into memory. Rooms write one at a time, and change a value that several rooms may change with Save.update, which reads and writes it with no other room's save in between. Arrays and hashes saved there may hold any number of things (only their nesting is limited, to 16 levels). Keep each player's data under their identity, as Online services shows; with many players, a key per player (Save["player:#{identity}"]) reads and writes one player instead of all of them.

A copy of the database for a backup is taken with sqlite3 save.sqlite3 ".backup copy.sqlite3", or by copying the folder while the server is stopped.

The server faces the internet. It keeps every limit a hosted game and the relay have (message sizes, how much each player may send, connections per address, spawned objects), lets go of machines that stay silent and of players who say nothing to the game for five minutes (a game left paused counts), and keeps out addresses that guess at room codes. Messages are not encrypted. Players are let in without asking unless the game decides who plays: see Online services.

docs.title: The editor
docs.text:
./build/src/redgem games/platformer          # opens the editor
./build/src/redgem games/platformer --play   # just plays the game

The editor is built with Dear ImGui (dark theme, Inter and JetBrains Mono fonts, Font Awesome icons):

  • Toolbar: move / rotate / scale gizmos, local or world axes, the pivot several selected objects turn and scale around (their middle, or the first one selected), grid snapping (or hold Ctrl while dragging), Play / Pause / Stop, and Build.
  • Hierarchy: the object tree with search. Click to select, Ctrl+click to add an object to the selection or take it away, Shift+click to select every row from the last one clicked; double click to frame, drag onto another object to parent it (or onto empty space to unparent; a row of the selection takes the whole selection along), right click for actions (on the whole selection) and to create objects. Scripts and models from the Project panel can be dropped on it.
  • Scene: hold the right mouse button and use WASD/QE to fly, wheel to dolly, F to frame the selection, click to pick objects (Ctrl or Shift + click adds or takes away), drag a rectangle to select what shows inside it (with Ctrl or Shift held, added to the selection), W / E / R switch the gizmo. Drop a model on the ground to place it there, or a script on an object to attach it.
  • Inspector: name, tag, visible, Template (hidden in the game, copied with Scene.spawn), then one card per component: Transform, Mesh with its materials (color, metallic, roughness, emission and their pictures, see Material pictures), Light (type, color, intensity, range), Camera (field of view, clipping), one card per Ruby script, Physics (body, trigger, collider, mass), vehicle wheels and custom properties. Add Component adds scripts (existing or new), a physics body, a trigger or a property. With several objects selected it shows what they have in common: tag, visible, Template and the Transform, a dash where their values differ. An edit applies to all of them.
  • GameObject menu: terrain you sculpt with a brush (see Levels), empty objects, cube / sphere / plane / cylinder / capsule (with colliders), directional / point / spot lights, cameras, and the game's models.
  • Your own models, sounds and pictures: drop .glb files (exported from Blender), .wav / .ogg / .mp3 / .flac files and .png / .jpg / .jpeg / .webp pictures from your file manager onto the editor window. They are copied into the game's models/, sounds/ and images/ folders and show up in the Project panel.
  • Project: the game's scripts, models, sounds, scenes and images. Double click a script to edit it, a model to add it to the scene, a sound to hear it, a scene to open it (see Scenes), a picture to see it in your system's viewer. New script creates a Behaviour from a template, New scene a scene; Open folder shows the files.
  • Console: engine and Ruby output (filter by level), including script errors with backtraces.
  • Scripts: each open Ruby file gets its own tab next to the Scene. Drag tabs to split the view anywhere (or press Split right), like a code editor's editor groups. Ctrl+S saves and checks the syntax (errors show the line); Open externally uses your default editor. Play saves all open scripts and reloads them.
  • View menu: hide the Hierarchy (Ctrl+B), the Inspector (Ctrl+Alt+B) or the bottom panels (Ctrl+J) to give the scene or the code more room; the toolbar's outer buttons toggle the sides.
  • Play / Pause / Stop (Ctrl+P, Esc): runs the game inside the Scene view with the current edits and fresh scripts; Stop restores the scene exactly as it was.
  • Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo, Ctrl+D duplicate, Del delete, Ctrl+X / Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V cut, copy and paste, Ctrl+S save. Help > Keyboard Shortcuts lists them all. File > New / Open Game goes back to the hub.

docs.title: Material pictures
docs.text:
Under a material's color, metallic, roughness and emission, the Inspector lists its five texture slots, each with the picture it shows or None:

  • Color map: the surface's colors, tinted by the material's color.
  • Surface map: roughness in the green channel and metalness in the blue one (glTF's metallic-roughness map), scaled by the sliders.
  • Normal map: small bumps and grooves, as a tangent-space normal map.
  • Occlusion map: how much ambient light reaches each spot, in the red channel.
  • Glow map: where the surface glows, tinted by the emission color.

Click a slot to pick one of the pictures of the game's images/ folder (or None), or drag a picture from the Project panel's Images onto it. The picture goes inside the scene's .glb (the same picture used twice is stored once), so the scene still shows it in Blender and when copied to another scene; a picture no material shows any more is left out when the scene is saved. Each change is one undo step. PNG, JPEG and still WebP pictures can be used.

docs.title: Several objects at once
docs.text:
Everything selected moves, turns and scales together with the gizmo (around the middle of the selection, or around the first object selected: the toolbar's pivot button; a scale goes along the pivot's axes, and an object turned another way and stretched unevenly takes the nearest placement without shear), and Duplicate, Delete, Cut, Copy and Paste act on all of it. A child goes along with its selected parent. Each of these is one undo step, however many objects it touches.

Copy takes the selected objects with everything under them: their meshes, materials, pictures, skeletons and animations, scripts and properties, lights and cameras. Paste (Ctrl+V) puts them next to the selected object, or at the top level when nothing is selected; Paste as Child (Ctrl+Shift+V, or the Hierarchy's menu) puts them under the selected object. They land where they were in the world, and a name that is already taken gets a number (Crate.001). Paste works in the scene they came from, in another scene of the game (open it and paste), and in another editor window: the copy goes on the system's clipboard as text. A copy bigger than 64 MB stays in the editor's own clipboard and pastes only in the window it was copied in.

A pasted object has its own copy of its meshes and pictures, even in the scene it was copied from (Duplicate shares them instead).

Undo goes back up to 200 steps, and keeps at most 256 MB for them (its copies of the objects and terrains, and what deleted objects and undone imports were made of: vertices, pictures and their bytes in the scene's file; an estimate, counted as each step begins): past either, the oldest steps go, and what no step can bring back any more is let go of, so a long session with many imports does not keep growing. The latest step always stays, however big.

Saving rewrites the open scene's file in place (only the glTF JSON; meshes and textures are untouched), so the file still opens in Blender. When the file changes on disk (e.g. you re-export from Blender) the editor reloads it automatically, unless you have unsaved edits.

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
A game can have several scenes: levels, missions, menus. Each is a .glb file, known by the name a script loads it with:

Scene File Loaded with main scene.glb Game.load_scene("main") level2 scenes/level2.glb Game.load_scene("level2")

The game always starts on main (scene.glb); scripts move to the others with Game.load_scene. The editor opens on main too, and edits one scene at a time:

  • Open another scene with a double click in the Project panel's Scenes folder, or with File > Open Scene. When the open scene has unsaved edits, the editor asks first (Save, Discard or Cancel), like when closing. Each scene has its own undo history: it starts empty when the scene opens.
  • New scene (File > New Scene, or New scene in the Scenes folder) makes scenes/<name>.glb with ground, a sun and a camera, and opens it. Names are lowercase letters, digits, _ and -, starting with a letter (level2, boss-fight); main is taken.
  • Save (Ctrl+S) writes the open scene back to its own file. File > Save Scene As writes it as a new scene of the game, which is then the one open. A scene that uses files next to it (textures exported outside the .glb) is not saved into another folder that way, where it would not find them: export it from Blender as a .glb with its textures in it first.
  • Play starts the game on the open scene as it is edited, under its own name (Game.scene_name, and its scripts/<name>_scene.rb runs). Stop comes back to it.

The window title and the status bar name the open scene, and the editor follows that scene's file for changes made outside. Built games carry every scene: Build copies the whole game folder, scenes/ included.

docs.title: Your first game
docs.text: You will create a game from a template, change it, write a behaviour in Ruby and export it.

docs.title: 1. Create the game
docs.text:
Start RedGem with no arguments. In the project hub, pick the Platformer template, type a name and create it. The same from a terminal:

./build/src/redgem new ~/RedGemGames/my_game --template platformer
./build/src/redgem ~/RedGemGames/my_game

With Docker, write tools/docker/editor.sh wherever this manual says ./build/src/redgem.

The editor opens:

  • Scene (center): the level. Hold the right mouse button and use WASD to fly, scroll to move closer, click an object to select it.
  • Hierarchy (left): every object of the level.
  • Inspector (right): what the selected object is made of.
  • Project and Console (bottom): the game's files, and messages from the engine and from your scripts.

docs.title: 2. Play it
docs.text: Press Play in the toolbar (or Ctrl+P). The game runs inside the Scene view: WASD moves, Space jumps. Press Esc or Stop to go back to editing. The level returns exactly to how it was.

docs.title: 3. Change the level
docs.text:
1. Click a coin in the Scene view.
  2. Drag the arrows of the gizmo to move it somewhere harder to reach.
  3. Press Ctrl+D to duplicate it and move the copy too.
  4. Press Ctrl+S to save.

Ctrl+Z undoes any of this.

docs.title: 4. Write a behaviour
docs.text:
Make the hero's coins worth collecting: a platform that moves up and down.

  1. In the menu, GameObject > 3D Object > Cube. Scale and place it as a platform.
  2. In the Inspector, Add Component > Script, type bob and press New.
  3. The script opens in a tab next to the Scene. Replace its contents with:
# Moves the object up and down.
class Bob < Behaviour
  HEIGHT = 2.0   # meters
  SECONDS = 4.0  # per cycle

  def start
    @origin = transform.position
  end

  def update(_dt)
    wave = Math.sin(Time.elapsed / SECONDS * 2 * Math::PI)
    transform.position = @origin + Vector3.up * (wave * HEIGHT)
  end
end
  1. Press Ctrl+S. The tab shows Syntax OK, or the line of the mistake.
  2. With the cube selected, find the Physics card in the Inspector and set Body to kinematic, so the hero can stand on it while it moves.
  3. Press Play.

If a script fails while the game runs, the game keeps going: that behaviour is switched off and the error, with its line, appears in the Console.

docs.title: 5. Share it
docs.text: Build in the toolbar (or redgem build <game> <folder>) makes a folder with your game's executable and its files, for Linux, Windows or (from a Mac) macOS. Zip it and send it. See Building and sharing.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
