  • Gameplay recipes: input, movement, pickups, HUD, sound, levels.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: RedGem is experimental. The editor is developed on Linux; there are Windows and macOS downloads too. Pick one of the ways below.

docs.title: Download (easiest)
docs.text:
System Download Linux (x86_64) redgem-linux-x86_64.tar.gz Windows (x86_64) redgem-windows-x86_64.zip macOS (Apple Silicon) redgem-macos-arm64.zip macOS (Intel) redgem-macos-x86_64.zip

Unpack it anywhere and run bin/redgem (Linux), redgem.exe (Windows) or open RedGem.app (macOS). Nothing is installed: delete the folder to remove it. The demos are in its games/ folder.

  • Linux needs a desktop with OpenGL 3.3, a processor with AVX2 and glibc 2.39 or newer (Ubuntu 24.04 and later). It builds games for Linux, Windows and Android.
  • Windows is compiled from Linux and has only been tried under Wine, not on a real Windows machine yet. It builds games for Windows.
  • macOS needs macOS 11 or newer. It is built and tested on GitHub's Mac machines (macOS 14 on Apple Silicon, macOS 15 on Intel), which are virtual machines with no graphics card OpenGL can use: there the editor opens, edits, plays and saves a game drawn by Apple's software renderer. It has not been tried on a real Mac yet. It builds games for the Mac only. The app is not signed by a registered Apple developer nor notarized, so macOS refuses it the first time: right-click RedGem.app and choose Open (on macOS 15 and later: try once, then System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway), or run xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine RedGem.app in the unpacked folder.

Wherever this manual says ./build/src/redgem ..., write bin/redgem ... (or redgem.exe ..., or RedGem.app/Contents/MacOS/redgem ... on macOS).

docs.title: With Docker
docs.text:
You need Docker and a desktop session using X11.

git clone https://github.com/carlosdanielpohlod/redgem.git
cd redgem
tools/docker/editor.sh

The first run builds the image, which takes a few minutes. After that the editor opens in seconds.

  • Games you create are saved in ~/RedGemGames on your machine.
  • The demos are in the games/ folder of the checkout: tools/docker/editor.sh games/platformer.
  • The script takes the same arguments as redgem itself, so wherever this manual says ./build/src/redgem ..., write tools/docker/editor.sh .... Paths must be inside ~/RedGemGames or the checkout's games/ folder: the container sees nothing else.
  • The container has no sound.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
You need a C++17 compiler, CMake 3.24 or newer, Ninja, Ruby with rake, and the X11 and OpenGL development files. On Ubuntu or Debian:

sudo apt install build-essential cmake ninja-build git ca-certificates xz-utils ruby rake bison \
  libgl1-mesa-dev libx11-dev libxrandr-dev libxinerama-dev libxcursor-dev libxi-dev libasound2-dev

On macOS: the Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install), then brew install cmake ninja and a Ruby with rake (the CI builds with Ruby 3.3).

Then:

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build
./build/src/redgem

CMake downloads the libraries RedGem is built on at fixed versions. The first build takes a few minutes.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
./build/src/redgem (or tools/docker/editor.sh) opens the project hub. Choose Platformer under New game, give it a name, and the editor opens with a level you can play right away: press the Play button, move with WASD, jump with Space.

./build/src/redgem --version says which version you have (RedGem 0.4.0, say): give it when you report a problem. (redgem --help lists everything else the command line does.)

docs.title: Blender (optional)
docs.text: You can make whole games without it. Install Blender 4.x when you want to model your own objects or build levels there: see Levels, lighting and Blender.

docs.title: How a scene is made
docs.text:
1. Model the level in Blender. Gameplay is configured with custom properties (Object Properties → Custom Properties), e.g. script = "coin.rb", trigger = true.
  2. Export to scene.glb (glTF binary). The exporter writes custom properties to each node's extras.
  3. The runtime loads the .glb with cgltf, reads the extras, builds physics bodies and instantiates the Ruby class named after each script (camera_follow.rb → CameraFollow).

A game is just a folder:

games/platformer/
  scene.glb          # exported from Blender
  platformer.blend   # the editable source
  scripts/*.rb       # behaviours

docs.title: Look of a scene: environment, lights and effects
docs.text:
Scenes are drawn in HDR and finished with bloom (bright things glow), filmic tone mapping, a vignette and anti-aliasing. One object with the property environment = true (GameObject > Environment in the editor, or a Blender empty) sets the mood through its properties:

Property Meaning sky_top, sky_horizon, ground_color colors of the sky gradient, as #rrggbb; they also light the scene fog_color, fog_density distance fog (it follows the horizon color unless given its own) ambient, exposure strength of the sky's light, overall brightness bloom, vignette, sun_glow glow around bright things, dark corners, the sun's disc and halo (0 turns each off) wind how much foliage sways shadows darkness of the sun's shadows (0 = none, 1 = full) ambient_occlusion darkening of creases and contact areas (0 = none, 1 = full) contrast, saturation the finished picture's grade: 1 leaves it as it is grain, aberration film grain, and color fringes toward the corners as through a lens (0 turns each off) sky_image, sky_rotation, sky_intensity a picture of the sky in the game's images/ folder, drawn behind everything and lighting the scene (see "A sky picture"), the degrees it is turned around the vertical, and its brightness (1 = as the picture is) msaa samples per pixel of the scene's picture (2, 4 or 8; 0, the default, is one): smoother edges, and grass and leaves whose cut-out edges are smoothed too antialias "temporal" smooths edges with the frames before (see "Large outdoor scenes"); anything else, the default, smooths them after the picture is drawn shadow_cascades, shadow_distance sun shadows over a large area: 1 to 4 maps, each farther from the camera, reaching shadow_distance meters (150 unless given) shadow_softness how wide the sun is, in degrees: shadows grow softer the farther they fall from what casts them (the real sun is about 0.5; 0, the default, keeps every edge equally soft) glow_limit the brightest glowing particles together make a pixel, in linear light (2 to 4 suits fire): many flames or sparks over each other come near it and keep their color instead of washing out to white (0, the default, sets no limit)

Without one, scenes get a clear day. Other things worth knowing: the 16 point lights nearest to the camera are used each frame (so a street can have dozens of lamps); the sun casts soft shadows around the camera; and materials use their glTF normal, roughness/metallic, occlusion and emission textures. A light's intensity and color can change while the game runs (see Gameplay recipes).

docs.title: See-through materials and wind
docs.text:
Blender's material settings decide how a material shows what is behind it (the glTF exporter writes them as the material's alpha mode):

Alpha mode Drawn as For Opaque whole: its alpha is not looked at almost everything Mask (alpha clip) cut out where its alpha is below the material's cutoff leaves, grass, fences Blend see-through: mixed with what is behind it by its alpha glass, hair cards, fur, smoke on a card

A blended material is drawn in two steps. What of it is nearly opaque (alpha 0.9 and above) is drawn with the opaque surfaces, so that a dozen hair cards over each other still sort themselves out; the rest is drawn after every opaque surface, mixed with what is behind it, one object at a time from the farthest to the nearest. Two see-through parts of the same object are not sorted between themselves, nor are copies scattered with Scatter.place. For many layers of fine cards (fur, a mane), give the material the custom property transparency = "dithered" (Material Properties → Custom Properties, exported when the exporter's Custom Properties is on): its texels are then left out in a fine pattern that thins with their alpha, which needs no sorting at all, at the price of a slight grain.

Wind. Textured cut-out and blended materials are foliage: drawn on both sides, and swaying with the environment's wind. An object whose foliage must stay still gives itself sway = false; objects moved by a skeleton (characters, and so their hair) do not sway unless they say sway = true. Copies scattered from an object sway as it does.

Glossy surfaces reflect their surroundings: the engine keeps capturing the scene around the camera (one cube face per frame) and uses it for reflections and ambient light.

A sky picture. sky_image = "meadow_sky" puts a picture of the whole sky around the scene (images/meadow_sky.hdr, .png or .jpg): an equirectangular picture, twice as wide as it is high, the kind sites of free skies offer and Blender takes as a world texture. It is laid as Blender lays it (the middle of the picture toward +X; sky_rotation turns it), and it lights the scene in place of the gradient: matte surfaces take the light of the sky around them, and glossy ones reflect it, sharper the smoother they are. Give the picture's sun a sun light of its own pointing the same way (the picture's own sun is held down in the light it gives, so that it does not light the scene twice) and set ambient to 1 for the sky's light as the picture has it. A Radiance picture (.hdr) holds light brighter than white, as a real sky has; a PNG or JPEG stops at white, and sky_intensity makes up for it. Pictures are read up to 8192 pixels a side; the sky drawn behind everything is kept at 4096 pixels across, its light is worked out from a smaller copy when the scene is loaded (a fraction of a second).

Large outdoor scenes. With shadow_cascades = 4 the sun's shadows reach shadow_distance meters, sharp up close and coarser far away; shadow_softness = 1.5 widens their edges with the distance to what casts them (a tree's shadow is sharp at its trunk and soft at its crown). Each cascade draws the scene's casters once more: a forest of tens of thousands of copies costs more with four than with one. msaa = 4 smooths edges with four samples a pixel; cut-out materials (grass, leaves) then let those samples smooth their edges too, which keeps a meadow from shimmering as the camera moves. Without it, cut-out edges are smoothed afterwards with the rest of the picture.

antialias = "temporal" goes further: each frame the view moves by less than a pixel, a different amount every frame, and the frames before, followed to where each pixel was then, are mixed into this one. Thin grass, leaves and the glints of shiny surfaces stop shimmering, and copies fading out by distance turn from a fine pattern into an even shade. What moves is followed, characters' bones and swaying foliage included; what is no longer there (a lightning flash, a character running past, the camera cutting to another place) is not smeared over the picture; particles take less of the frames before. A new scene, a new window size and a camera that jumps start over. It works with msaa on or off and costs one more pass over the scene's opaque surfaces. History fades out locally between 16 and 32 pixels of motion per frame, and at large motion splits around opening edges. Fast scenery therefore favors current detail, while a tracked subject with little screen motion still accumulates samples. Reprojected previous-frame depth rejects hidden or newly revealed surfaces, including moving and skinned objects. A still view holds still and its edges, against the sky or other surfaces, settle smooth: depth is compared around where each pixel was, so a silhouette keeps its history. Thin cut-outs and very fast details can still shimmer as fewer temporal samples are retained.

Animated characters. glTF skeletons and animations are supported: skinned meshes are deformed on the GPU (up to 1024 bones per skeleton, 4 per vertex: a character with fingers has about 65) and every animation in the scene plays in a loop until a script says otherwise (see Control animations). The editor keeps skeletons and animations when saving, reordering or importing models. tools/blender/walk_rig.py gives a scanned standing person leg bones and a walk cycle.

Per-object color. The property tint = "#rrggbb" multiplies the colors of an object's mesh, so copies sharing one mesh (cars, crates) can each have their own color.

No shadow. cast_shadow = false keeps an object out of the sun's shadows (a sky dome, a glow, a light's shade): it is still drawn and still receives shadows.

Graphics card. On laptops with two cards the engine asks for the dedicated one and logs which card it got. To choose: Edit > Graphics Card in the editor (saved in ~/.config/redgem/settings.json, used from the next start), the REDGEM_GPU environment variable (read by redgem and redgem-test), or --gpu auto|dedicated|integrated for one run. The command line wins over the environment, which wins over the saved setting.

Performance. Objects outside the view, and parts too small to see from where the camera is, are not drawn. Objects that share a mesh (linked duplicates in Blender, Alt+D, or copies of one model) and come one after the other in the level are drawn together, every copy of a part in one call, however many there are: a street of the same building costs little more than one. Blender keeps duplicates together by their names (Tree, Tree.001, Tree.002...); copies whose turn comes between other objects are drawn in that order, so that surfaces lying on each other look as they did. What still costs is the number of different meshes on screen, and of separate parts in each: join the parts of a model that share a material, and give heavy models lighter versions for far away with visible_from and visible_to.

docs.title: Coated materials
docs.text:
Blender's Principled BSDF coat is read through KHR_materials_clearcoat. A polished coating can sit above rough paint, wood or a textured base. Its weight and roughness have independent linear maps (red and green channels respectively), and its normal map does not change the base normal. The coating reflects the sun, point lights and the environment while attenuating the base layer and emission by Fresnel, rather than adding unlimited brightness.

Export the coat with the material in glTF. A zero coat weight preserves the original shading. The editor keeps its factors, texture references and normal scale through import and saving. The layering follows the glTF clearcoat extension.

docs.title: Grass, forests and cities
docs.text:
Tens of thousands of copies (a meadow's grass, a forest) are too many to be objects: a script scatters them instead (Scatter.place, see the API reference). Model one tuft or one tree, give it prefab = true so the template itself is hidden in the game, and scatter it over the ground from a scene script's setup:

Scatter.place("GrassTuft", count: 50_000, area: [Vector3[-80, 0, -80], Vector3[80, 0, 80]],
              ground: find("Ground"), seed: 7, scale: 0.7..1.4, align: true)
Scatter.place("Tree", count: 2_000, area: [Vector3[-140, 0, -140], Vector3[140, 0, -90]],
              ground: find("Ground"), seed: 8, scale: 0.8..1.5)

The copies take the template's own mesh (a model whose parts are children: join them), its scale, tint, visible_from / visible_to and cast_shadow. They are only drawn: nothing collides with them (give the trees a collider of their own, or invisible objects, where players must not walk through) and no script runs on them. The same seed places them the same on every machine of a game.

They are drawn by patches of ground 16 m across: a patch out of view, or too far for its biggest copy to show, is skipped whole. Like any object, they cast shadows, and small things (grass) only near the camera: a tuft half a meter high stops casting one about 50 m away, a tree hundreds of meters away. Their foliage sways in the wind (wind on the environment), each copy with its own phase, so a field does not move in step.

How the copies look can vary too, the same for the same seed on every machine:

Scatter.place("GrassTuft", count: 50_000, area: field, ground: find("Ground"), seed: 7, align: true,
              tints: [[0.85, 1.0, 0.7], [1.05, 1.0, 0.8]],  # each a color between these
              tint_variation: 0.12,                         # and a little brighter or darker
              fade: 10.0,                                   # fading out over the last 10 m
              normals_up: 0.7)                              # lit as the meadow, not as flat cards

fade makes copies near the template's visible_to thin out pixel by pixel over that many meters instead of popping away (and fade in after its visible_from, when it has one: two levels of detail whose distances overlap by the fade cross over without a gap). normals_up bends the copies' normals toward their own up: grass cards are then lit as the ground they stand on, so a field does not show the cards' faces turning light and dark with the sun.

docs.title: Scatter distance LODs
docs.text:
Use lighter templates to keep vegetation visible far away without drawing the full mesh:

forest = Scatter.place("Tree", count: 2_000, area: [corner_a, corner_b], seed: 7,
                       fade: 8.0, lods: [["TreeMid", 40.0], ["TreeFar", 120.0]])

All levels share the base template's placement, scale, tint, wind and shadow settings. Each replacement contributes only its mesh and materials; model it with the same origin, orientation and dimensions. The base template's visible_from and visible_to bound the whole chain.

At 40 meters the middle mesh begins appearing; over the next 8 meters it replaces the near mesh through complementary dithered pixels. The far mesh takes over from 120 to 128 meters. A zero fade switches immediately. Up to three replacements are supported. Distances must increase, leaving more than fade meters between transitions and before visible_to.

count reports placed copies and remove removes the whole chain. Each representation uses one drawing record per copy: this example uses 6,000 of the scene's 262,144-record budget. An invalid chain or an exhausted budget adds nothing. Omitting lods keeps the original rendering.

docs.title: Terrain
docs.text:
GameObject > Terrain adds a square of ground, 100 m across, that you shape with a brush. It comes selected with the brush on: mountains, holes and plateaus are a drag of the mouse away.

  1. Drag the left mouse button over the ground in the Scene view. A ring shows the brush.
  2. In the Inspector's Terrain card, pick what the brush does (Sculpt turns the brush off and on again, to move the terrain itself with the gizmo):
Brush Effect Raise Piles ground up under the brush (hold Shift to dig instead) Lower Digs (hold Shift to pile up) Smooth Softens bumps and edges Flatten Levels the ground to the height at the brush's center: plateaus, roads

Radius is the size of the brush in meters, Strength how fast it works. Each stroke is one undo step. Untick Sculpt to select and move objects again.

The terrain's collider follows its shape, so characters walk and things roll on the hills you make. Its color and roughness are in the Mesh card, like any object's. A terrain is made and shaped in the editor; one re-exported from Blender is an ordinary mesh.

docs.title: Editing the level in Blender
docs.text:
blender games/platformer/platformer.blend           # edit, save
blender -b games/platformer/platformer.blend \
  --python tools/blender/export_scene.py -- games/platformer/scene.glb

tools/blender/run.sh build_platformer.py games/platformer (or build_driving.py games/driving) regenerates a whole level from code; tools/blender/scene_kit.py has helpers to build levels with bpy.

docs.title: Custom properties
docs.text:
Property Values Meaning script "player.rb" or "a.rb, b.rb" Behaviours to attach, loaded from scripts/ body static, dynamic, kinematic, character, vehicle Physics body (characters use Jolt's CharacterVirtual, vehicles its VehicleConstraint) wheel true On a child of a vehicle: it becomes a wheel (model it with its axle along X) collider box, sphere, capsule, mesh Shape, sized from the mesh bounds × object scale. collider alone = static body trigger true Trigger volume: fires on_trigger_enter/exit, does not collide mass number Mass of dynamic bodies (and of kinematic ones, should a script make them dynamic) layer a layer of game.json, e.g. "enemy" Collision layer of the body or trigger: what it meets (see "Collision layers" in the gameplay recipes). Without it, default tag string Used by Scene.find_all(tag) and game_object.tag? visible false Hide the mesh (the object still exists) prefab true A template: hidden and inert in the game, copied by Scene.spawn visible_from, visible_to meters The object is drawn only while that far from the camera: give a model a detailed version up close and a light one far away tint "#rrggbb" Multiplies the colors of this object's mesh (copies sharing a mesh can differ) cast_shadow false Keeps the object out of the sun's shadows (a sky dome) sway true / false Whether the wind sways its foliage: unless said, yes, except on objects a skeleton moves (see "See-through materials and wind") environment true This object's properties set the sky, fog and effects (see "Look of a scene") anything number / string / bool Available in Ruby as props[:name] / prop(:name, default)

Cameras and lights (sun, point) are taken from the Blender scene. Spot lights are loaded but lit like point lights (in every direction). Parenting is preserved.

Vehicles. Give the chassis body = "vehicle" and parent the wheel meshes to it with wheel = true. Wheels in front of the center (Blender +Y) steer, the rear ones get the hand brake, and every axle is driven. Wheel radius and width come from the wheel mesh. See tools/blender/build_driving.py. Blender is Z-up; the engine is Y-up like glTF: Blender (x, y, z) is engine (x, z, -y) (Vector3.blender(x, y, z) does the conversion). Forward is -Z (Blender +Y).

docs.title: Water surfaces
docs.text:
A horizontal, upward-facing mesh becomes water when its material has the Blender custom property water = true. Enable custom properties in the glTF export. The surface is drawn after opaque geometry: it refracts that picture, absorbs light through the depth behind it, and reflects on-screen objects with a sky and surroundings fallback. The material's base color is its deep-water color and roughness controls its reflections. Its alpha is ignored; transparency comes from water depth and absorption instead.

Material custom property Default Meaning water false Use water shading. wave_height 0.08 Maximum vertical displacement in world meters, from 0 to 10. wavelength 3 Dominant wavelength in meters, from 0.05 to 1000. wave_speed 1 Wave clock multiplier, from 0 (still) to 10. absorption_red 0.35 Red light absorption per meter, from 0 to 10. absorption_green 0.08 Green light absorption per meter, from 0 to 10. absorption_blue 0.035 Blue light absorption per meter, from 0 to 10. foam_width 0.12 Nominal local horizontal width of a shore foam band, in meters; 0 disables it. World-space patches vary its reach from 0.85 to 1.15 times this value. refraction 0.035 Refraction strength, from 0 to 0.1; the default uses water's IOR of 1.333 and 0 keeps the bottom undistorted.

The Blender helper scene_kit.water_material("Pond", wave_height=0.04, wavelength=2.0) creates the material and its custom properties. Optional keyword arguments override the table above. The material preview has water's IOR and transmission; runtime waves and depth-based color are applied by the engine after export.

Use a subdivided mesh: vertex spacing at most one tenth of the smallest visible geometric wavelength avoids angular silhouettes. Three traveling waves displace geometry; finer ripples change normals. Smooth spatial phase variation curves the crests without changing the maximum height. The pattern is in world coordinates, so adjacent patches share phase and mesh scale does not change the wavelength. Wave displacement follows the renderer's clock, including fixed-step recordings, and the temporal coverage pass uses the same displaced geometry. Water does not cast an opaque shadow. Objects keep their authored collision shapes.

Dynamic and kinematic physics bodies automatically disturb horizontal water meshes when they cross the surface or travel through it. Each contact sends a short, outward-moving wave packet; its strength follows motion and its initial width follows the body's footprint. No script call is needed. The visual effect displaces vertices and bends the lighting normal with the same radial wave, so use a subdivided surface when the silhouette needs to move.

Impulses belong to one object and one original mesh primitive. Copies that share a mesh or material, and other water primitives in that mesh, remain independent. The simulation keeps at most 16 impulses for three seconds; drawing never advances their ages. Pausing simulation freezes them, and recording uses the same simulation steps. They reset when the world changes. Temporal motion uses the last snapshot actually drawn; a newly observed impulse starts with its current age in both poses to avoid an invented first-frame velocity. These ripples are a visual response: they do not apply buoyancy or forces to physics bodies and are not network-synchronized.

Contact detection uses the actual water triangles with a cached spatial tree. It supports rigid, horizontal planar mesh primitives; skinned or tilted surfaces and Scatter copies do not generate contacts. Body footprints use conservative world-aligned collider bounds, including spheres and capsules. A small surface margin, emission cooldown and travel spacing suppress resting jitter. Scripted position changes of dynamic bodies, characters and vehicles are treated as teleports; scripted kinematic movement can create entry waves and wakes.

Work is bounded to the first 128 eligible water objects, 128 valid water primitives and 262,144 triangles per world, 256 moving bodies and 1,024 active body/surface pairs. Tilted or oversized candidates still occupy a water-object slot. A primitive that exceeds the remaining triangle budget is ignored as a whole. These bounds keep interaction work predictable for large scenes.

This first water material is for views above a lake or sea surface. Refraction samples only opaque geometry visible on screen; transparent objects and other water layers are absent from that snapshot. Screen-space reflections miss off-screen and hidden geometry and use the environment capture when a ray misses. There is no planar reflection pass. Shore foam approximates the horizontal distance to the intersection of the local water and visible-bottom tangent planes, without breaking-wave simulation. Its world-space patches and softer pockets form an irregular band rather than a uniform intersection line. Low-density pockets leave water uncovered; even dense patches preserve some transmission instead of replacing the whole shallow surface with white. Coverage fades in over a short contact distance and fades out across the authored horizontal width; larger foam_width values broaden the band. The pattern stays fixed in world space and does not drift with the render clock. Fine pores are filtered by their projected footprint and converge to expected mean coverage when unresolved. Flat shallow plateaus with no local shore intersection receive no foam. The local plane estimate uses the primary opaque depth, not the refracted optical path. Occluded or off-screen bottom geometry, depth discontinuities, and degenerate or almost parallel tangent planes produce no foam; they do not invent a hidden shore. Curved terrain is only locally approximated, and rejected curvature can leave gaps. Nearly vertical bottom walls are supported without dividing by the bottom normal's vertical component.

Traveling waves combine seven non-harmonic scales with distinct phases around one prevailing direction. Slow spatial envelopes vary crest height; displacement and shading use the same analytic gradient. Positive amplitude weights sum to one, and the envelopes never exceed one, so wave_height remains the maximum displacement used by visibility bounds. Fragment normals fade each traveling component when its phase becomes too fine for a pixel; discarded slope variance adds bounded reflection roughness. Geometry and motion retain the full wave shape. This is a procedural surface approximation, without wave interactions or a fluid spectrum simulation. Refraction traces the visible depth field. When the refracted surface is hidden or outside the screen, it keeps the undistorted opaque sample instead; this fallback cannot reveal geometry absent from the snapshot. Depth discontinuities use a guarded, texel-matched color sample. When a ray misses, the visible bottom's local tangent plane may estimate its absorption distance; this remains an approximation for hidden or curved geometry. Absorption filters the transmitted picture, but does not yet attenuate lighting on its way to submerged objects; a lit bottom can therefore be brighter than in a full participating-medium render. There is no underwater camera mode, buoyancy, fluid simulation, or wave collision. Use ordinary scene meshes for water surfaces rather than Scatter copies.

The optical comparison records a fixed-camera Cycles reference and the remaining differences around refraction and incident lighting.

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text:
Start a local MCP server for one game:

redgem mcp /path/to/game --read-only

Configure your MCP client to launch the redgem executable with those arguments. It reads newline-delimited JSON-RPC from standard input and writes only protocol responses to standard output. Native library output goes to standard error. Closing input stops the server. By default it opens no listening socket and works on files. Add --editor to connect to an editor that explicitly enabled its local bridge (see below).

The server supports the MCP 2026-07-28 per-request metadata protocol and the 2025-11-25 initialization handshake. Modern clients can discover capabilities with server/discover and must supply their protocol version and client capabilities in each request's params._meta. Legacy clients send initialize, then notifications/initialized, before using tools.

docs.title: Tools and permissions
docs.text:
Tool What it does scene_list Lists objects, taking optional scene, limit and depth. scene_get Reads one object by persistent #id, unique name or hierarchy path. scene_edit Takes action (set, add, remove), object and optional assignments (key=value strings), from, parent, scene. Removal requires confirm: true. Saves the scene file. scene_diff Compares with an earlier scene file named by against, inside the game. game_run Plays headlessly with frames (default 60, maximum 600), seed, input, assert, until, print, every, scene. game_check Checks scripts, scenes and assets; does not run the game's test files. api Reads the API index, a class, or a search. events Reads this server's log history with since, limit (default 20, maximum 32), level.

--read-only exposes only scene_list, scene_get, scene_diff, api and events. It also rejects calls to disabled tools, even if the client remembers an earlier tool list. For a smaller surface, add an exact comma-separated allow list:

redgem mcp /path/to/game --read-only --allow scene_list,scene_get,api,events

Without --read-only, the tools can save edits and execute the configured game's Ruby scripts. Run only games you trust. A run expression can mutate state or use networking; read-only mode disables execution entirely. The configured game directory stays fixed for the life of the process. Input replay and comparison files must be regular files inside it, without symbolic links. These restrictions protect tooling paths; they do not sandbox native game code.

Without --editor, edits go through the file-based scene commands. Close the editor while editing its files this way. Keep an earlier save and inspect scene_diff after an edit. from is available only in file mode; parent also works when adding a live empty object.

docs.title: Live editor
docs.text:
Start the editor with its bridge explicitly enabled:

redgem /path/to/game --editor-bridge

The terminal prints the path of a private connection.json in the user's RedGem data folder. Pass that file to the MCP server for the same game:

redgem mcp /path/to/game --editor /path/to/connection.json

Scene listing, object details and scene comparison now read the editor's unsaved document. scene_edit supports set, add and remove. add creates an empty object, optionally under parent, with initial assignments; attach scripts and properties as with the CLI. from (asset-backed duplication) remains file-only. remove deletes a subtree and requires confirm: true. Every call is one undo step: invalid assignments or exceptions roll it back without losing earlier undo/redo. Changes update the viewport and remain unsaved until save.

The editor tool takes these actions:

Action Result status Scene, play state, dirty flag, selection, undo/redo and external-conflict state. select Select the requested object. undo, redo, save Apply the corresponding editor command. Saving is explicit. play, pause, resume, stop Control the editor's game, using its normal input, audio and viewport. step Advance a paused game by exactly one fixed frame, keeping it paused. capture Return the last completed viewport as an MCP PNG image, without writing a file.

capture accepts max_size (default 512, range 128–1024), the longest output side. Images are reduced further when necessary to stay below 128 KiB before base64 encoding. Only the scene viewport is captured, never the desktop or other applications. object is accepted only by select; max_size only by capture. Read-only mode permits status and capture only.

Edits and document commands are refused while playing, during gestures/dialogs, or with an external file conflict pending. Play starts a copy of the unsaved scene; Stop discards that runtime and restores the edited document. Pause/resume/stop/step control that runtime, not the file. Read operations still describe the edited document, not runtime-mutated objects. An explicit scene must match the open scene; requests never switch or discard scenes.

events reads the editor's log history. api, game_run and game_check remain ordinary CLI tools: runs/checks read saved files rather than the unsaved editor scene. Runtime object inspection and arbitrary live eval are not exposed by this release.

The bridge binds only to IPv4 loopback and requires a random credential on every request, with the game directory checked at both ends. Its connection file stays outside the repository and is removed on clean shutdown. On POSIX it is owner-only inside an owner-only directory; on Windows it inherits the user's profile access controls. Treat the file as a credential granting control of that editor. MCP read-only and allow-list options restrict that client's calls.

At most four connections are handled at once, on the editor thread between frames. Requests are limited to 64 KiB and replies to 256 KiB. Transport waits expire after five seconds. If an edit times out, it may have completed: inspect status and the object before retrying. There is no automatic retry or fallback to editing the file when an editor connection fails. After a crash a stale connection file can remain; reconnect using the new editor instance's file.

docs.title: Bounded results
docs.text:
Each request is at most 64 KiB with at most 16 JSON nesting levels. Ordinary tool text is limited to 8 KiB with a truncation notice; narrow the scene list or API query for more detail. Invalid arguments return JSON-RPC errors. A valid command that fails returns isError: true with the engine's diagnostic.

Event results also contain structuredContent: events, cursor, dropped, more and cursor_ahead. Pass the returned cursor in the next since. Each event's text is capped at 256 UTF-8 bytes, with truncated when shortened. The cursor belongs to this server process; it is not a cursor into an unrelated editor or game (with --editor, it belongs to that editor). Events include engine log messages, not raw standard output. Process history is bounded, so dropped identifies overwritten messages.

Requests run one at a time. A cancellation notification cannot interrupt a native command already running; frame limits and the game's script budget bound headless work. A slow native operation can still delay completion. Clients can terminate and restart a server that stops responding.

The protocol follows the official stdio binding and tool messages.

docs.title: Rendering regression validation
docs.text: These synthetic scenes isolate temporal detail and opening-edge rejection. They are renderer regressions, not a claim of photographic scene quality. The images come from the native renderer.

docs.title: Fast camera
docs.text:
A tracked subject travels with the camera while a striped roadside wall crosses the screen at more than 32 pixels per frame. The camera stays below the global camera-cut threshold. The reference uses the same final view and jitter phase without accumulated history.

Previous resolve Updated resolve Fresh reference

The mean sum of absolute RGB byte differences per pixel in the wall region was 41.1073 with the previous shader. The updated resolve meets the regression threshold of 0.5, with both zero and four MSAA samples. Temporal antialiasing disabled produces the same final pixels as a fresh view. Existing static and slowly moving foliage tests still pass.

docs.title: Opening edge
docs.text:
A foreground card moves about 7.7 pixels while its background moves about 1.6 pixels. Both remain below the fast-motion threshold. The regression selects 51 freshly revealed black pixels next to the card. Their mean sum of absolute RGB byte errors falls from 588 to zero.

Previous resolve Updated resolve

The previous shader fails both regressions. These original controls isolate current motion and neighbor disagreement; the additional depth validation below covers surfaces that disappear without leaving a motion discontinuity. Fine moving detail can still trade smear for shimmer.

docs.title: Particle shadows and water refactoring
docs.text:
Particle render tests distinguish receiver darkening from the visible sprite, compare circular and rectangular silhouettes, check transparent flipbook cells and lifetime alpha, clear expired casters, and require identical disabled frames before and after an enabled frame.

The water shader is divided into small helpers for intersection, reflection, lighting, transmission, foam and composition. Each function body is at most 13 lines. All 28 water regression images remain pixel-identical across this refactoring. Across existing non-temporal scenes, 83 shared screenshots remain pixel-identical to the earlier renderer.

docs.title: Validation environment
docs.text:
On a GeForce RTX 4050 Laptop GPU, the combined change passed 1,193 C++ unit/integration cases (41,877 assertions), 23 Ruby suites and 52 render cases (655,490 assertions). Include-direction checks pass. The lit, depth, motion, particle-shadow and temporal programs also compile and link as GLSL ES 3.00 through native Mesa Intel EGL. This is not Android-device validation.

With 60 warm-up frames and 600 measured frames at 1600 x 900, without vertical synchronization, the scatter field measured 3.107 ms average / 3.106 ms median and the local showcase scene 5.091 ms average / 5.075 ms median. These are measurements of this run, not a controlled claim of speedup over another revision. Showcase assets are local and are not included here.

docs.title: Previous-frame depth validation
docs.text:
The temporal history stores logarithmic view distance in its existing alpha channel. The motion pass stores the expected previous view distance alongside its velocity, using the previous object and bone transforms. Color history is read where the surface was, without either frame's Halton shift: the history is the average over every shift, so a still view holds still. Only the depth lookup accounts for the current and previous shifts, because each stored depth is the previous frame's jittered sample. The pixel's own previous depth is looked for where its own motion takes it, even where its color follows the nearest surface's motion at an edge. Depth is checked over that texel and its eight neighbors, each with a slope margin for its own distance: one match keeps the history (the previous sample may have landed one texel over at a silhouette, against the sky or another surface), none rejects it. Where only some match (a depth edge), the filtered color is kept within the four nearest texels' colors, so the spline's outer taps add no color from across the edge. Where the pixel's own texel held another surface and the surfaces around it separate slowly (under two pixels a frame), the color is instead held to the colors of the matching texels: an object moving away leaves no ghost. An uninitialized frame cannot accumulate history; its output still initializes depth for the next frame. Sky (any depth below half the near plane's) and points behind the previous camera have distinct markers. Deliberately stochastic coverage (distance fades and dithered transparency) has signed depth metadata, allowing covered samples and sky holes to accumulate. An opaque center pixel still requires its own depth match; a neighboring stochastic surface cannot make unrelated opaque history valid.

Logarithmic distance avoids overflowing half-float channels for distant geometry. A bounded comparison margin allows half-float rounding and the depth change across a subpixel footprint; it cannot grow without limit at a silhouette. The existing targets and render passes are reused. The first temporal frame now also draws the motion pass so its depth history starts initialized.

Isolated resolve tests distinguish depth rejection from color clipping and velocity rejection. They cover zero-motion disocclusion, expected previous depth, invalid history, sky, jittered depth edges, colors beside a depth edge, a slow object moving away, a pixel whose neighbor moves differently, a sloped surface, a near plane of one millimeter and distant values. Scene regressions additionally exercise a stopped foreground object that disappears and approaching rigid and skinned geometry, with zero and four MSAA samples. The approaching surfaces use dithered coverage so discarding all history cannot pass as a fix. A still, turned cube in front of the sky and of a wall checks that the settled picture changes by less than 0.7 bytes per cube pixel from frame to frame (about 6 when the color lookup followed the jitter, about 1 when history was rejected at every silhouette) and that its silhouette gains partly covered pixels over a single sample.

The opaque-neighbor control selects 51 newly revealed black edge pixels beside a surviving white surface. With four MSAA samples, the previous renderer retains a mean sum of absolute RGB byte errors of 732; depth validation reduces that selected-edge error to zero. This does not claim that every pixel in an accumulated frame matches a fresh frame. Both renderers produce pixel-identical fresh reference pictures.

Previous history Previous-depth validation

The crops cover [124, 100, 138, 156] in the original 256 by 256 picture and are enlarged eight times with nearest-neighbor sampling. The previous result retains a bright column from the removed opaque card. The corrected edge agrees with the freshly rendered background.

The combined render suite passes 97 cases and 655778 assertions; the full unit suite passes 1215 cases and 42068 assertions. The thirteen new depth/scene cases also pass on llvmpipe. The previous renderer fails eight of ten isolated depth cases and both disappearing-object scene cases (six failed assertions). The approaching rigid/skinned scene remains a positive history-preservation control. Five native GLES shader pairs compile and link; this does not replace Android packaging.

A render-only ABBA comparison uses temporal anti-aliasing in both versions, a fixed 0.5-second animation clock, 1600 by 900 pixels, 60 warmup frames and 600 measured frames. The baseline uses the same twelve-wave water detail as the candidate. Physical interaction detection and game logic are excluded.

Scene Previous medians (ms) Depth-validation medians (ms) Pair averages (ms) Scatter field 3.913, 3.846 3.876, 3.844 3.880 to 3.860 Coastal water 12.573, 12.664 12.659, 12.675 12.619 to 12.667

These small differences are comparable to repeat variation; they do not establish a speedup or a precise overhead. The added motion pass on the first temporal frame is outside the warmed measurement. No additional history texture or steady-state render pass is allocated.

docs.title: Building and sharing
docs.text:
Build in the editor's toolbar, or from a terminal:

./build/src/redgem build my_game dist/my_game

This makes a folder with an executable named after your game (dist/my_game/my_game) and a game/ folder with its files. Whoever receives the folder runs the executable: they do not need RedGem, Ruby or Blender installed.

That executable is the player: a copy of redgem-player, a small program that plays the game in the game/ folder beside it and does nothing else. The editor, the project hub and the other tools you make the game with are not in it. A build looks for the player beside the redgem program that builds: redgem-player in the same folder for the system you are on, and runtimes/<system>/ in that folder for the others (runtimes/windows/redgem-player.exe, runtimes/android/<abi>/libredgem.so). When one is missing the build says which file it looked for.

docs.title: Icon, version and splash picture
docs.text:
A game says in its game.json what it is shown by; all of it is optional:

{
  "title": "My Game",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "icon": "images/icon.png",
  "splash": "images/splash.png",
  "network": true
}
  • version is a semantic version: three numbers, then optionally a pre-release (2.0.0-beta.1) or build part (1.0.0+build.5). Scripts read it with Game.version (nil when there is none). Android shows it as the app's version, and a Mac app carries its three numbers. A game without one is version 1.0 there.
  • icon is a square PNG in the game's folder, 1024×1024 at best (it is scaled down to every size a system wants; a smaller one is scaled up, and looks it). Every build turns it into its system's own icon (see each system below). A game without one keeps the engine's icon on Windows and has the system's default icon elsewhere.
  • splash is a PNG in the game's folder shown over the whole window, fitted with black bars around it, from when the window opens until the first frame of the game is drawn: while the world is built, the scripts start and the scene goes to the graphics card. (Reading the scene's file happens before the window opens: a big level still takes that long with no window.) It is shown by built games and --play, not by the editor.
  • network says whether the game plays online (Network) or makes web requests (HTTP): its Android app asks for the network only when it does, since an app that asks for what it does not use worries players and stores. When game.json does not say, a build looks at the scripts: one that calls Network. or HTTP. gets the network, and the build warns to say "network": true. "network": false keeps the app offline even then (with a warning). On computers it changes nothing.

A build refuses a game.json that says one of these and cannot be used (a version that is not one, a picture that is not a PNG in the game's folder, an icon that is not square), saying which. A game played that way logs it as a warning and plays as if the line were not there.

docs.title: For Windows
docs.text:
On Linux, RedGem builds games for Linux, Windows and Android (the experimental Windows download builds Windows games, the macOS one Mac games: --target macos, see For macOS). In the editor, Build asks which one; from a terminal:

tools/windows/build_runtime.sh                                   # once: builds the player for Windows
./build/src/redgem build my_game dist/my_game_win --target windows

The first command downloads a Windows compiler into the project (no administrator rights needed) and builds redgem-player.exe into build/src/runtimes/windows/; it takes a few minutes and is only needed once, or again after updating RedGem. The build then makes dist/my_game_win/my_game.exe next to its game/ folder. The game's icon goes inside the .exe (at 16 to 256 pixels): the file manager, the taskbar and shortcuts show it. Nothing has to run on Windows for that: the build puts the pictures into its copy of the player, in place of the engine's. The player RedGem makes is not signed; a player that was would lose its signature there (it would no longer match), so a game you release is signed afterwards, by you. A player that cannot take the icon (one made without an icon of its own, or with no room left in its headers) is left as it is, and the icon goes beside it as my_game.ico, with a warning. It needs 64-bit Windows 10 or later and a graphics card with OpenGL 3.3; nothing has to be installed with it.

docs.title: For Linux
docs.text: A build for Linux also writes my_game.desktop, a menu entry, and the icon as my_game.png (256 pixels) beside the executable. The entry names the program and its icon by name (Exec=my_game, Icon=my_game), the way a package installs them: an AppImage, a Flatpak or a distribution's package takes both files as they are. On its own, the folder runs from a file manager or a terminal; the entry needs installing to show up in a menu.

docs.title: For macOS
docs.text:
On a Mac, --target macos (the default there) makes an app: dist/my_game/My Game.app, named after the game's title. It holds everything, so it can be moved and opened like any Mac app:

My Game.app/Contents/Info.plist              its name, id, version and icon
My Game.app/Contents/MacOS/my_game           the player
My Game.app/Contents/Resources/game/         the game's files
My Game.app/Contents/Resources/my_game.icns  the icon (16 to 1024 pixels)
My Game.app/Contents/Resources/licenses/

The app's id is the game's id (with _ written as -), or com.redgem. and its name. The build signs the app ad hoc (with no identity), which an Apple Silicon Mac requires to open it. That is not a developer's signature: a Mac that downloads the app warns that its developer cannot be verified until it is signed with a paid Apple Developer ID and notarized, which the build does not do.

docs.title: For Android
docs.text:
tools/android/build_runtime.sh                                   # once: builds the player for Android
./build/src/redgem build my_game dist/my_game_android --target android

The result is dist/my_game_android/my_game.apk, with the game's files inside it. Install it on a phone with adb install, or copy the file to the phone and open it. tools/android/run_on_device.sh my_game builds, installs, starts the game on the phone or emulator that adb sees, and shows its log.

What it needs on your machine:

  • The Android SDK with its build-tools and one platform (sdkmanager "build-tools;35.0.0" "platforms;android-35"), and ANDROID_HOME pointing at it.
  • Java (the SDK's signing tool runs on it).
  • The first command downloads the Android compiler (NDK) into the project and builds the engine for phones (arm64) and for emulators (x86_64); it takes several minutes, once.

What changes on a phone:

  • The game fills the screen: it keeps the height from game.json and gets the width that fits.
  • Touch controls appear by themselves and act as a gamepad: a stick under the left thumb, A and B under the right, Start in the corner. A game that plays with a gamepad plays on a phone as it is; taps also work as mouse clicks, so UI.button menus work. A game with a touch interface of its own hides them with Input.touch_controls = false.
  • Characters may have as many bones on a phone as on a computer (up to 1024 per skeleton).
  • There is no on-screen keyboard yet, so text fields cannot be typed in.
  • Phones are slower than computers: keep levels light (few lights, modest textures) and test on a real device. It needs Android 8 or later with OpenGL ES 3.

  • The APK is signed with a key the engine makes on your machine the first time (~/.config/redgem/android-debug.keystore). It never leaves your machine and is different on everyone's; it is good for your own devices and for sharing the file.

  • The app's launcher icon is made from the game's icon, at every screen density (48 to 192 pixels). Its version is the game's version unless the android section gives another.

  • The app asks for the network (the INTERNET permission) when game.json says "network": true, or says nothing and the scripts call Network. or HTTP. (see above). Without it, Network and HTTP cannot reach anything on a phone.

docs.title: For Google Play: an App Bundle
docs.text:
Google Play takes App Bundles (.aab), not APKs. --bundle makes one:

./build/src/redgem build my_game dist/my_game_play --target android --bundle

It makes dist/my_game_play/my_game.aab, signed with the same key an APK would be (for Google Play, your own: see below). An App Bundle is made with Google's bundletool, which is not part of the SDK: put a bundletool program on the PATH, or download bundletool-all-<version>.jar and point REDGEM_BUNDLETOOL at it (it runs with Java). zip and unzip must be installed too. A bundle is not installed on a phone by itself: bundletool build-apks makes the APKs Play would.

docs.title: Your own app id, version and key
docs.text:
A game says these in the android section of its game.json; all are optional:

{
  "title": "My Game",
  "android": {
    "package": "com.mystudio.mygame",
    "version_code": 3,
    "version_name": "1.2",
    "keystore": "../keys/release.keystore",
    "key_alias": "mygame"
  }
}
  • package is the app's id on the phone. Without it the app goes by the game's id (see below), and a game with no id by its folder name.
  • version_code goes up with every release: a phone only updates to a higher one.
  • version_name is the version players see; without it, the game's own version (1.0 when it has none).
  • keystore and key_alias sign the app with a key of your own, which is what a release needs: players can only update a game signed with the same key as the one they have. Make it once with Java's keytool and keep it safe (and backed up): there is no getting it back.
  • The key's password is never written in a file. Give it when building:
REDGEM_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD='...' ./build/src/redgem build my_game dist/android --target android

(REDGEM_KEY_PASSWORD too, when the key has a password of its own.) - Keep the keystore outside the game's folder. If one is left there anyway, builds leave it out: a signing key never travels with a game.

docs.title: Recording a video
docs.text:
redgem <game_dir> --record out.mp4 plays the game into a video. You need ffmpeg on the PATH; without it RedGem says so and does not start.

redgem games/arena --record trailer.mp4 --record-fps 30 --record-size 3840x2160 --record-scale 1920x1080 --record-seconds 20
  • Each frame moves the game on by exactly 1/--record-fps seconds (30 unless given), however long it takes to draw. A scene too heavy to play smoothly still comes out smooth in the video, and so do the wind, film grain and everything else that moves with time.
  • --record-size is the size the game is drawn at, off screen (the window's own size unless given). It is not limited by the window or the desktop, and the window shows a fitted copy. --record-scale sets the video's size; frames are scaled down to it with lanczos, so drawing at 4K and scaling to 1080p gives very clean edges.
  • Recording ends after --record-seconds, when a script calls Game.stop_recording (the game keeps running in the window), or when the game quits.
  • Frames are read back from the graphics card a few frames late, so drawing never waits for it. They are encoded as H.264 (-crf 16, preset medium, yuv420p), which plays everywhere.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The executable needs the game/ folder next to it.
  • game.json says what the game is and how its window opens:
{ "id": "com.mystudio.mygame", "title": "My Game", "window_width": 1280, "window_height": 720 }
  • id is what the game is known by: its save follows it when the folder is moved or renamed, and its Android app is named after it. redgem new writes one (my-game-3fa2c1b0); change it to your own before the first release and leave it alone after. It is small letters, digits, ., - and _, starting and ending with a letter or a digit. Two games with the same id share a save: a game started as a copy of another needs a new one. A game with no id keeps its save by where its folder is, and starts a new save when it is given one.

  • game.json may also say how the game is shown until its player chooses otherwise: "fullscreen": true, "vsync": false, "fps_cap": 144 (0 for no cap), "render_scale": 0.75 (the world drawn at 75% of the window's size) and "quality": "medium" (low, medium, high, ultra). What the player chooses (see Settings in the API reference) is kept in the user's settings file, by the game's id.

  • Everything in the game folder is copied, including the scripts as plain .rb files.

  • Check the licenses of the models and sounds you include. A license that allows using an asset in a game does not always allow shipping its original file.

docs.title: Installing RedGem somewhere else
docs.text:
cmake --install build --component redgem --prefix <folder> copies the programs out of the build folder, laid out the way builds expect:

<folder>/bin/redgem            the editor, the project hub and the command line
<folder>/bin/redgem-player     what a game built for this system is a copy of
<folder>/bin/redgem-relay      the meeting point for games over the internet
<folder>/bin/redgem-server     runs a game on a server, for players to join (see Dedicated server)
<folder>/bin/redgem-test       the tool that runs a game's tests
<folder>/bin/runtimes/         the players for other systems that were built before installing

docs.title: Testing your game
docs.text:
The example below tests the game made in Your first game.

A system test is a Ruby script that plays your game: it holds keys, waits, checks what happened and can take screenshots. It runs the real game, frame by frame, at the same pace on any machine.

# tests/collect_coin_test.rb
SystemTest.define do |t|
  t.wait(30)                                   # frames
  t.hold(:w, frames: 60)                       # walk forward for a second
  t.wait_until(frames: 30) { Scene.find("Coin1").nil? }
  t.assert("the score counts the coin") { Scene.find("Player").get_component(Player).coins == 1 }
  t.screenshot("coin_collected")
end

Run it with redgem-test, the program that runs tests (it is built next to redgem):

./build/src/redgem-test my_game tests/collect_coin_test.rb --screenshots shots

The command exits with an error when an assertion fails or a script raises, so it fits in any automated check. Add --headless to run without opening a window (no screenshots then); redgem-test --help lists every option.

To run every test of a game at once, each system test with no window, and get a line per file (PASS or FAIL with the first error it said):

./build/src/redgem-test --all my_game

redgem check my_game --run-tests does the same after looking the game over (see The command line).

redgem-test is a development tool. It is not part of a built game: the program your players receive (what redgem build and the editor's Build make) contains no test code at all, and SystemTest and the rest of what tests are written with do not exist in the Ruby your game runs in. They are only there while redgem-test plays it.

docs.title: What a test can do
docs.text:
Call Effect t.wait(frames) Lets the game run t.hold(:w, :a, frames: 60) Holds keys for that long t.press(:space) Taps a key t.move_mouse(x, y), t.click(x, y) Moves the mouse; clicks there with the left button t.type("Ana") Types a text (what Input.text and UI.text_field read) t.tilt(:left_y, -1.0, frames: 60) Pushes a gamepad stick (or pulls a trigger) for that long t.press_button(:a), t.hold_button(:a, frames: 30) Taps or holds gamepad buttons t.hold_until(:w, frames: 300) { ... } Holds keys until the block is true t.wait_until(frames: 120) { ... } Waits until the block is true, or fails t.assert("message") { ... } Fails the test when the block is false t.screenshot("name") Saves a picture of the next frame as name.png in the screenshots folder (--screenshots <dir>, screenshots unless said)

Inside the blocks you have the whole scripting API, so a test can also move objects or read any behaviour's state. Taking pictures is something only tests do: a game's own scripts have no call for it. What the game saves with Save goes to a file of the test's own, which starts empty: a test never sees or changes your real progress.

docs.title: Testing Ruby code by itself
docs.text:
Code that needs no running game (a formula, a helper class) can be tested without one. A file of unit tests defines classes that inherit from RedGemTest::Case; every method whose name starts with test_ is a test:

# tests/score_test.rb
class ScoreTest < RedGemTest::Case
  def test_a_coin_is_worth_ten_points
    assert_equal 10, 1 * 10
    assert_in_delta 0.5, Vector3.new(0.5, 0, 0).length
  end
end

./build/src/redgem-test --ruby tests/score_test.rb

It runs in the same Ruby a game runs in, with the scripting API and an empty scene. The assertions are assert, refute, assert_equal, assert_nil, assert_in_delta, assert_vector and assert_raises; a system test has them too.

To test the game's own classes, say which game they are from: they then load by name from its scripts folder, as they do when the game runs (without --game, from the test file's folder).

./build/src/redgem-test --ruby tests/score_test.rb --game .

A test may reopen one of the game's classes to add to it, a trace or a stand-in for a method:

# tests/fighter_trace_test.rb
class Fighter
  alias untraced_strike strike
  def strike(*args) = (Debug.log("strike #{args.inspect}"); untraced_strike(*args))
end

A class or module line at the top of the file (not indented) loads that class from the game's scripts first, so the line reopens the game's Fighter instead of making a new, empty one.

docs.title: What RedGem does not do yet
docs.text:
Knowing this up front saves time:

  • Input is keyboard, mouse and one gamepad. Keys and buttons cannot be rebound by the player.
  • In-game interface is texts, rectangles, images, buttons and text fields you draw each frame. There are no sliders or layout containers.
  • Particles are let out in bursts, as dots or pictures. They do not collide and are not lit.
  • Animation: a character plays one clip with a second mixed over it. There are no blend trees, no animation events and no inverse kinematics.
  • Multiplayer has no matchmaking and no lag compensation; playing over the internet needs a relay you run, or a forwarded port (see Multiplayer).
  • Platforms: the editor is developed on Linux; the Windows and macOS downloads are experimental (macOS has only run on GitHub's virtual Macs, drawn by Apple's software renderer). Games are built for Linux, Windows and Android, and for the Mac from the Mac's editor (no iOS, no web).
  • macOS says the app cannot be opened ("unidentified developer", or "damaged"): the app is not signed by a registered Apple developer. Right-click RedGem.app and choose Open (on macOS 15 and later: System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway), or run xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine RedGem.app in the unpacked folder.
  • Scripts are loaded when you press Play; they are not reloaded while the game runs.
  • Scene size: a scene (or a model) that would need more than 4 GB of memory, counting its file, its vertices as the engine keeps them and its pictures as they are once decoded, is refused with a message saying how much it needs. The biggest demo scene comes to about 1.8 GB. This is an estimate of the memory the game holds, not a limit on the graphics card's memory.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text:
The editor does not open from Docker. Your session must use X11 (echo $XDG_SESSION_TYPE prints x11). The launcher tools/docker/editor.sh allows the container on your display and removes that permission when the editor closes.

The build fails looking for X11 headers. Install the development packages listed in Install. If you cannot install packages, tools/setup/fetch_x11_headers.sh extracts the headers into the project.

My script does nothing. Look at the Console: a script with an error is switched off and reported there. Check that the class name matches the file name (moving_door.rb defines MovingDoor) and that it inherits from Behaviour.

The game freezes for a moment and a behaviour stops, with ScriptTimeout in the Console. A call into that behaviour ran longer than the scripts' budget (1000 ms unless game.json says otherwise): it is stuck in a loop, or does far too much in one go. See Behaviours.

A built game closed by itself. A game that crashes writes a report and tells the player where it is (in a message box on Windows; on Linux and the Mac on its error stream, which a terminal shows). The report is a text file beside the game's save, in the player's home folder, in a folder named after the save:

.config/redgem/saves/by-id/<id>-crashes/crash-<date>-<time>.log                 Linux, Windows
Library/Application Support/RedGem/saves/by-id/<id>-crashes/crash-<date>-<time>.log   macOS

(A game with no id uses saves/<folder>-<digits>-crashes/.) It says the game, the engine's version, the system, the time in UTC, what happened (the signal, such as SIGSEGV, or the exception and its message) and, where the system can say, the functions the program was in. Send it with a bug report. The save itself loses nothing: it is written to the disk on every change. A built game for Android writes no report yet: look in adb logcat.

on_trigger_enter never fires. The object needs Trigger on, and the thing entering must be a character, a dynamic body or a kinematic body. Static scenery does not set triggers off.

The hero falls through a platform I move from a script. Give the platform a kinematic body. A static body is not meant to move.

The game is slow on a laptop with two graphics cards. RedGem asks for the dedicated card and logs which one it got when it starts. To choose: Edit > Graphics Card in the editor, or start with --gpu dedicated.

Joining fails with "this game runs protocol 1, the other side 2". The two machines (or the game and the relay or server it meets on) run versions of RedGem whose network messages differ. Build every copy of the game, the relay and the server from the same version.

I want to see what the machines of a game say to each other. Start the game, the relay or the server with REDGEM_LOG_MESSAGES=1 in its environment: every message it sends and receives is written to its log, as JSON text.

I changed the level in Blender and the editor did not update. It reloads scene.glb by itself when you have no unsaved edits. With unsaved edits it asks.

docs.title: Coastal water validation
docs.text: The current coastal result combines guarded refraction, a horizontal shore band and a broader micro-wave field. The practical target is stable, detailed real-time water. Distant reflections remain more regular than the reference, and filtered-normal roughness is an approximation; passing geometric and temporal controls does not establish photographic fidelity.

docs.title: Broader micro detail
docs.text:
Twelve wavelengths spanning approximately 3 to 51 centimeters replace four dominant carriers. Directions and phases vary deterministically, reducing parallel streaks near the camera. Equal slope weights preserve the previous sum of squared coefficients, 0.30. Macro displacement, physical impact ripples, foam, lighting and the roughness mapping remain unchanged. This is a finite artistic height field, not a fluid or ocean-spectrum simulation.

Both pictures below use the same new field, frozen camera, 0.5-second clock, exposure 0.8 and foam disabled. The Cycles control uses analytic, ray-facing macro/micro gradients and 96 samples. The older four-carrier references below remain as historical controls; changing the wave field also changes the reference, so scores across those two targets do not prove a general fidelity gain.

Runtime, twelve micro waves Matched analytic-normal Cycles control Region Rectangle RGB MAE RGB SSIM Distant water [40, 260, 1560, 325] 10.256 0.5699 Foreground water [200, 740, 1350, 880] 28.602 0.6621

Four near-origin positions and animation times check resolved slopes against independent height finite differences. Separate controls cover wavelength/direction participation and transfer of unresolved micro energy to variance. Their tolerance is unchanged from the earlier energy probe. Both focused micro cases also pass on llvmpipe. These controls do not establish gradient accuracy at arbitrary large world coordinates.

A render-only ABBA run at 1600 by 900 measured medians of 15.998 and 16.150 ms for the previous four-carrier version, versus 16.068 and 16.316 ms for twelve carriers. The pair averages are 16.074 and 16.192 ms. The 0.118 ms difference is smaller than the candidate repeat spread; it is not a precise overhead estimate. Do not combine this thermal session with the earlier costs below.

An internal fixed-step recording was checked at frames 0, 90, 180 and 239: eight seconds, 30 fps, 240 frames, rendered at 3840 by 2160 and downsampled to 1920 by 1080. The complete render suite passes 84 cases and 655741 assertions with this detail field.

docs.title: Horizontal shore band
docs.text:
Optical path length previously placed foam across broad shallow terraces. The band now uses the horizontal distance to the intersection of visible bottom and water tangent planes. foam_width is a horizontal width in meters, with 15 percent spatial reach variation. Parallel shallow plateaus receive no foam. Centimeter pores fade to their expected mean coverage when unresolved; even dense coverage retains at least 28 percent of the transmitted light.

This is a local screen-space estimate, not a complete shoreline field. Discontinuous or missing depth suppresses coverage; curved terrain can produce gaps or differ from the nearest shore. The pattern is stationary and has no advection, accumulation or breaking-wave simulation.

Physical controls require support inside 0.5 meters and none beyond 1.25 meters for a nominal one-meter band, across three bottom slopes and two camera angles. Separate controls cover a sloping water surface over flat ground, a vertical wall and a shallow plateau without a shore. Close-up pores retain the original minimum counts and transmission requirement. A separate frequency probe rejects decimeter clouds; minified coverage agrees with a resolved area quadrature.

Before the micro-detail update, the complete render suite passed 83 cases and 655739 assertions. The ten initial foam cases also pass on NVIDIA and llvmpipe. The two additional geometry controls pass on both renderers. The new helpers received an independent correctness review; this does not establish photographic acceptance.

Restoring optical-path coverage and decimeter pores makes all five selected negative controls fail: the flat plateau gains roughly 50000 changed pixels, the visible band edge moves by 0.5 to 0.8 meters across slope/camera changes, and the fine-pore probe finds only 31 crossings instead of the required 100. These controls retain the same geometric and frequency thresholds.

docs.title: Optical validation correction
docs.text: Earlier image metrics in this study are withdrawn: the preview helper changed the clock reset in recording shutdown instead of setting the clock before normal presentation. Those previews therefore used wall time. Automated render tests, internal video recordings and the frame-time benchmarks set their clocks independently and are unaffected. Replacement previews must pass a repeated-capture check before being used for image comparisons.

docs.title: Historical four-carrier optical study
docs.text:
Both views use the same scanned coast, camera, sun, sky, seven-component wave field and 0.5-second clock at 1600 by 900 pixels. Foam is disabled in both optical views. Exposure is 0.8 with the same display transform; there is no alignment or exposure fitting. The corrected runtime capture is repeated in a separate process: the distant-water rectangle is pixel-identical, while five foreground pixels differ by one RGB byte. Its clock is set before normal frame presentation, independently of elapsed loading or rendering time. The reference uses Cycles with 32 samples, denoising, IOR 1.333, roughness 0.07 and the same absorption coefficients. Its isotropic volume scattering is a physical approximation of the runtime body-light term; atmospheric fog and derivative filtering do not have identical models. The micro-height field is represented by bump shading in the reference. The reference's macro normals come from the displaced radial mesh, while the runtime uses analytic gradients. At a radius of 100 meters its radial and tangential edges are about 1.58 and 1.64 meters, exceeding the shortest macro wavelength of 0.90 meters. Distant normal convergence must therefore be checked before attributing the image difference to shading alone.

Runtime Cycles reference

The finite scan ends above a separate deeper substrate. Both pictures show that geometric edge; it must be distinguished from duplicated or displaced refraction samples.

Fixed rectangles exclude the shore and sky. Coordinates are [left, top, right, bottom] in original pixels. MAE is the mean absolute RGB byte difference. SSIM uses an 11-pixel Gaussian window with sigma 1.5, population covariance, constants 0.01 and 0.03, and a five-pixel border removed from the result. Values below are computed from the lossless pictures above.

Region Rectangle RGB MAE RGB SSIM Distant water [40, 260, 1560, 325] 10.213 0.5131 Foreground water [200, 740, 1350, 880] 29.062 0.6843

These values replace the withdrawn wall-clock comparisons. They do not establish photographic acceptance or a causal improvement over earlier shader variants, which need fresh timed captures.

A separate normal-field control keeps the camera, displaced mesh, material, illumination and display transform, but replaces smooth mesh normals plus bump with the analytic total macro/micro height gradient. Its normal is oriented per incoming ray, matching Cycles' geometry-normal convention. Independent finite differences check that gradient. This control addresses mesh normal undersampling; it does not make the runtime's BSDF, screen-space visibility or fog identical.

Region Runtime versus analytic-normal control: RGB MAE RGB SSIM Distant water 10.415 0.5643 Foreground water 28.459 0.7075

The control's 32-versus-96 sample difference is 3.371 MAE / 0.9280 SSIM at distance and 2.580 / 0.9482 in the foreground. Sampling error is not zero; small candidate deltas need further integration checks. Both the original reference and this control are retained.

docs.title: Correctness controls
docs.text:
• Isolate screen-space reflection from transmission using submerged and exposed emissive objects.
  • Compare transmitted silhouettes with an independent CPU Snell-law intersection, including supported interior coverage and false copies outside the postprocess footprint.
  • Compare absorption outside a partially exposed object's silhouette against the identical unobstructed flat or inclined floor.
  • Reproduce a missed inclined-depth root when search and refinement use different samplers.
  • Require a soft, irregular foam band, open water pockets and partial bottom transmission.
  • Check displacement bounds, analytic gradients, stationary clocks and filtered normal energy.

The current full render suite passed 84 cases and 655741 assertions. The previous full unit run passed 1215 cases; the current shader-generation checks pass 14 cases and 147 assertions. Local shader-validation binaries rebuild shader construction and changed tests while reusing unchanged CPU libraries. Clean builds remain a CI requirement. The actual GLES shader pairs for lighting, motion, depth, particle shadows and temporal resolve all compiled and linked on a native GLES context. This does not replace an Android package build.

Negative controls remove micro-normal variance or restore the continuous foam coverage floor: they respectively lose energy at 4608 distant probe pixels and produce no open pockets in 1089 shallow-shelf samples. Restoring nearest-depth bracketing makes the inclined-root probe return the wrong sample coordinate. The corrected versions pass those checks.

docs.title: Smooth specular normalization
docs.text:
The direct-light GGX distribution now preserves narrow specular lobes. Its previous additive denominator floor suppressed their energy: at roughness 0.07, the analytic peak is about 13257, while the floored expression returned 0.24. The equivalent positive denominator is evaluated without that floor; callers already bound perceptual roughness to at least 0.045. This intentionally affects direct specular lighting on all materials, including water. It does not change the sky prefilter or establish agreement with the coastal reference.

A GPU probe checks the production distribution against an independent double-precision reference at roughness 0.045, 0.07, 0.15 and 0.4, using 512 projected-distribution samples each. Both peak and projected mass checks pass on NVIDIA and software rendering. Restoring the old denominator fails all eight peak/mass checks. Foam envelope checks average 21 shoreline profiles so individual pores cannot determine band width; the existing width, softness and independent porosity requirements remain unchanged. The correction received a separate correctness review before publication.

The historical four-carrier runtime pictures include both this correction and the horizontal shore band. Foam is disabled for the optical comparison and enabled for the separate shore-band picture.
