docs.title: Assets
docs.text: The local study uses Coast Rocks 01, by Rico Cilliers and Rob Tuytel, and Ballito Rocky Beach, from Poly Haven under CC0. Only rendered validation pictures are included here; source assets and the demonstration project remain local.

docs.title: Water interaction validation
docs.text: Physical bodies generate local water impulses automatically. Entry, exit and motion along the surface produce radial packets with finite lifetimes. Detection uses conservative collider bounds against the rendered water triangles, with a cached spatial index. The water mesh needs no collider. Impulses belong to one object and original primitive, even when meshes and materials are shared. See Water surfaces for supported geometry and limits.

docs.title: Native impact study
docs.text:
A dynamic stone falls into a procedural pond. The game script contains no effect or splash call; physics and water interaction detection produce the waves. The native test captures the scene before entry, at impact and during propagation.

Before entry Impact Propagation

This is a functional study with placeholder materials. Optical artifacts around submerged edges remain under investigation. Fluid simulation, buoyancy, splashes, breaking waves and network replication of impulses remain unsupported.

docs.title: Correctness and code review
docs.text:
The regression suite covers fast swept crossings, entry/exit and wakes, dry materials, holes, shared meshes/primitives, geometry caching, stationary jitter, destroyed handles, teleports, kinematic movement from scripts, pause, expiry and world replacement. Living bodies can visit more than the retained-contact budget without permanently exhausting it.

Contacts retain their wet-state hysteresis and cooldown through small oscillations inside the surface band. Exit impulses use the final contact at the shoreline or along an upward path, rather than the body's position before leaving. Dedicated regressions reproduce both failures against the preceding detector.

Rendering tests check owner isolation, canonical simulation ages, repeated drawing, public snapshot validation, previous-frame packets, expiration, asset reload and temporal antialiasing with zero/four MSAA samples. Rendering never advances the simulation. The previous packet comes from the last frame actually drawn. Empty snapshots preserve the existing draw path.

The complete build passed 1,212 C++ cases (42,022 assertions), 23 Ruby suites and 60 native render cases (655,534 assertions). All 1,509 checked include directions are allowed. A comparison with the preceding renderer found 106 shared screenshots pixel-identical; three grass images use a real-time wind clock and differ between runs. The lit, depth, motion, temporal and particle-shadow programs also compile and link as GLSL ES 3.00 through native Mesa Intel EGL. Phone hardware has not been tested.

New C++ methods pass the project's size and complexity limits. The water shader uses small helpers for propagation, gradients, intersections, lighting and composition.

docs.text:
GeForce RTX 4050 Laptop GPU, 1600 x 900, fixed render clock, vertical synchronization disabled, 60 warm-up frames and 600 measured frames:

Pond render mode Mean Median No impulses 4.967 ms 4.926 ms One impulse 5.091 ms 5.110 ms Sixteen impulses 5.593 ms 5.615 ms

These modes measure rendering, excluding the CPU contact detector. The impulses have fixed ages, so simulation changes do not confound the comparison.

In alternating comparisons without active impulses, the preceding field renderer measured 3.631/3.740 ms median and this renderer 3.463/3.533 ms. The local showcase measured 6.388 ms before and 6.414 ms after. Earlier isolated runs varied with machine power and thermal state; these results do not establish a speedup. Local showcase assets are not included.

docs.title: Water optical comparison
docs.text:
This fixed-camera study isolates refraction and absorption from incident lighting. The bottom and stones emit their own color; the sun and environment are black, and water has no body color. The reference uses Cycles with a transmitting surface and an absorption volume. Geometry, camera, wave phase, small ripple height field, absorption coefficients and display curve are matched. All scene geometry was created for this study; no vehicle or production-scene assets are included.

The images are 1600 × 900, with the wave clock fixed at 0.5 seconds. Water has a maximum wave height of 0.045 m, dominant wavelength of 2.3 m, roughness of 0.065, IOR of 1.333 and absorption coefficients (0.42, 0.07, 0.035) per meter. Shore foam is disabled. The display uses exposure 0.8, the runtime's ACES fit and gamma 2.2. The Cycles reference uses 64 samples and denoising.

Runtime refraction SSIM against reference Mean absolute RGB error One projected depth estimate 0.9210 0.02019 Bounded depth intersection with filtered depth 0.9479 0.01057

RGB error is measured on display values normalized to [0, 1]. SSIM uses an 11-pixel Gaussian window with sigma 1.5. The newer implementation reduces mean error by about 48% in this control. This measures an optical improvement, not completion of the visual-quality target.

docs.title: After
docs.text:
Screen-space refraction cannot recover hidden or off-screen geometry. A failed intersection keeps the undistorted opaque sample; differences remain around occlusion boundaries. The runtime also uses a different reflection and sampling approximation from the offline reference.

A separate study with a lit bottom remains less accurate: water attenuates the bottom-to-camera path, but not incident illumination on submerged geometry. That approximation is recorded in the known limitations and must be addressed separately; these control images do not remove it.

docs.title: Design: online games
docs.text: Status: implemented (see Online services for how a game uses it, and "As built" at the end for where the implementation differs). What RedGem needs so a game can be played online with accounts and saved data, built the way online games are commonly made, and generic: the engine provides the pieces, the game chooses its services.

docs.title: Common practice
docs.text: Need Common practice Talking to web services A generic, asynchronous HTTP client with HTTPS in the scripting API, available on every platform. Accounts and login The engine ships no account system of its own. Games log in through an authentication service or the developer's own backend, over HTTPS, and get a session token. Letting a player into a server Connection approval: the client sends a payload when it connects (usually that token), and the server decides whether to accept it. Saved data on a server The ordinary save API writes to the server's disk. Anything bigger goes to a database behind a backend or service, reached over HTTP. Databases Never opened by the game itself. A backend owns the database; the game server calls the backend. Encrypting the game connection Offered by the transport, usually optional.

docs.title: The design
docs.text:
phone / PC                          dedicated server                 services
 ┌──────────────┐  1 log in (HTTPS)                                  ┌──────────────┐
 │  game        │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ │ auth service │
 │  (Ruby)      │ ◀───────────────── session token ───────────────── │ or backend   │
 │              │                   ┌───────────────────┐            │              │
 │              │ 2 join + token ─▶ │ redgem-server     │ 3 verify ─▶│              │
 │              │ ◀── approved ──── │ (Ruby: the game)  │ ◀──────────│              │
 │              │ 4 play ◀───────▶  │                   │ 5 save ──▶ │ database     │
 └──────────────┘                   └───────────────────┘   (HTTPS)  └──────────────┘

The password never travels over the game connection: it goes from the device to the service over HTTPS. The game connection carries only the token, then gameplay.

docs.title: 1. HTTP: a web client for every game
docs.text:
Asynchronous (the frame never waits), HTTPS by default, on Linux, Windows, macOS, Android and the dedicated server. The answer arrives in a block on the game's own thread, like every other callback.

HTTP.post("https://api.mygame.com/scores", json: { player: id, points: 120 },
          headers: { "Authorization" => "Bearer #{token}" }) do |response|
  next Debug.warn("scores: #{response.error}") unless response.ok?

  show_ranking(response.json[:top])
end

HTTP.get("https://api.mygame.com/news") { |response| @news = response.json }
  • HTTP.get/post/put/patch/delete(url, json:, body:, headers:, timeout:); the block gets a response with ok?, status, headers, body, json and error.
  • Limits: answer size (8 MB), requests in flight per game (16), a timeout (15 s default). URLs must be https://, or http:// to a local or private address (a backend on the same machine or network).
  • Certificates are checked against the system's store, or a bundled one on Android.
  • Built on the engine's sockets and mbedTLS (Apache 2.0), on a worker thread.

docs.title: 2. Connection approval
docs.text:
The joining side sends a payload; the server's game decides. Without a handler on the server everyone is let in, as today.

# on the device, after logging in to the service
Network.join("play.mygame.com", auth: { token: session_token })

# on the server
Network.authenticate do |peer, auth, decide|
  HTTP.get("https://auth.mygame.com/user",
           headers: { "Authorization" => "Bearer #{auth[:token]}" }) do |response|
    next decide.deny("not logged in") unless response.ok?

    decide.accept(identity: response.json[:id], name: response.json[:name])
  end
end

Network.identity(peer)   # => "user-4821" once accepted, on the server
Network.on_join { |peer| greet(Network.identity(peer)) }
  • on_join fires only once a player is accepted; a denied player gets on_fail with the reason.
  • Approval has a deadline (10 s): a server that never decides denies.
  • Works the same with a player hosting, but is meant for dedicated servers.

docs.title: 3. Saving on a server
docs.text:
Save keeps working everywhere. On a dedicated server it is written to the server's data folder (--data <dir>, default next to the game), so it survives restarts. Data per player is kept under the player's identity:

Network.on_leave do |peer|
  Save.update("players", {}) do |players|      # no other room's change gets lost in between
    players.merge(Network.identity(peer) => { level: @level, coins: @coins })
  end
end

One row per key in a database (SQLite), each written as it changes. For queries such as a ranking, the game sends its data to a backend with HTTP.

docs.title: 4. Guides, not built-in services
docs.text:
The manual gets two worked examples, both with the platformer:

  • A hosted service (Supabase, which has a free tier): log in, keep each player's progress, a ranking.
  • Your own backend in a few lines of Sinatra with SQLite, for those who want it all on their own machine.

No service is built into the engine and none is required.

docs.title: Later
docs.text: • Encrypted game connections (TLS over the same mbedTLS), optional, for games that carry anything sensitive over the game connection.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Passwords never reach the game server or the game connection.
  • Every HTTP answer and every auth payload is untrusted input: size limits, types checked, timeouts.
  • A server's game decides who plays; tokens are checked by the service that issued them.
  • Scripts still cannot read or write files on the player's device; only HTTP reaches out.

docs.title: As built
docs.text:
• HTTP lives in src/net/http_* (Mbed TLS 3.6, one thread per request), its Ruby side in ruby/engine/http.rb. http:// is allowed when the address a name leads to is this machine's or a private network's, checked once connected (nothing is sent otherwise). Redirects are not followed. On Android the certificates are not bundled: the engine reads the system's own (/apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts, then /system/etc/security/cacerts), which every app can read and which stays up to date. A level loaded while requests are on their way drops their blocks (the requests still go out); a game that ends gives them up.
  • Connection approval: the name is Network.player_name(peer); on_fail gets the reason. The hello carries auth under a new key, and the host answers with two new kinds of message ("the game is deciding", "refused, and why"); no version field was needed. A client of 0.2.0 joins as before (it carries nothing); against a host that decides, it ignores "deciding", so it gives up after its own 5 seconds if the game takes longer, and a refusal reaches it as a plain failure. In a room on a relay the game of whoever opened it decides, and the relay decides nothing: the opener tells it whether its game decides (a new kind of message), the relay holds the newcomer with the id it would have and hands the opener what its hello carried, and passes the decision back (two more).
  • Saving on a server: the data folder defaults to <game>-data beside the game's folder. It holds a SQLite database (save.sqlite3, src/server/save_database.*): one row per key, each change its own transaction, used by the rooms' threads one call at a time. Saved arrays and hashes are no longer limited to 4096 things (that limit is a message's); only their nesting is. Save now keeps arrays, hashes and Vector3 as well (the example above needs a hash); hashes come back with string keys. A server's secrets (a backend's key) go in its own save.
  • Guides: the manual's Online services page; the platformer logs in when ACCOUNTS is set (scripts/accounts.rb, scripts/server_gate.rb) and joins as a guest otherwise. The backend's essential code is shown in the guide; no example app is kept in the repository.

docs.title: On the wire
docs.text:
What the machines of a game (and the relay and the dedicated server between them) say to each other, since protocol version 1. The code is in src/net/wire* and src/net/pose_*.

  • Frames. Every message travels as its length (4 bytes, big-endian) and then its bytes, at most 1 MiB. A message is a MessagePack map whose keys are single letters (k its kind, f from, t to, n a game message's name, d its data, and a few more for joining). A game's data is MessagePack's nil, booleans, integers, floats, strings (UTF-8), arrays and maps; a Vector3 is {"$v": [x, y, z]}. A message to everyone does not say so (no t).
  • Version. Every connection starts with v, the protocol's version: in the newcomer's hello, and in the first thing it gets back, a welcome, a refusal or "the game is deciding" (and in a game's answer to a LAN search). The version of a connection's first message is read before anything else of it, since another version's messages may hold what this one's may not. A host, a relay or a server's lobby refuses a hello of another version with "this game runs protocol 1, the other side 2" and logs it; the machine turned away says the same, from its side, in its on_fail and its log. A game of another version found on the local network is not listed (the log says why, once). Nothing is kept for older versions; what the first words look like (a frame holding a map with k, v and a reason y) is the one thing every version keeps the same.
  • Limits, the same as with JSON: a message's data nests at most 16 deep, an array or a map holds at most 4096 things, names and hash keys are at most 64 bytes, a join's auth at most 4096 bytes written out, a refusal's reason 256. What arrives is untrusted: depth and counts are checked while it is read (arrays nested deeper than a message may be are stopped before they are built), text must be UTF-8, and bytes, infinity and NaN are no game data. The allowances of a relay and a server (bytes a second, messages a poll) are unchanged; since messages are smaller, they now hold more of them.
  • Poses (NetworkSync) are a kind of message of their own, o, whose d is bytes:
part size what flags 1 byte which parts follow: where it is, how far it moved, its rotation key size, key 1 byte + up to 128 the object's key (UTF-8) where it is 12 bytes x, y, z as 32-bit floats or how far it moved 6 bytes x, y, z as 16-bit steps of 1/1024 m since the last pose sent rotation 4 bytes "smallest three": the largest part's index (2 bits), the others in 10 bits each

A part that did not change since the last pose sent is left out; an object standing still sends its key alone, which keeps the others' interpolation on time. Positions are floats, as the engine keeps them, so a whole pose is exactly the sender's however far from the middle of the world, and a move is counted from the last pose sent, so its precision (half a millimeter) does not depend on where the object is either; a power of two times a whole number is exact in a float, so the moves add up to the same place on every machine. A rotation comes back within 0.3 degrees. Every object's pose is sent whole first, again every 40 sends (two seconds), and as soon as someone joins; a machine ignores moves of an object until it has its whole pose. The receiving side hands whole poses to the scripts as the $sync message, as before. - Debugging. With REDGEM_LOG_MESSAGES=1 in its environment, a game, relay or server writes every message it sends and receives to its log as JSON text.

A typical pose (a player running and turning, key hero-2) took about 110 to 140 bytes as JSON; it now takes 34 (30 when it only moves, 24 standing still, 40 when whole). The load test's game message (a shot: where, how hard, when) went from 143 bytes to 66, framing included.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:

It measures the bytes each player sends and receives, the server's processor time per frame (its process, lobby included, at 60 frames a second) and how long a shot takes from one player to the others (through the server, which passes messages on once a frame). docs.title: Animation graphs
docs.text:
Animation::Graph describes named states and transitions for one character. Install it with game_object.animation.use(graph). A graph can be reused: each character owns its clocks and parameter values. Installation validates the whole definition before changing the character.

graph = Animation::Graph.new(initial: :grounded, parameters: {speed: 0.0, grounded: true})
graph.blend_1d(:grounded, parameter: :speed,
               clips: [[0.0, :Idle], [1.5, :Walk], [5.0, :Run]])
graph.clip(:airborne, :Jump, loop: false)
graph.transition(:grounded, :airborne, parameter: :grounded, equals: false, fade: 0.15)
graph.transition(:airborne, :grounded, parameter: :grounded, equals: true, fade: 0.2)
animation.use(graph)

# In the character's update:
animation.set(:speed, velocity.length)
animation.set(:grounded, grounded?)

Declare every parameter and its default in parameters:. Values are booleans or finite numbers; a parameter keeps its declared type. Blend parameters must be numeric. Clips must exist in the loaded scene, state names must be unique, and every state must be reachable from initial. For numeric conditions use exactly one of equals:, above: or below:; comparisons are strict for above and below. For booleans use equals:. The first matching transition in declaration order wins, and at most one transition is taken per frame.

One-dimensional blend points must have strictly increasing finite thresholds. Outside their range, the nearest endpoint plays alone. Inside, the two neighboring clips mix linearly. Clips share normalized phase; their weighted duration determines the cycle length. A missing channel contributes the character's rest pose. Rotations mix normalized quaternions on the same hemisphere. Installation and parameter updates reject synchronized clip speeds outside the representable float range, preserving the active controller and its previous parameter values.

For movement on two axes, use a complete rectangular grid. Points can be in any order; each combination of the distinct x and y coordinates must appear exactly once, with at least two coordinates per axis. Both parameters must be distinct, declared numbers. Missing corners, duplicate points, unknown clips and nonfinite coordinates are rejected at installation.

graph = Animation::Graph.new(initial: :move, parameters: {strafe: 0.0, forward: 0.0})
graph.blend_2d(:move, parameters: [:strafe, :forward], clips: [
  [[-1.0, -1.0], :BackLeft], [[1.0, -1.0], :BackRight],
  [[-1.0, 1.0], :ForwardLeft], [[1.0, 1.0], :ForwardRight]
])
animation.use(graph)
animation.set(:strafe, sideways_speed)
animation.set(:forward, forward_speed)

The four corners of the enclosing cell mix bilinearly. Outside the grid, each axis clamps to its nearest endpoint. Zero-weight corners are omitted; shared phase and weighted cycle duration work as for one-dimensional blends. The evaluated tracks are replicated by NetworkSync. The larger snapshots use protocol version 2; machines with different protocols cannot join.

clip, blend_1d and blend_2d accept loop: and speed:. Negative speed plays backwards; a nonlooping state holds its endpoint. State fades keep the source and destination playing and use at most eight clips (four per side for two-dimensional states). A fade completes before another transition is evaluated at the next frame boundary; changing parameters during a fade does not interrupt it.

animation.state returns the current destination state's name as a String, including during a fade, or nil under manual control. clip and time refer to the dominant destination clip; equal weights choose the earlier blend point (grid points are ordered by y, then x). pause freezes the graph's clocks and fade. Calling use again installs a fresh controller with its defaults.

mix and unmix retain the graph and affect the separate overlay as usual. A valid manual play or follow_scene detaches the graph immediately. Fades across this control boundary are not supported; fades between graph states are. An invalid manual clip request preserves the active graph.

NetworkSync sends the evaluated clips, times, weights and speeds, including remaining fade time. Receivers advance those tracks without installing a graph or evaluating its conditions. Only the owner changes parameters. Every machine needs the same clips; malformed or unknown graph tracks are ignored without replacing the active controller. Graphs currently support flat clip states, one-dimensional blends and rectangular two-dimensional grids; there are no hierarchical trees or irregular point-cloud blends.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The scripting API of RedGem games: the classes and methods scripts use. Generated from docs/scripting/api.json, which tests keep in step with the engine.

Class What it is Behaviour A Ruby class attached to an object: the engine calls its methods as the game runs. GameObject An object of the scene, as scripts see it. Transform Where an object is, how it is turned and how big it is. Vector3 A point or a direction in meters: x, y, z. Scene The objects of the running scene. SceneScript Sets a level up from Ruby when it loads: scripts/_scene.rb. Input Keyboard, mouse, gamepad and touch, read every frame. Time The game's clock (added to Ruby's Time). Physics Questions to the physics world: rays, moving shapes and shapes in place. Joint What holds two bodies together, or one to the world (made by Physics.joint). CharacterController The body of an object with body = "character": walks, jumps, climbs steps. Rigidbody The body of an object with body = "dynamic" or "kinematic" (or a vehicle's chassis). Vehicle The body of an object with body = "vehicle" and wheels. Camera The camera the game is seen through. Light game_object.light: the light an object shines with. Animation The scene's own animations (exported from Blender), by name. Animator game_object.animation (animation in a behaviour): an object's own clips. Animation::Graph Named states and transitions for one character (animation.use(graph)). Audio Sounds and music from the game's sounds/ folder. UI What a script draws over the game this frame: texts, rectangles, pictures, buttons. UI::Focus Which widget of a screen the keyboard and a gamepad work: up and down move it, wrapping. Debug Messages to the console (and to redgem run). Game The game itself. Settings How the player chose the game to be shown and heard; a change takes effect at once. GameMenu A behaviour: title screen, pause menu, end screen and settings screen with its controls page; arrows or the D-pad move the focus, Enter or A picks. GameMenu::Screen A screen of the GameMenu. Particles Short-lived sparks, smoke and dust. Particles::Emitter A continuous particle effect attached to an object, returned by Particles.emitter. Scatter Great numbers of copies of a mesh (grass, trees, rocks), drawn only. Save What the game keeps between runs. HTTP Web requests; the answer comes to the block. HTTP::Response What a web request's block is given. I18n The game's texts in several languages (locales/*.json). Network Games played together: on a local network, through a relay or on a dedicated server. Network::Decision What an authenticate block decides with. NetworkSync A behaviour: the same object in the same place on every machine.

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
A Ruby class attached to an object: the engine calls its methods as the game runs. See behaviours.md.

  • start: called once, before the first update
  • update(dt): called every frame; dt is the seconds since the last one
  • fixed_update(dt): called 60 times a second, with the physics
  • on_trigger_enter(other): something entered this object's trigger, or it entered one
  • on_trigger_exit(other): something left this object's trigger
  • on_collision_enter(other): this object's body touched another
  • on_collision_exit(other): this object's body stopped touching another
  • on_destroy: the object is being destroyed
  • game_object: the object this behaviour is attached to
  • name: the object's name
  • transform: the object's Transform
  • character: the object's CharacterController, or nil
  • rigidbody: the object's Rigidbody, or nil
  • vehicle: the object's Vehicle, or nil
  • animation: the object's own Animator
  • props: the object's custom properties, as a Hash
  • prop(key, default = nil): a setting: what add_component was given, else the object's property, else the default
  • find(name): the object called name, or nil
  • find!(name): find that stops with a clear error when the object is missing
  • find_all(tag): every object with that tag
  • destroy(target = game_object): removes an object (this one unless said) at the end of the step
  • get_component(klass): another behaviour of this object, or nil
  • after(seconds, &block): runs the block once, that many seconds from now
  • every(seconds, &block): runs the block every that many seconds
  • tween(seconds, ease: :smooth, &block): calls the block with t from 0 to 1 over that many seconds
  • cancel_timers: stops every after, every and tween of this behaviour

docs.title: GameObject
docs.text:
An object of the scene, as scripts see it. See behaviours.md.

  • name: its name
  • id: its number in the running game
  • tag: its tag property
  • tag?(value): whether its tag is value
  • props: its custom properties
  • alive?: false once it was destroyed
  • destroy: removes it at the end of the step
  • visible: whether it is drawn
  • visible = value: shows or hides it
  • behaviours: its behaviours
  • parent: the object it is under, or nil
  • children: the objects under it
  • transform: its Transform
  • character: its CharacterController, or nil
  • rigidbody: its Rigidbody, or nil
  • vehicle: its Vehicle, or nil
  • light: the Light it shines with, or nil
  • animation: its Animator
  • animation_offset: seconds its animations run ahead of the original's (a spawned copy)
  • animation_offset = seconds: sets that offset
  • get_component(klass): one of its behaviours, or nil
  • add_component(klass, **settings): attaches a behaviour; settings are what its prop reads
  • tint: the color its colors are multiplied by
  • tint = color: multiplies its colors: [1.0, 0.5, 0.5]

docs.title: Transform
docs.text:
Where an object is, how it is turned and how big it is.

  • position: its position in the world (Vector3)
  • position = vector: moves it; a physics object is teleported
  • local_position: its position relative to its parent
  • local_position = vector: moves it relative to its parent
  • rotation: its rotation, Euler degrees (Vector3)
  • rotation = degrees: turns it to those Euler degrees
  • rotate(degrees): turns it by those Euler degrees
  • look_at(target, up = Vector3.up): turns it to face a point
  • translate(offset): moves it by an offset
  • scale: its scale (Vector3)
  • scale = vector: resizes it
  • forward: the direction it faces (-Z)
  • right: its right (+X)
  • up: its up (+Y)

docs.title: Vector3
docs.text:
A point or a direction in meters: x, y, z.

  • Vector3.new(x, y, z): a vector
  • Vector3[x, y, z]: the same as new
  • Vector3.zero: (0, 0, 0)
  • Vector3.one: (1, 1, 1)
  • Vector3.up: (0, 1, 0)
  • Vector3.down: (0, -1, 0)
  • Vector3.left: (-1, 0, 0)
  • Vector3.right: (1, 0, 0)
  • Vector3.forward: (0, 0, -1)
  • Vector3.back: (0, 0, 1)
  • Vector3.blender(x, y, z): a vector given in Blender's axes (Z up)
  • x: its x
  • y: its y
  • z: its z
  • + other: sum
  • - other: difference
  • -@: the opposite vector
  • * number: scaled
  • / number: divided
  • == other: whether the numbers are exactly the same
  • dot(other): dot product
  • cross(other): cross product
  • length: its length
  • length_squared: its length squared (faster)
  • normalized: the same direction, length 1
  • clamped(max_length = 1.0): the same direction, no longer than max_length
  • lerp(other, t): the point t of the way to other
  • flat: the same with y = 0
  • with(x:, y:, z:): a copy with some parts changed: v.with(y: 0)
  • distance_to(other): the distance to another point
  • approx?(other, tolerance = 0.0001): whether two vectors are about the same
  • to_a: [x, y, z]
  • set(x, y, z): changes it in place
  • add!(other): adds in place
  • sub!(other): subtracts in place
  • scale!(number): scales in place
  • normalize!: normalizes in place

== compares the numbers exactly, and equal vectors are one key of a Hash. A vector used as a key must not be changed in place (set, add!...) while the Hash holds it: use a dup as the key. The scene keeps positions, rotations and scales in 32-bit floats, so a vector that goes through it comes back rounded: compare what comes back from the scene with approx?(other, tolerance). The in-place methods change the vector and hand it back: dup one you got from someone else first. Arithmetic whose result would not fit a float, and dividing by zero, raise an ArgumentError; a vector changed in place is then left as it was.

docs.title: Scene
docs.text:
The objects of the running scene. See gameplay.md.

  • Scene.find(name): the object called name, or nil
  • Scene.find!(name): find that stops with a clear error when the object is missing
  • Scene.find_all(tag): every object with that tag
  • Scene.objects: every object
  • Scene.spawn(template, position: nil, rotation: nil, physics: true): copies a prefab = true template, with its physics and scripts; returns the copy

docs.title: SceneScript
docs.text:
Sets a level up from Ruby when it loads: scripts/_scene.rb. See behaviours.md#setting-a-level-up-in-ruby.

  • setup: runs when the level loads, before any behaviour starts
  • find(name): the object called name, or nil
  • find!(name): find that stops with a clear error when the object is missing
  • find_all(tag): every object with that tag

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Keyboard, mouse, gamepad and touch, read every frame. See gameplay.md.

  • Input.axis(name): :horizontal or :vertical, from -1 to 1 (keys, stick)
  • Input.down?(key): whether a key is held
  • Input.pressed?(key): whether a key went down this frame
  • Input.released?(key): whether a key went up this frame
  • Input.action?(name): whether a named action (game settings) is held
  • Input.action_pressed?(name): whether a named action started this frame
  • Input.action_released?(name, pad: 0): whether a named action ended this frame
  • Input.define_action(name, *bindings, keys: [], buttons: []): adds an action of the game's own (besides game.json's input section)
  • Input.define_axis(name, negative: [], positive: [], pad_axis: nil, invert: false): adds an axis of the game's own: define_axis(:steer, negative: ["key:a"], positive: ["key:d"])
  • Input.actions: the names of the actions
  • Input.axes: the names of the axes
  • Input.axis_stick(name): the stick that moves an axis (:left_x), the game's for every player; nil when none does
  • Input.bindings(name, pad: 0): what a player bound to an action: ["key:space", "pad:a"]
  • Input.bindings_changes: a count that goes up whenever actions, axes or bindings may have changed
  • Input.bind(name, binding = nil, key: nil, button: nil, side: nil, pad: 0): binds a key or a button to an action; kept between runs
  • Input.unbind(name, binding = nil, key: nil, button: nil, side: nil, pad: 0): takes a binding off an action
  • Input.reset_bindings(name = nil, pad: nil): back to the game's own bindings (of one action, or all; of one pad, or all)
  • Input.capture_next(cancel: ["key:escape", "pad:b", "pad:back"], &block): the next key or button pressed, to the block: |binding, pad| (nil: called off)
  • Input.capturing?: whether a capture waits for a key
  • Input.capturing_for?(block): whether a capture still waits to call that block (not once another took its place)
  • Input.cancel_capture: calls a capture off
  • Input.mouse_x: the pointer's x, in pixels
  • Input.mouse_y: the pointer's y, in pixels
  • Input.mouse_dx: how far the mouse moved this frame, across
  • Input.mouse_dy: how far the mouse moved this frame, up and down
  • Input.mouse_wheel: how far the wheel turned this frame
  • Input.mouse_down?(button): whether a mouse button (:left, :right, :middle) is held
  • Input.mouse_pressed?(button): whether a mouse button went down this frame
  • Input.mouse_released?(button): whether a mouse button went up this frame
  • Input.mouse_locked = locked: hides the pointer and keeps it in the window (first-person cameras)
  • Input.mouse_locked?: whether the pointer is locked
  • Input.pads: the numbers of the gamepads plugged in
  • Input.gamepad?: whether a gamepad is connected
  • Input.gamepad_axis(axis): :left_x, :left_y, :right_x, :right_y, :left_trigger, :right_trigger
  • Input.gamepad_down?(button): whether a gamepad button (:a, :b, :x, :y...) is held
  • Input.gamepad_pressed?(button): whether a gamepad button went down this frame
  • Input.gamepad_released?(button): whether a gamepad button went up this frame
  • Input.text: what was typed this frame
  • Input.touch_controls = on: shows the on-screen stick and buttons of a phone
  • Input.touch_controls?: whether they are shown

Every action, axis, binding and gamepad call takes pad: (0 to 3: the player; 0 when left out). Actions and axes come from game.json's input section and define_action/define_axis; a player's bindings are kept between runs, beside the game's save. See Controls.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
The game's clock (added to Ruby's Time).

  • Time.delta: seconds since the last frame
  • Time.fixed_delta: seconds of a physics step (1/60)
  • Time.elapsed: seconds since the game started
  • Time.frame: how many frames have run
  • Time.scale: how fast game time runs (1 is normal)
  • Time.scale = value: slows or speeds the game; 0 pauses it

docs.title: Physics
docs.text:
Questions to the physics world: rays, moving shapes and shapes in place. See gameplay.md.

  • Physics.raycast(origin, direction, max_distance = 1000, skip = nil, layers: nil, ignore: nil): the first thing a ray hits: {object:, point:, normal:, distance:}, or nil (skip: an object it sees through)
  • Physics.raycast_all(origin, direction, max_distance = 1000, layers: nil, ignore: nil): everything a ray hits, nearest first
  • Physics.sphere_cast(from, to, radius, layers: nil, ignore: nil): the first thing a ball moving from from to to touches, or nil
  • Physics.box_cast(from, to, size, rotation: nil, layers: nil, ignore: nil): the same for a box (its whole size; rotation in degrees)
  • Physics.capsule_cast(from, to, radius, height, rotation: nil, layers: nil, ignore: nil): the same for an upright capsule (height end to end)
  • Physics.overlap_sphere(center, radius, layers: nil, ignore: nil): the hits of everything inside a ball, nearest first
  • Physics.overlap_box(center, size, rotation: nil, layers: nil, ignore: nil): the same inside a box
  • Physics.overlap_capsule(center, radius, height, rotation: nil, layers: nil, ignore: nil): the same inside a capsule
  • Physics.layers: the game's collision layers, as Symbols (game.json's physics layers)
  • Physics.joint(kind, object, other = nil, anchor: nil, other_anchor: nil, axis: nil, limits: nil, motor_speed: nil, motor_torque: nil, min: nil, max: nil, spring: nil, damping: nil, break_force: nil): joins two objects, or one to the world (other nil): :fixed, :hinge, :slider, :point or :distance

layers: is a layer's name or a list of them (every layer when nil); ignore: is an object or a list of objects to see through. Hits are {object:, point:, normal:, distance:}, each object once, nearest first, at most 64; triggers are never hit. A cast that starts inside something hits it at distance 0.

docs.title: Joint
docs.text:
What holds two bodies together, or one to the world (made by Physics.joint). See gameplay.md.

  • kind: :fixed, :hinge, :slider, :point or :distance
  • object: the object it holds
  • other: the other object it holds, or nil for the world
  • alive?: whether it still holds them
  • broken?: whether it was pulled past its break force
  • remove: lets go
  • enabled?: whether it holds right now
  • enabled = flag: lets go for a while, or holds again
  • break_force: the pull (newtons) or twist (newton meters) it breaks at; 0 never breaks
  • break_force = newtons: sets the pull it breaks at
  • motor(speed, torque): a hinge turns at that speed (degrees per second) with at most that torque; 0 torque lets it go
  • angle: how far a hinge turned from where it started, in degrees

Points and axes are in world space; anchor: defaults to the object's position, other_anchor: (a distance joint's other end) to the other object's, axis: to up. A hinge's limits: are degrees [low, high] from where it starts (low -180 to 0, high 0 to 180), a slider's are meters along its axis; a hinge's motor_speed: needs a motor_torque:. A distance joint keeps between min: (0) and max: (how far apart the ends are) apart, springy with spring: (hertz) and damping:. Each kind refuses options it has no use for, and motor and angle raise for anything but a hinge. A joint needs a dynamic body at one end (one whose bodies were all made kinematic since holds nothing until one is dynamic again); it goes when either object is destroyed or the scene changes.

docs.title: CharacterController
docs.text:
The body of an object with body = "character": walks, jumps, climbs steps. See gameplay.md.

  • move(velocity): walks with that velocity (m/s) this frame
  • jump(speed): jumps up at that speed
  • grounded?: whether it stands on something
  • velocity: its velocity
  • layer: its collision layer, a Symbol
  • layer = name: moves it to another collision layer

docs.title: Rigidbody
docs.text:
The body of an object with body = "dynamic" or "kinematic" (or a vehicle's chassis). See gameplay.md.

  • velocity: its velocity
  • velocity = vector: sets its velocity
  • add_impulse(vector): pushes it
  • add_force(force, at: nil): pushes it during the next step (newtons); at a point (world space), it also turns it
  • add_torque(torque): turns it during the next step (newton meters)
  • angular_velocity: how fast it spins, degrees per second around each axis
  • angular_velocity = vector: sets how fast it spins
  • mass: its mass in kilograms
  • mass = kilograms: changes its mass (more than 0)
  • kinematic?: whether scripts move it (instead of forces)
  • kinematic = flag: turns a dynamic body kinematic, or back
  • dynamic?: whether forces move it
  • dynamic = flag: turns a kinematic body dynamic, or back
  • gravity_scale: how much gravity pulls it (1 is normal)
  • gravity_scale = scale: 0 floats, 2 falls twice as hard
  • sleep: stops simulating it until something touches it
  • wake: simulates it again
  • sleeping?: whether it sleeps
  • layer: its collision layer, a Symbol
  • layer = name: moves it to another collision layer

Forces and torques act during the next physics step only: add them every fixed_update to keep pushing. A body made dynamic again starts at rest. kinematic= and dynamic= raise for a vehicle.

docs.title: Vehicle
docs.text:
The body of an object with body = "vehicle" and wheels. See gameplay.md.

  • drive(throttle: 0.0, steering: 0.0, brake: 0.0, handbrake: 0.0): drives it this frame (each from -1 or 0 to 1)
  • stop: brakes fully
  • speed: its speed in m/s, signed
  • velocity: its velocity

Wheel meshes must have their rotation applied (the axle along X). drive's inputs are the one setting the engine clamps, since an analog stick may push a little past full.

docs.title: Camera
docs.text:
The camera the game is seen through.

  • Camera.main: the object holding the camera
  • Camera.screen_ray(x, y): [origin, direction] through a pixel of the screen
  • Camera.fov: its vertical field of view, in degrees
  • Camera.fov = degrees: sets the field of view
  • Camera.motion_blur: how much the picture streaks with speed, 0 to 1
  • Camera.motion_blur = amount: sets it

docs.title: Light
docs.text:
game_object.light: the light an object shines with. See gameplay.md#light-that-flickers-and-fades.

  • intensity: watts for a point or spot light, lux for the sun
  • intensity = value: sets it; shows from the next frame
  • color: its color [r, g, b], 0 to 255
  • color = color: :orange or [r, g, b] from 0 to 255

docs.title: Animation
docs.text:
The scene's own animations (exported from Blender), by name. See animation.md.

  • Animation.names: the names of the scene's animations
  • Animation.play(name, loop: true, speed: 1.0, restart: false): plays one
  • Animation.pause(name): pauses one
  • Animation.stop(name): stops one
  • Animation.playing?(name): whether it plays
  • Animation.time(name): where it is, in seconds
  • Animation.duration(name): how long it is, in seconds
  • Animation.seek(name, seconds): jumps to a moment

docs.title: Animator
docs.text:
game_object.animation (animation in a behaviour): an object's own clips. See animation.md.

  • play(name, loop: true, speed: 1.0, fade: 0.0, restart: false): plays a clip, fading from the last one
  • mix(name, weight: 1.0, loop: true, speed: 1.0): plays a clip over the one playing
  • unmix: stops the clip mixed over
  • pause: pauses its clips
  • follow_scene(fade: 0.0): goes back to the scene's animations
  • clip: the clip playing
  • playing?: whether a clip plays
  • time: where the clip is, in seconds
  • use(graph): installs an Animation::Graph
  • set(parameter, value): sets a parameter of the graph
  • state: the graph's state, or nil

docs.title: Animation::Graph
docs.text:
Named states and transitions for one character (animation.use(graph)). See animation.md.

  • Animation::Graph.new(initial:, parameters: {}): a graph starting at a state, with its parameters and their defaults
  • clip(name, clip, loop: true, speed: 1.0): a state that plays one clip
  • blend_1d(name, parameter:, clips:, loop: true, speed: 1.0): a state that blends clips by a number: clips: [[0.0, :Idle], [5.0, :Run]]
  • blend_2d(name, parameters:, clips:, loop: true, speed: 1.0): a rectangular two-dimensional grid: parameters: [:x, :y], clips: [[[x, y], :Clip], ...]
  • transition(from, to, parameter:, equals: nil, above: nil, below: nil, fade: 0.0): goes from one state to another when a parameter says so

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
Sounds and music from the game's sounds/ folder.

  • Audio.play(name, volume: 1.0, pitch: 1.0): plays a sound once
  • Audio.music(name, loop: true, volume: 0.7): plays music
  • Audio.stop_music: stops the music
  • Audio.music_pitch = pitch: changes the music's pitch
  • Audio.music_volume = volume: changes the music's volume
  • Audio.volume = volume: the volume of everything
  • Audio.play_at(name, position, loop: false, volume: 1.0, pitch: 1.0, reference_distance: 1.0, max_distance: 50.0): plays a sound at a place in the world; returns its id, or nil
  • Audio.listener(position, forward, up): where the ears are (move it with the camera)
  • Audio.move(id, position): moves a sound played with play_at
  • Audio.playing?(id): whether that sound still plays
  • Audio.stop(id): stops that sound
  • Audio.stop_sources: stops every sound played with play_at

play_at sources use stereo panning and inverse-distance volume, fading to silence at max_distance. volume must be 0 or more and pitch from 0.01 to 8; 0 < reference_distance < max_distance. Positions and directions may be arrays or Vector3. Update Audio.listener(position, forward, up) when the camera moves: nothing follows an object by itself. At most 64 sources play at once; old ids are never reused.

docs.title: UI
docs.text:
What a script draws over the game this frame: texts, rectangles, pictures, buttons. See gameplay.md.

  • UI.text(str, x:, y:, size:, color:, alpha:, align:): draws a text
  • UI.rect(x:, y:, width:, height:, color:, alpha:, radius:): draws a rectangle
  • UI.image(name, x:, y:, width:, height:): draws a picture of images/
  • UI.button(label, x:, y:, width:, height:): draws a button; true the frame it is clicked
  • UI.text_field(value, x:, y:, width:, height:, max_length:, secret:): a field to type in; returns the new value
  • UI.width: the width of the screen, in pixels
  • UI.height: the height of the screen, in pixels
  • UI.text_width(str, size:): how wide a text is, in pixels (in the face selected)
  • UI.toggle(label, on, x:, y:, width:, height:, focused: false): an on/off row of a settings screen; returns whether it is on
  • UI.choice(label, choices, index, x:, y:, width:, height:, focused: false): a row that picks one of choices; returns the index chosen
  • UI.slider(label, value, x:, y:, width:, height:, min: 0.0, max: 1.0, step: 0.05, focused: false): a row with a slider; returns the value
  • UI.font: the face texts are drawn with: a file name of fonts/, or nil for the built-in one
  • UI.font = name: draws the next texts with fonts/.ttf or .otf (nil: the built-in face)

    A focused widget (focused: true) is worked by Enter or a gamepad's A, and left and right change it. The built-in face adds glyphs as they are asked for (Greek, Cyrillic, accented letters, €); for another face or script, put a .ttf or .otf in fonts/ and set UI.font. A missing or unreadable face falls back to the built-in one, with a warning; glyphs a face lacks show as ?; there is no bidirectional layout or complex-script shaping.

docs.title: UI::Focus
docs.text:
Which widget of a screen the keyboard and a gamepad work: up and down move it, wrapping. See gameplay.md.

  • UI::Focus.new: a focus on the first widget
  • update(count): moves it among count widgets, as up or down was pressed this frame
  • at?(index): whether the widget of that index has it: pass it as focused:
  • move_to(index): puts it on a widget (one clicked, or the one a screen comes back to)
  • index: the widget that has it
  • reset: back to the first widget

docs.title: Debug
docs.text:
Messages to the console (and to redgem run).

  • Debug.log(message): says something
  • Debug.warn(message): warns
  • Debug.error(message): reports an error

docs.title: Game
docs.text:
The game itself.

  • Game.load_scene(name): switches to scenes/.glb ("main" is scene.glb); Ruby globals survive
  • Game.scene_name: the scene running
  • Game.title: the game's title
  • Game.quit: ends the game
  • Game.stop_recording: ends a video recorded with --record; the game goes on
  • Game.version: the version in game.json ("1.2.0"), or nil

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
How the player chose the game to be shown and heard; a change takes effect at once. See ../shipping.md#notes.

  • Settings.window_mode: :windowed, :fullscreen or :borderless
  • Settings.window_mode = mode: changes it
  • Settings.fullscreen?: whether the game fills the screen
  • Settings.fullscreen = on: fullscreen, or back to a window
  • Settings.resolution: [width, height] of the window, in pixels
  • Settings.resolution = size: resizes the window: one of resolutions
  • Settings.resolutions: the sizes the monitor offers: [[w, h], ...]
  • Settings.render_scale: the share of the window's size the world is drawn at (0.5 to 2)
  • Settings.render_scale = scale: changes it
  • Settings.vsync: whether frames wait for the screen
  • Settings.vsync = on: changes it
  • Settings.fps_cap: frames a second at most; nil for none
  • Settings.fps_cap = cap: changes it
  • Settings.quality: :low, :medium, :high, :ultra or :custom
  • Settings.quality = quality: the most a level's environment gets of what it asks for
  • Settings.quality_details: what the custom quality allows: {msaa:, antialias:, shadow_cascades:, ...}
  • Settings.quality_details = details: changes some of them, and makes the quality :custom
  • Settings.volume: the player's volume, 0 to 1 (it multiplies Audio.volume)
  • Settings.volume = volume: changes it
  • Settings.save: keeps them for the next runs; false where they last for the run only

Until the player chooses, everything is what game.json says. Settings.save keeps them only in a built game a player plays: in the editor's Play, redgem run, a server's rooms and tests they last for the run, and save returns false.

docs.title: GameMenu
docs.text:
A behaviour: title screen, pause menu, end screen and settings screen with its controls page; arrows or the D-pad move the focus, Enter or A picks. See gameplay.md#pause-and-the-flow-between-screens.

  • GameMenu.instance: the menu of the scene, or nil
  • show(screen): opens a screen: :title, :pause, :over, :settings or one of the game's
  • show_settings: opens the settings screen (window, resolution, quality, volume...; its Controls button opens the controls page)
  • resume: closes the menu and goes on
  • restart: starts the scene again
  • finish(message): opens the end screen with a message
  • open?: whether the menu is open
  • screen: the screen open
  • screens: the screens, by name (:title, :pause, :over, :settings, :controls and the game's own)
  • button_box(index): where the menu's button of that index is: [x, y, width, height]

docs.title: GameMenu::Screen
docs.text:
A screen of the GameMenu. See gameplay.md#pause-and-the-flow-between-screens.

  • GameMenu::Screen.new(heading:, options:, back:): a screen with a heading and options: [[label, action], ...]
  • add_option(label, index:, &action): adds an option
  • heading: its heading
  • heading = text: changes its heading
  • options: its options
  • back: the screen Esc goes back to
  • opened: called when it is shown
  • closed: called when it is left
  • draw(first_button): draws what else it shows
  • space_above: pixels kept between its heading and its buttons
  • typing?: whether letters are typed into it
  • rows: how many widgets it draws above its buttons that take the focus
  • first_button_share: where its first button sits, a share of the height (nil: the menu's)
  • focus: its UI::Focus, which the menu gives it
  • focus = focus: sets it

docs.title: Particles
docs.text:
Short-lived sparks, smoke and dust. See gameplay.md#sparks-dust-and-smoke.

  • Particles.burst(position, count:, color:, alpha:, glow:, lit:, cast_shadow:, soft:, direction:, spread:, speed:, life:, size:, gravity:, image:, frames:, fps:, spin:): adds particles; returns how many (size, color and alpha may be lists over their life)
  • Particles.emitter(object, rate: 24, offset: Vector3.zero, **settings): starts a continuous local effect; returns a Particles::Emitter handle; uses burst settings except count
  • Particles.count: how many are alive
  • Particles.clear: removes all particles and stops every emitter

Emitters follow game time and stop on object destruction or scene changes. They are local visual effects, not replicated. Without a presenter, creation returns an inactive handle and no emitter is allocated or simulated. Births follow ordinary movement; movement over 10 meters per update starts them at the destination. Up to 256 emitters fairly share 4096 live particles; missed births are dropped.

docs.title: Particles::Emitter
docs.text:
A continuous particle effect attached to an object, returned by Particles.emitter. See gameplay.md#sparks-dust-and-smoke.

  • active?: whether this emitter is still emitting from a live object
  • stop: stops new births; existing particles finish their lives

docs.title: Scatter
docs.text:
Great numbers of copies of a mesh (grass, trees, rocks), drawn only. See ../levels.md#grass-forests-and-cities.

  • Scatter.place(template, count:, area:, ground: nil, seed: 0, scale: 1.0, align: false, tints:, tint_variation:, fade:, normals_up:, lods:): places copies; returns a set (count, remove)
  • Scatter.clear: removes every set
  • count: how many copies a set placed
  • remove: removes a set

docs.title: Save
docs.text:
What the game keeps between runs. See online-services.md#saving-on-a-server.

  • Save.get(key, default = nil): a value, or the default
  • Save.set(key, value): keeps a value (nil removes it)
  • Save[key]: the same as get
  • Save[key] = value: the same as set
  • Save.update(key, default = nil, &block): reads and writes a key with nothing in between
  • Save.delete(key): removes a key
  • Save.clear: removes everything
  • Save.keys: every key

Values are numbers, texts, true/false, Vector3, and arrays and hashes of those; hashes come back with string keys.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
Web requests; the answer comes to the block. See online-services.md#http.

  • HTTP.get(url, headers: {}, timeout: 15, &block): GET
  • HTTP.post(url, json: nil, body: nil, headers: {}, timeout: 15, &block): POST
  • HTTP.put(url, json: nil, body: nil, headers: {}, timeout: 15, &block): PUT
  • HTTP.patch(url, json: nil, body: nil, headers: {}, timeout: 15, &block): PATCH
  • HTTP.delete(url, headers: {}, timeout: 15, &block): DELETE
  • HTTP.request(verb, url, json: nil, body: nil, headers: {}, timeout: 15, &block): any verb

docs.title: HTTP::Response
docs.text:
What a web request's block is given. See online-services.md#http.

  • ok?: whether it came back with a 2xx status
  • status: its status
  • headers: its headers
  • body: its body
  • json: its body read as JSON
  • error: why there was no answer, or nil

docs.title: I18n
docs.text:
The game's texts in several languages (locales/*.json). See i18n.md.

  • I18n.t(key, **values): the text of a key in the language in use, its {placeholders} filled
  • I18n.locale: the language in use (:en)
  • I18n.locale = language: changes the language
  • I18n.available_locales: the languages of the game's locales/ files

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Games played together: on a local network, through a relay or on a dedicated server. See multiplayer.md.

  • Network.host(port: 7777, name: nil, visible: true, room: false): hosts a game
  • Network.join(address = nil, port: 7777, room: nil, auth: nil): joins a game (an address, or a room code)
  • Network.leave: leaves the game
  • Network.online?: whether this machine is in a game
  • Network.connecting?: whether a join is on its way
  • Network.host?: whether this machine hosts
  • Network.server?: whether this machine is a dedicated server
  • Network.id: this machine's peer id
  • Network.peers: the peers of the game
  • Network.players: the peers without a dedicated server
  • Network.port: the port of the game
  • Network.room: the room code, on a relay
  • Network.relay: the relay's address
  • Network.relay = address: sets the relay's address
  • Network.search: looks for games on the local network
  • Network.searching?: whether it is looking
  • Network.stop_search: stops looking
  • Network.games: the games found
  • Network.discovery_port: the port games are looked for on
  • Network.discovery_port = port: changes it
  • Network.emit(name, data = nil, to: :all): sends a message (:all, :host or a peer id)
  • Network.on(name, &block): receives a message: |data, from|
  • Network.on_connect(&block): this machine is in the game
  • Network.on_disconnect(&block): the game is gone
  • Network.on_join(&block): someone arrived: |peer|
  • Network.on_leave(&block): someone left: |peer|
  • Network.on_fail(&block): a join did not work out: |reason|
  • Network.authenticate(&block): decides who gets in: |peer, auth, decide|
  • Network.identity(peer): who a peer was accepted as
  • Network.player_name(peer): a peer's name
  • Network.spawn(template, owner: Network.id, position:, rotation:): spawns a copy on every machine
  • Network.allow_spawn(*templates): lets guests spawn those templates

docs.title: Network::Decision
docs.text:
What an authenticate block decides with. See online-services.md.

  • accept(identity:, name: nil): lets the peer in
  • deny(reason = "not let in"): keeps the peer out

docs.title: NetworkSync
docs.text:
A behaviour: the same object in the same place on every machine. See multiplayer.md#objects-in-the-same-place-everywhere.

  • mine?: whether this machine owns it
  • owner: the peer that owns it
  • owner = peer: gives it to a peer
  • key: the name it is known by on every machine
  • assign(owner:, key:): sets its owner and key

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Script errors are logged with a backtrace and only disable the failing behaviour; the game keeps running. Every method takes finite numbers a float can hold: infinity, NaN or a number too large raises an ArgumentError instead of reaching the scene. A setting with a range raises outside it and says the range; nothing is quietly clamped, except Vehicle#drive's inputs. Assigning transform.position to a physics object teleports it (moving bodies also stop); changing its rotation keeps its velocity. Images may be PNG, JPEG or static WebP (a name without an extension looks for .webp last), at most 8192 pixels a side; animated WebP and KTX2/Basis are not read. Missing or unreadable images (scene textures, UI.image, particle images) show an opaque magenta-and-black checkerboard, with a warning; a material that never named a texture keeps its plain color, and no path reads outside the game's folder.

docs.title: Behaviours
docs.text:
A behaviour is a Ruby class that inherits from Behaviour. Attached to an object, it gets one instance for that object, and the engine calls its methods as the game runs.

class Door < Behaviour
  def start; end                      # once, before the first update
  def update(dt); end                 # every frame; dt is seconds since the last one
  def fixed_update(dt); end           # 60 times per second, with the physics
  def on_trigger_enter(other); end    # something entered this object's trigger (or it entered one)
  def on_trigger_exit(other); end
  def on_collision_enter(other); end  # this object's body touched another
  def on_collision_exit(other); end
  def on_destroy; end
end

Define only the ones you need. other is the other object (a GameObject).

docs.title: Files and class names
docs.text:
The file name decides the class name: camera_follow.rb must define CameraFollow. Scripts live in the game's scripts/ folder.

You never require another script. The first time you use a class name, RedGem loads the file it should be in (Patrol loads scripts/patrol.rb). That works for plain helper classes too.

docs.title: Attaching a behaviour
docs.text:
There are three ways, and they mix freely:

  • In the editor: Inspector > Add Component, or drag a script from the Project panel onto an object.
  • In Blender: the custom property script = "door.rb" (several: "door.rb, sound.rb").
  • From Ruby: object.add_component(Door, speed: 2.0).

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
A behaviour reads its settings with prop:

def start
  @speed = prop(:speed, 3.0)   # 3.0 when nothing sets it
end

prop(:speed, default) returns, in this order: what add_component was given, the object's custom property speed (set in the Inspector or in Blender), or the default. So the same script can be tuned per object without changing code.

docs.title: Reaching things
docs.text:
Inside a behaviour:

You write You get game_object, transform, name this object, its transform, its name character, rigidbody, vehicle this object's physics body of that kind, or nil find("Hero"), find_all(:coin) an object by name, all objects with a tag get_component(Health) another behaviour on the same object other.get_component(Player) a behaviour on another object destroy or destroy(other) removes an object from the game

docs.title: Objects that are gone
docs.text:
destroy takes an object out at the end of the step: its on_destroy still runs, and until then it can be used as usual. After that, a reference you kept (in a variable, a global, a timer's block) stands for that object only. alive? says false, name and tag still answer, and anything else raises game object "Coin" (id 12) was destroyed, even once a newly spawned object sits in the same place (its id) or the level was switched. A kept reference never starts acting on another object.

@target = nil unless @target&.alive?   # forget an enemy someone else destroyed

docs.title: Setting a level up in Ruby
docs.text:
Instead of attaching scripts object by object, a level can have a scene script: scripts/main_scene.rb for scene.glb, scripts/level2_scene.rb for scenes/level2.glb. Its setup runs when the level loads, before any behaviour starts.

class MainScene < SceneScript
  ENEMY_SPEEDS = { "Slime" => 1.5, "Bat" => 4.0 }

  def setup
    find!("Player").add_component(Player, speed: 6.0)
    ENEMY_SPEEDS.each { |name, speed| find!(name).add_component(Patrol, speed: speed) }
    find_all("coin").each { |coin| coin.add_component(Coin) }
  end
end

find! is find that stops with a clear error when the object is missing. With a scene script the level file says what is there and where, and Ruby says what it does.

docs.title: When a script fails
docs.text: An error in a behaviour does not stop the game. That behaviour is switched off, and the Console shows the error with the file and line. Fix it, press Play again.

docs.title: A script that never returns
docs.text:
Every call the engine makes into the scripts (a behaviour's start and update, a contact, a scene script, a network handler) has a budget of time: 1000 ms unless the game's game.json says otherwise. A call still running past it (a loop {} with no break, a while true waiting for something that never comes) is stopped with a ScriptTimeout error. The behaviour is switched off like one that raised, the Console says which behaviour and method it was and how long it ran, and the game goes on. The game freezes for the length of the budget, once.

{ "id": "com.mystudio.mygame", "title": "My Game", "script_budget_ms": 2000 }

script_budget_ms is a whole number of milliseconds from 1 to 60000. It applies the same way to a game you play, to Play in the editor and to every room of a dedicated server, where each room has its own scripts and its own budget. Raise it for a scene script that builds a large level in one go; a frame's update should never come near it.

ScriptTimeout is not a StandardError, so rescue => e does not catch it. A call over its budget is stopped once, where it stands, and has 50 ms more to unwind: its ensure clauses run, so it can put back what it changed. If it is still running after that (an ensure that loops, a rescue Exception that carries on), it is stopped again at every step until it has returned.

What counts is the time spent in the call's own Ruby. Not counted: the work of the engine known to take long (spawning objects, placing scatter copies), and the calls the engine makes into the scripts from inside it, such as the start of a behaviour a spawned object brings, which each have a budget of their own. Up to four budgets of that are forgiven in one call: a loop that does nothing but spawn is stopped after about five. The engine's methods are never cut off halfway: the call stops at its next line of Ruby.

A recursion that never ends stops on its own, with SystemStackError, long before the program's stack runs out, and is handled the same way: its behaviour is switched off. redgem-test runs a file of Ruby tests with no budget, as one call.

docs.title: Gameplay recipes
docs.text: Short answers to "how do I...". Each snippet goes inside a behaviour.

docs.title: Read the keyboard
docs.text:
Input.axis(:horizontal)        # -1..1: A/D or left/right arrows
Input.axis(:vertical)          # -1..1: S/W or down/up arrows
Input.action_pressed?(:jump)   # true on the frame Space goes down
Input.action?(:run)            # true while Left Shift is held
Input.down?(:e)                # any key: held
Input.pressed?(:e)             # any key: went down this frame

Built-in actions: :jump (Space), :fire (Left Ctrl or Enter), :run (Left Shift). A game declares its own and lets players change them: see Controls.

docs.title: Read a gamepad
docs.text:
A game written with axes and actions already works with a gamepad: the left stick moves :horizontal and :vertical (by as much as it is pushed), and A, X and B are :jump, :fire and :run. For the rest, ask the gamepad itself:

Input.gamepad?                        # is one plugged in?
Input.gamepad_axis(:right_x)          # -1..1: left_x, left_y, right_x, right_y (left and up are negative)
Input.gamepad_axis(:right_trigger)    # 0..1: left_trigger, right_trigger
Input.gamepad_down?(:start)           # held; also gamepad_pressed? and gamepad_released?

Buttons are named as on an Xbox pad: :a, :b, :x, :y, :left_bumper, :right_bumper, :back, :start, :dpad_up, :dpad_down, :dpad_left, :dpad_right, :left_stick, :right_stick. To walk slowly with a half-pushed stick, use clamped instead of normalized:

direction = Vector3.new(Input.axis(:horizontal), 0, -Input.axis(:vertical)).clamped

Up to four gamepads are read at once, numbered from 0. Each is a player: pad: picks whose actions, axes or buttons to read, and leaving it out reads the first.

Input.pads                              # [0, 1]: the gamepads plugged in
Input.action_pressed?(:jump, pad: 1)    # the second player jumped
Input.axis(:horizontal, pad: 1)         # the second player's stick
Input.gamepad_down?(:start, pad: 1)

The keyboard belongs to the first player (pad 0). The other players start with the gamepad's bindings only, unless a player binds keys of their own (two players sharing one keyboard).

Gamepads cannot rumble: the window library the engine uses on desktops has no vibration, and neither does Android's.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
A game names what its players do (actions, which are on or off, and axes, from -1 to 1) and says what triggers them. Scripts then read the names, never the keys, so players can change the keys. The built-in :jump, :fire, :run, :horizontal and :vertical are always there; a game adds its own, or binds one of those anew, in the input section of its game.json:

{
  "input": {
    "actions": {
      "dash": ["key:e", "pad:b"],
      "jump": ["key:space", "key:w", "pad:a"]
    },
    "axes": {
      "steer": {"negative": ["key:a", "pad:dpad_left"], "positive": ["key:d", "pad:dpad_right"], "pad_axis": "left_x"},
      "climb": {"pad_axis": "right_y", "invert": true}
    }
  }
}

A binding is key: with a key's name (key:space, key:left_shift, key:7) or pad: with a gamepad button's (pad:a, pad:dpad_up). An axis' pad_axis is a stick that moves it too, by as much as it is pushed; invert runs that stick the other way (up is negative on a stick). A binding the engine does not know is left out with a warning, and the game plays on. Scripts can declare names too, before using them. There, a binding may also be a Symbol (a key) or {keys: [...], buttons: [...]}, mixed as one likes:

Input.define_action(:dash, keys: [:e], buttons: [:b])     # or define_action(:dash, :e, "pad:b")
Input.define_axis(:steer, negative: [:a, "pad:dpad_left"], positive: {keys: [:d], buttons: [:dpad_right]},
                  pad_axis: :left_x)
Input.actions                   # [:dash, :fire, :jump, :run]
Input.action_released?(:dash)   # true on the frame the last of its keys and buttons lets go

Declaring a name again binds it anew; declaring it as the other kind (an axis that was an action) also takes away what players had bound to the old one.

docs.title: Letting players rebind
docs.text:
Each player (a gamepad's number, pad:, 0 when left out or nil) has bindings of their own:

Input.bindings(:jump)                         # ["key:space", "pad:a"]
Input.bindings(:horizontal)                   # {negative: ["key:a", "key:left"], positive: [...]}
Input.bind(:jump, key: :k)                    # Space and K both jump now
Input.bind(:jump, key: :j, button: :y)        # both given: both bound (unbind takes both away too)
Input.unbind(:jump, key: :space)              # only K
Input.unbind(:jump)                           # nothing: every key and button taken away
Input.bind(:fire, button: :y, pad: 1)         # the second player's Y fires
Input.bind(:horizontal, key: :j, side: :negative)   # an axis says which way the key pushes it
Input.reset_bindings(:jump)                   # back to the game's, for every player
Input.reset_bindings(pad: 1)                  # all of the second player's, back to the game's

What players bind is kept between runs in the user's RedGem folder, under bindings/, named as the game's save is (by-id/<game id>.json, or after the game's folder for a game with no id). It is written at the end of the frame in which it changed, once however many calls changed it, and not at all when it ends up as the file already says. A player binds an axis' keys and buttons only: its stick, and whether the stick is inverted, are always the game's, so a game's "invert Y" option (declaring the axis again with invert:) reaches every player.

One key may be bound to several actions, and every action it is bound to sees it: Enter can both :fire in the game and :confirm in a menu. A settings screen that wants each key to do one thing checks Input.bindings of the other actions before binding it.

A "press a key" screen asks for the next key or button pressed. The block gets the binding as text, and the gamepad's number (nil for a key); a key already held when it asks does not count. Escape, or a gamepad's B or Back, calls the capture off instead: the block gets nil for the binding, so the player can back out (cancel: lists other bindings for that, cancel: [] none). Whatever went down on the frame a capture ends is the capture's: no action fires and no menu opens with it.

Input.capture_next do |binding, pad|
  next if binding.nil?   # called off: jump stays as it was

  Input.unbind(:jump, pad: pad)
  Input.bind(:jump, binding, pad: pad)
end
Input.capture_next(cancel: ["key:backspace"]) { |binding, pad| ... }   # Escape can be bound
Input.capturing?       # still waiting
Input.capturing_for?(block)   # still waiting to call that block (not once another capture took its place)
Input.cancel_capture   # stop waiting (the block is never called)
Input.bindings_changes # a count that goes up whenever actions, axes or bindings may have changed

Sticks and triggers are not caught, only keys and buttons. Input.axis_stick(:horizontal) says which stick moves an axis (:left_x, or nil): it is the game's, the same for every player.

docs.title: The controls page
docs.text:
GameMenu's settings screen has a Controls button that opens a ready-made controls page (the :controls screen). At its top, a choice of the player whose bindings it shows (1 to 4: the first also has the keyboard). Under it, a row for each action and one for each side of each axis, every one the game declared, in two cells: the player's keys, and their gamepad buttons (an axis' stick shows among them, though no player rebinds it). Up and down move between the rows, left and right between a row's two cells.

Enter, a gamepad's A or a click on a cell (which also moves the focus there) waits for the next key (the keys' cell) or button (the buttons' cell): that one takes the place of everything the cell had, and the row's other cell keeps its own. A button pressed for the keys' cell (or a key for the buttons'), or a button of another player's gamepad, is not for it, and it waits on; any keyboard key is taken for any player. Escape or a gamepad's Back calls the wait off (and B too, for a keys' cell), so those are never bound there. A key bound to two rows is allowed, as above, and both cells show it in orange with a !. "Reset to defaults" puts all of the shown player's bindings back to the game's; Back (or Esc) goes back to the settings, on their Controls button (the settings were kept on the way in). What players bind is kept for the next runs as it changes. A game adds options to both screens as to any other (add_option): they come after the engine's buttons unless an index: says otherwise.

A row is named by the game's translation files, as game.controls.action_<name> (an axis' sides as game.controls.action_<name>_negative and _positive); without one, its name is made readable (:air_dash is "Air dash", the sides of :steer "Steer -" and "Steer +"). The engine names its own (:jump is "Jump", the negative side of :horizontal "Move left") and the keys and buttons ("Space", "Left Shift", "A button", "Left stick X"), as game.controls.* texts a game may change too.

docs.title: Read the mouse
docs.text:
Input.mouse_x, Input.mouse_y        # pixels from the top-left corner
Input.mouse_dx, Input.mouse_dy      # how far it moved since the last frame
Input.mouse_down?(:left)            # :left, :right or :middle, held
Input.mouse_pressed?(:left)         # went down this frame
Input.mouse_released?(:left)        # went up this frame
Input.mouse_wheel                   # notches turned this frame

To turn a first-person camera with the mouse, hide the pointer and keep it in the window, then use how far it moved:

def start = Input.mouse_locked = true

def update(_dt)
  transform.rotate(Vector3.new(0, -Input.mouse_dx * 0.1, 0))
end

To click on things in the world, cast a ray from the camera through the pointer:

if Input.mouse_pressed?(:left)
  origin, direction = Camera.screen_ray(Input.mouse_x, Input.mouse_y)
  hit = Physics.raycast(origin, direction, 100.0)
  hit[:object].destroy if hit
end

docs.title: Move a character
docs.text:
Give the object a character body: set Body in the Inspector's Physics card (objects made in the editor already have one), or use Add Component > Physics body on an object without physics. A character walks on floors, climbs slopes and is stopped by walls.

def update(_dt)
  direction = Vector3.new(Input.axis(:horizontal), 0, -Input.axis(:vertical)).normalized
  character.move(direction * 6.0)                                    # meters per second
  character.jump(9.0) if Input.action_pressed?(:jump) && character.grounded?
end

docs.title: Push things around
docs.text:
A dynamic body falls, rolls and gets pushed. From a script:

rigidbody.add_impulse(Vector3.up * 5.0)
rigidbody.velocity = Vector3.new(0, 0, -10)

A kinematic body is moved by your script (set transform.position) and carries what stands on it: platforms, lifts, doors.

Forces push for one physics step, so a steady push goes in fixed_update:

def fixed_update(_dt)
  rigidbody.add_force(Vector3.up * 30.0)                                  # newtons: a hovering crate
  rigidbody.add_force(transform.forward * 5.0, at: transform.position + Vector3.up)   # also tips it
  rigidbody.add_torque(Vector3.new(0, 2, 0))                              # spins it around y
end

rigidbody.mass, gravity_scale (0 floats), angular_velocity (degrees per second) can be read and changed while the game runs. rigidbody.kinematic = true hands a falling crate to your script (a crane picks it up); rigidbody.dynamic = true drops it again, at rest. rigidbody.sleep keeps a body still until something bumps it or wake is called.

docs.title: Doors, ropes and chains: joints
docs.text:
A joint holds two bodies together, or one to the world (give nil as the other). Points and axes are in world space.

A door on a hinge that pushes open up to 110 degrees, and that its motor pulls shut (back to the 0 degrees it started at, its other limit):

class Door < Behaviour
  def start
    pin = transform.position + Vector3.left * 0.5            # its left edge
    @hinge = Physics.joint(:hinge, game_object, nil, anchor: pin, axis: Vector3.up, limits: [0, 110])
  end

  def close = @hinge.motor(-60, 50)                           # degrees per second, newton meters
  def let_go = @hinge.motor(0, 0)
end

A rope of distance joints: each link may come closer to the one above it, never farther.

hook = Vector3.new(0, 8, 0)
above = nil
links.each do |link|                                          # dynamic spheres, top to bottom
  Physics.joint(:distance, link, above, other_anchor: above ? nil : hook)
  above = link
end

spring: 2, damping: 0.3 makes it a bungee. Other kinds: :fixed glues two bodies as they are, :slider lets one slide along an axis (limits: in meters), :point lets it turn every way (a ball and socket). break_force: 500 breaks a joint pulled harder than 500 newtons, or twisted harder than 500 newton meters (joint.broken? then says so); joint.remove lets go; destroying either object removes it.

docs.title: Collision layers
docs.text:
Bullets that fly through pickups, ghosts that walk through walls: give each body a layer and say in game.json which layers meet. Up to 16 layers; default is always there.

"physics": {
  "layers": ["default", "player", "enemy", "bullet", "pickup"],
  "collides": {"bullet": ["enemy", "default"], "pickup": ["player"]}
}

A layer with no collides entry meets every layer; two layers meet only when each lets the other in, so above bullets hit enemies and walls but pass through players, pickups and other bullets, and pickups only notice players. Put an object on a layer with the layer custom property (in Blender or the Inspector), or from a script:

bullet = Scene.spawn("Bullet", position: muzzle, rotation: transform.rotation)
bullet.rigidbody.layer = :bullet
bullet.rigidbody.velocity = transform.forward * 40.0

Triggers only notice bodies whose layer meets theirs, and queries look at the layers they are given.

docs.title: Drive a car
docs.text:
Give the chassis a vehicle body and mark its wheel children with wheel = true.

def fixed_update(_dt)
  vehicle.drive(throttle: Input.axis(:vertical), steering: Input.axis(:horizontal),
                handbrake: Input.down?(:space) ? 1.0 : 0.0)
end

vehicle.speed is in meters per second, negative in reverse.

docs.title: Pickups and zones
docs.text:
Tick Trigger in the object's Physics card (it stops being solid) and react when something enters:

class Coin < Behaviour
  def on_trigger_enter(other)
    return unless other.get_component(Player)

    Audio.play(:coin)
    destroy
  end
end

Only moving things (characters, dynamic and kinematic bodies) set triggers off.

docs.title: Spawn objects
docs.text:
