Mark an object as a Template in the Inspector (prefab = true). It disappears from the game and becomes something to copy:

bullet = Scene.spawn("Bullet", position: transform.position, rotation: transform.rotation)
bullet.add_component(Bullet, speed: 30.0)

The copy comes with the template's physics and scripts.

docs.title: Look ahead with a ray
docs.text:
hit = Physics.raycast(transform.position, transform.forward, 20.0, game_object)
Debug.log("I see #{hit[:object].name} #{hit[:distance]} m away") if hit

The last argument is an object the ray ignores (usually the one casting it). Every query also takes layers: (a layer or a list) and ignore: (an object or a list):

# Everything a laser goes through, nearest first.
Physics.raycast_all(eye, forward, 50.0, layers: [:enemy, :default], ignore: [game_object, gun])

# Would a ball of radius 0.4 get from here to there? (nil: the way is clear)
blocked = Physics.sphere_cast(transform.position, target, 0.4, ignore: game_object)

# An explosion: everything on the enemy layer within 5 m.
Physics.overlap_sphere(transform.position, 5.0, layers: :enemy).each do |hit|
  hit[:object].rigidbody&.add_impulse((hit[:point] - transform.position).normalized * 20.0)
end

box_cast, capsule_cast, overlap_box and overlap_capsule work the same way. Hits come nearest first, each object once, at most 64.

docs.title: Show text on screen
docs.text:
Call it every frame from update:

UI.text("Coins #{@coins}/#{@total}", x: 20, y: 40, size: 28, color: :gold)

Colors: :white, :black, :red, :green, :blue, :yellow, :gold, :orange, :gray, or [r, g, b].

To show it in the player's language, keep the text in the game's translation files and show it with I18n.t("hud.coins", coins: @coins, total: @total): see Texts in several languages.

docs.title: Menus, buttons and images
docs.text:
Everything in UI is drawn the frame you call it, so a menu is just a behaviour that draws itself every frame. UI.button returns true on the frame it is clicked:

def update(_dt)
  UI.rect(x: 0, y: 0, width: UI.width, height: UI.height, color: :black, alpha: 170)
  UI.text("My Game", x: UI.width / 2, y: 120, size: 72, align: :center)
  UI.image(:logo, x: 40, y: 40, width: 128)            # images/logo.png
  start_game if UI.button("Play", x: UI.width / 2 - 140, y: 300, width: 280, height: 58)
  Game.quit if UI.button("Quit", x: UI.width / 2 - 140, y: 374, width: 280, height: 58)
end

UI.width and UI.height are the size of the screen, so layouts can be centered. Pictures go in the game's images/ folder (.png or .jpg).

A text field hands back what is in it after this frame's typing, so keep the value and pass it in again (Input.text is what was typed this frame, for anything else):

@name = UI.text_field(@name, x: 40, y: 200, width: 320, height: 48, max_length: 12)

docs.title: Pause, and the flow between screens
docs.text:
Time.scale = 0 freezes the game: physics stops and behaviours get an update with a delta of 0, so a menu keeps working while everything else stands still. Time.scale = 1 resumes.

The usual flow of a game is made of three things:

  • A title screen: a menu that starts open, with the game frozen behind it.
  • Pause: the same menu opened by a key.
  • Other screens and levels: Game.load_scene("level2") to move on, and Game.load_scene(Game.scene_name) to restart the current one.

GameMenu is all of this, ready made: a title screen, a pause menu on Esc, P or a gamepad's Start, an end screen, and a settings screen (see A settings screen). Up and down move the focus between its buttons; Enter or a gamepad's A picks the focused one. Put it on an object from the scene's script, and end the game from anywhere:

class MainScene < SceneScript
  def setup
    Camera.main.add_component(GameMenu)   # title: "...", start_open: false
  end
end

GameMenu.instance.finish("You win!")

Its screens are :title, :pause, :over, :settings and :controls. A game adds options and screens of its own:

menu = GameMenu.instance
menu.screens[:credits] = GameMenu::Screen.new(heading: "Made by Ana", back: -> { menu.show(:pause) })
menu.screens[:pause].add_option("Credits", index: 1) { menu.show(:credits) }

back is what the pause keys do on that screen. A label or a heading may also be a lookup, -> { I18n.t("menu.credits") }, made each time it is shown (see Texts in several languages). A screen that draws more than buttons is a subclass of GameMenu::Screen (draw, space_above, opened, closed, typing?, and rows for widgets of its own that take the focus before its buttons, with focus): the platformer's multiplayer screen, games/platformer/scripts/multiplayer_screen.rb, is one.

docs.title: A settings screen
docs.text:
GameMenu has one ready, reached from its title and pause screens: window mode, resolution, render scale, vsync, frame-rate cap, quality and master volume, with a button to its controls page (see The controls page). A game builds its own with Settings and the widgets of UI, which the keyboard and a gamepad work through a focus:

def update(_dt)
  @focus ||= UI::Focus.new
  @focus.update(3)   # up and down (arrows, D-pad) move it among three widgets
  box = { x: 40, width: 480, height: 44 }
  on = UI.toggle("VSync", Settings.vsync, y: 100, focused: @focus.at?(0), **box)
  Settings.vsync = on unless on == Settings.vsync
  names = %w[Low Medium High Ultra]
  index = Settings::QUALITIES.index(Settings.quality) || 3
  picked = UI.choice("Quality", names, index, y: 152, focused: @focus.at?(1), **box)
  Settings.quality = Settings::QUALITIES[picked] unless picked == index
  volume = UI.slider("Volume", Settings.volume, y: 204, focused: @focus.at?(2), **box)
  Settings.volume = volume unless volume == Settings.volume
end

Each change shows at once; Settings.save keeps them for the game's next runs. A quality caps what the level's environment asks for (samples a pixel, temporal anti-aliasing, shadow cascades and distance, scattered copies and how far they show, the sky picture's size, ambient occlusion, bloom): :ultra draws the level as it was made, and nothing ever gets more than it asked for. What the graphics card cannot do is left out whatever the quality.

docs.title: Play sounds and music
docs.text:
Files go in the game's sounds/ folder.

Audio.play(:jump)                      # sounds/jump.wav (or .ogg, .mp3, .flac)
Audio.play(:hit, volume: 0.5, pitch: 1.2)
Audio.music(:theme, loop: true)
Audio.stop_music

docs.title: A sense of speed
docs.text:
rush = (speed / TOP_SPEED).clamp(0.0, 1.0)
Camera.fov = 52 + 10 * rush          # the view widens
Camera.motion_blur = 0.7 * rush      # the edges of the picture streak
Audio.music_pitch = 0.8 + 0.7 * rush # the engine's note climbs (Audio.music(:engine) is looping)

docs.title: Change level
docs.text:
Game.load_scene("level2")   # scenes/level2.glb; "main" is scene.glb

The switch happens at the end of the frame. Ruby global variables survive it, which is the simple way to carry a score or lives from one level to the next.

docs.title: Do something later, or over a while
docs.text:
Every behaviour has timers. They run on game time, so they wait while the game is paused, and they end with their object.

after(2.0) { destroy }                                   # once, two seconds from now
every(0.5) { Scene.spawn("Bullet", position: muzzle) }   # again and again
tween(0.4) { |t| transform.scale = Vector3.one * (1.0 + t) }   # every frame, t going from 0 to 1

after and every return a timer you can cancel; cancel_timers calls off all of a behaviour's. tween starts and ends gently; ease: :linear keeps a steady pace.

docs.title: Sparks, dust and smoke
docs.text:
Particles.burst lets out small dots that fly and fade. They are looks only: nothing collides with them.

# A coin picked up: gold sparks in every direction.
Particles.burst(transform.position, count: 24, color: :gold, glow: true)

# Smoke follows this object, from a local exhaust offset. Old puffs stay in the world.
@smoke = Particles.emitter(game_object, rate: 20, offset: [0, 0.5, 1], color: :gray,
                           direction: Vector3.up, spread: 20, speed: 1.0, life: 1.5,
                           size: 0.4, gravity: -0.05)

Particles.emitter(object, rate: 24, offset: Vector3.zero, **settings) returns a handle with active? and stop. It takes the burst settings below except count: rate is particles per game second, greater than zero and at most 4096. Offset uses the object's full world transform; direction follows its world rotation. Birth positions are spread along the object's movement between frames. Movement over 10 meters in one update is treated as a teleport: new particles start at the destination. Each birth is aged and advanced by the time since its birth within the frame. Emitted particles move independently in world space, without inheriting the object's velocity. Time.scale = 0 pauses emission.

Destroying the object or changing scenes ends its emitters; stopping one leaves its existing particles to finish their lives. Particles.clear removes particles and emitters together. Up to 256 emitters share the existing limit of 4096 live particles. When that limit is full, missed births are dropped rather than saved for a later burst. Priority passes to the next emitter that is waiting for space, so a full pool cannot permanently favor the first one. Emitter handles are never reused.

These are local visual effects, not replicated by NetworkSync. Start matching effects on each client through gameplay events. A game running without a presenter, including a dedicated server, returns inactive emitter handles and does not allocate or simulate emitters.

Setting Meaning Default count How many 12 color, alpha A color name or [r, g, b]; 0 to 255 :white, 255 glow Shines (sparks, magic) instead of covering what is behind (dust, smoke) false direction, spread Where they fly, and how many degrees they may stray: 180 is everywhere up, 180 speed, life, size Meters per second, seconds, meters across (each particle varies a little) 3.0, 0.8, 0.12 gravity 1 falls like everything else, 0 floats, negative rises 1.0 image A picture from the game's images/ folder drawn on each particle, tinted by color a soft dot frames, fps The image is a sprite sheet of [columns, rows] pictures, read like a page; fps of them a second, round and round, or all of them once over the particle's life without one one picture spin Degrees per second each picture turns 0 lit Takes the light of the sun, the sky and the lights near it, as smoke and dust do (glowing ones shine with their own light either way) false soft Meters over which it fades where it meets the ground or a wall, instead of cutting a hard line into it 0

A white picture with see-through edges works best, since the color tints it: Particles.burst(at, image: :smoke, color: :gray, alpha: 90, size: 1.2, life: 1.5, gravity: -0.05, spin: 40).

docs.title: Over their life
docs.text:
size, color and alpha may each be a list of up to 4 values, which every particle goes through evenly over its life, from the first at its birth to the last at its end. A single size or alpha does what particles always did: it holds for half the life, then the size shrinks to 0.3 of itself and the alpha fades out. A single color holds.

# A flame that licks (an 8 x 4 sheet at 30 pictures a second), shrinking from yellow to a dark ember.
Particles.burst(torch, count: 1, image: :flame_sheet, frames: [8, 4], fps: 30, glow: true, soft: 0.3,
                size: [0.5, 0.6, 0.15], color: [[255, 230, 160], [255, 120, 30], [70, 25, 15]], life: 0.6)

# Smoke that grows as it rises, fades in and out, and darkens in the shade.
Particles.burst(chimney, count: 1, image: :smoke, lit: true, soft: 1.0, size: [0.5, 2.5],
                alpha: [0, 120, 90, 0], gravity: -0.1, life: 3.0, spin: 20)

cast_shadow: true includes a particle in the directional sun's shadow cascades; it defaults to false. Its shadow is an alpha-cutout sprite facing the sun, using its current size, rotation, alpha and flipbook cell (or the circular dot mask without an image). Fragments whose combined texture and particle alpha is below 0.5 cast no shadow. Fading can therefore shrink or remove a shadow abruptly. This is a sprite approximation, not volumetric smoke: overlapping particles do not accumulate density, and soft: only fades the color pass against the camera's scene depth. Point lights do not cast particle shadows.

Lit particles are lit at their corners by the sun, the sky and the nearest lights, as a puff lit on about half of it. lit: true also receives the scene's filtered sun shadows, using the same shadow cascades as surfaces. Sun shadowing leaves sky and point-light contributions intact. Unlit particles, including unlit glowing ones, keep their own color in shadows.

docs.title: Light that flickers and fades
docs.text:
An object with a light (a lamp, a fire's glow, made in Blender like any light) can change how bright it shines and in what color while the game runs:

glow = Scene.spawn("FireLight", position: torch)
every(0.05) { glow.light.intensity = 40 + rand * 25 }           # a flame's flicker
tween(0.6) { |t| glow.light.intensity = 300 * (1 - t) }        # a blast that fades
glow.light.color = [255, 120, 40]                               # or a name: :orange

intensity is in the units Blender gives the light (watts for a point or spot light, lux for the sun) and is at least 0; color is three channels from 0 to 255, as a color picker shows them.

docs.title: Control animations
docs.text:
Every animation in a level plays in a loop from the start. Animation is for the ones that should not, by the name the action has in Blender:

Animation.stop(:DoorOpen)                              # in a scene script's setup: starts closed
Animation.play(:DoorOpen, loop: false)                 # opens once and stays open
Animation.play(:DoorOpen, loop: false, speed: -1.0)    # closes
Animation.pause(:Fan)                                  # freezes where it is; play carries on
Animation.playing?(:DoorOpen)                          # false once it reached its end

Animation.names lists the level's clips; time, duration and seek(name, seconds) are there for syncing things to a clip. A stopped clip lets go of its objects, so scripts can move them.

docs.title: Animate one character
docs.text:
Animation is for the whole level. A character with several clips (idle, walk, run) picks its own through animation, and so does each spawned copy of it:

def start = animation.play(:Idle)

def update(_dt)
  animation.play(moving? ? :Run : :Idle, fade: 0.2)   # blends from one to the other over 0.2 s
end

Playing the clip a character is already on just carries on, so it is fine to call every frame. loop: false plays once and holds the last pose; speed: and restart: true work as above. A second clip can be laid over the first:

animation.mix(:Wave)                 # a clip that only moves the arm: the legs keep walking
animation.mix(:Limp, weight: 0.5)    # half of it blended into everything
animation.unmix

animation.follow_scene(fade: 0.3) hands the character back to what the level plays, and animation.clip is the name of its own clip (nil while it follows the level).

docs.title: Save progress
docs.text:
Save keeps numbers, texts and true/false values between runs, in one file per game:

best = Save.get(:best_time, 999.0)    # the second value is what you get when nothing was saved
Save[:best_time] = time if time < best
Save[:name] = "Ana"
Save.delete(:name)
Save.clear                            # start from nothing

Whole numbers come back as integers (a saved 12.0 is read as 12): call .to_f on a value you divide.

The file is written on every change, to .config/redgem/saves/by-id/<id>.json in the player's home folder, where <id> is the game's id from its game.json: the save stays with the game when its folder is moved or renamed. A game with no id saves to .config/redgem/saves/<folder>-<digits>.json, with digits made from where its folder is. Tests get a save file of their own, empty at the start of each test.

Each change is flushed to the disk before it replaces the file, and the save before it is kept beside it as <name>.json.bak, written the same way. A save found damaged (cut short by a crash or a bad disk) is moved aside to <name>.json.damaged, never written over, and the backup takes its place; the log says so, naming both files. When the backup is damaged too, it is moved aside as well and the game starts from nothing. A save that cannot be read at all (another program holds it, say) is left alone: the game runs without saving, and the log says why.

docs.title: Keep score across objects
docs.text:
Put a manager behaviour on one object and let the others find it:

class GameManager < Behaviour
  attr_reader :coins

  def self.instance = Scene.find("GameManager")&.get_component(GameManager)

  def start = @coins = 0
  def collect_coin = @coins += 1
end

# anywhere else
GameManager.instance.collect_coin

docs.title: Time
docs.text: Time.elapsed is seconds since the game started, Time.delta the length of the last frame.

docs.title: Texts in several languages
docs.text: A game shows its players texts: a score, a hint, the end screen's message, the labels of its menus. Written straight into the scripts, they are in one language. Kept in translation files, the same game shows them in English to one player and in Portuguese to another.

docs.title: Translation files
docs.text:
They go in the game's locales/ folder, one per language, named for it: locales/en.json, locales/pt.json, locales/pt_BR.json. Each is a JSON object of keys and the texts they stand for:

{
  "hud.coins": "Coins {count}/{total}",
  "hud.hint": "Grab every coin, then reach the flag!",
  "over.win": "You win!"
}

A key is any name you like; words joined by dots keep them in order (hud.coins, menu.credits). A text names the values put into it in braces ({count}). A long text may be a list of lines, which are joined with line breaks: "credits": ["Made by Ana", "Music by Rui"].

English is the one every other language falls back to, so en.json has every key; a translation has the keys it translates, and a key it lacks shows in English.

The templates come with a locales/en.json, and the platformer's (games/platformer/locales/) is a full example.

docs.title: Showing a text
docs.text:
I18n.t gives the text of a key in the language in use, with its values filled in:

UI.text(I18n.t("hud.coins", count: @coins, total: @total), x: 20, y: 40, size: 28, color: :gold)
GameMenu.instance.finish(I18n.t("over.win"))

Each value is shown as its to_s. A number with a set number of decimals is formatted first: I18n.t("hud.best", seconds: format("%.1f", @best)). Keep a whole sentence in one text, values and all, rather than gluing pieces together: another language may want the values elsewhere, or a different word for one and for many ("{place}: 1 other player" and "{place}: {count} other players" are two keys).

A key no file has a text for shows as itself (hud.coins), so a missing text is easy to spot on the screen.

docs.title: The language
docs.text:
I18n.locale is the language texts are shown in, as a Symbol (:en). It starts as the player's: the language chosen in RedGem's settings, else the system's, matched with the game's files whatever their case and whether - or _ is written: the same language and region (pt_BR.json for pt-BR), else the language alone (pt.json), else another region of it. When the game has no file in the player's language, it starts in the language RedGem shows its own texts in (English when it has none in the player's). A text a region's file lacks is looked for in the language's own file (pt_BR, then pt). A game may offer a choice:

I18n.available_locales    # => [:en, :pt]: the languages the game has files for
I18n.locale = :pt         # from now on, in Portuguese

A text already looked up keeps its language. GameMenu looks its labels and headings up each time it draws them, so they follow I18n.locale; a game's own option or heading does too when it is given as a lookup rather than a text:

menu.screens[:pause].add_option(-> { I18n.t("menu.credits") }, index: 1) { menu.show(:credits) }
GameMenu::Screen.new(heading: -> { I18n.t("credits.heading") })

docs.title: The engine's own texts
docs.text:
The labels of GameMenu (Play, Quit, Play again, Resume, Restart, Paused, and those of its settings screen and controls page) come from the engine, in the player's language. A game's files may change them or translate them, with the same keys:

{
  "game.menu.play": "Start",
  "game.menu.resume": "Continuar"
}

The keys are game.menu.play, game.menu.quit, game.menu.play_again, game.menu.resume, game.menu.restart and game.menu.paused; the settings screen's are game.settings.*, and the controls page's game.controls.* (its rows, and the names of keys and buttons: see The controls page). A text is looked for in the game's files in the language in use, then among the engine's texts in that language, then in the game's English, then in the engine's English; else the key itself is shown. (So a game whose English changes a label still shows the engine's translation of it to a player who reads another language.)

docs.title: What is read, and what is not
docs.text:
Translation files travel with the game: builds, Android packages and dedicated servers carry the locales/ folder like the rest. They are read once, when the game's scripts start. Only files named <language>.json are read (a language's name is letters, digits, - and _), none larger than 1 MB and none reached through a symbolic link. A file that is not a translation file (broken JSON, or a value that is neither a text nor a list of lines) is left out whole: the log says which file and why, and the game goes on with the others.

On a dedicated server each room has its own I18n.locale. A text a server sends players, such as the reason a join was turned down, is in the server's language: a game that wants it in each player's sends a key and lets the player's machine look it up.

docs.title: Multiplayer
docs.text:
Games can be played together over a local network or the internet. One machine hosts the game and the others join it; every machine has an id (the host is 1, then 2, 3... as players arrive). Up to 16 machines play together.

A game that plays online says so in its game.json with "network": true: its Android app then asks the phone for the network, which an app without it does not get (a build of a game that says nothing guesses it from its scripts, and warns; see Building and sharing).

There are three ways for the others to get to the host, from the easiest, and a fourth where nobody hosts:

Where the players are How they join What it takes On the same network (same Wi-Fi) The game is found by itself Nothing Anywhere A room code like K7QM3P A relay running somewhere on the internet Anywhere The host's address The host's router forwarding a port Anywhere The server's address The game running on a dedicated server

docs.title: Host and join
docs.text:
Network.host                           # on one machine (port 7777; port: 9000 picks another)
Network.join("192.168.0.12")           # on the others: the host's address

Network.on_connect { start_round }     # this machine is in the game
Network.on_fail { |reason| show("Could not join: #{reason}") }  # reason: nil, the host's, or a timeout
Network.on_join { |peer| ... }         # someone else arrived
Network.on_leave { |peer| ... }        # someone else left
Network.on_disconnect { ... }          # the game is gone: the host left or the connection dropped

Network.online?, Network.host?, Network.id and Network.peers (everyone else's ids) tell where things stand. A join that hears nothing back for 5 seconds gives up, and on_fail gets "the game did not answer in time". That time, like every wait of the network, is real time: a game run with no window (a headless test) plays its frames faster than that, and they do not count. Network.leave leaves the game; when the host leaves, it ends for everyone.

Every machine in a game runs the same version of the engine's network protocol, and so do the relay and the dedicated server it meets on. A machine of another version is turned away: on_fail gets the reason ("this game runs protocol 1, the other side 2"), and both sides write it to the log.

A host lets 4 machines from one address be joining at the same moment (more are hung up on, and try again). Players behind one shared address (a campus, some mobile networks) joining together may need more: Network.host(waiting_per_address: 16), up to 32.

docs.title: Games on the same network
docs.text:
A hosted game answers the machines around it, so nobody types an address:

Network.host(name: "Ana's game")       # name: the game's title unless said; visible: false hides it

Network.search                         # on the others: start looking
Network.games                          # => [{ name: "Ana's game", address: "192.168.0.12", port: 7777, players: 1 }]
game = Network.games.first
Network.join(game[:address], port: game[:port])
Network.stop_search

Network.games changes as games come and go, so a menu draws a button for each one every frame. Every RedGem game looks on the same port, so games see each other's; a game that wants to see only its own picks another with Network.discovery_port = 7790 (the same on every copy).

docs.title: Over the internet: rooms
docs.text:
Home routers let connections out, not in, so two players at home cannot reach each other directly. They can both reach a relay: a small program on a machine with a public address. One player opens a room and gets a short code; the others join with the code:

Network.relay = "relay.example.com"    # where the relay runs ("host:port" for another port)

Network.host(room: true)               # then, once on_connect fired:
Network.room                           # => "K7QM3P": tell it to the others

Network.join(room: "K7QM3P")             # on the others

Everything else is the same in a room: messages, NetworkSync, Network.spawn. Whoever opened the room is the host; when they leave, the room closes.

The relay comes with the engine, as a program of its own: redgem-relay. It is small, opens no window and needs no graphics card or display, so it runs on any machine the players can reach (a small rented server is enough, it only passes messages on):

./build/src/redgem-relay               # listens on port 7778; --port <number> picks another
docker compose up relay                # or with Docker

One address may hold 24 machines and 8 open rooms on a relay. When many players share one address (a campus, some mobile networks), raise them: --per-address <number> (up to 1024) and --rooms-per-address <number> (up to 256).

While nobody talks to it the relay sleeps: it wakes when a machine connects or says something, and about once a second to let go of machines that went silent.

The relay expects strangers: one address can only open a few rooms and hold a few connections, guessing room codes gets it kept out for a while, and a machine that goes silent is let go, as is one that sends far more than a game does (each message counts for 64 bytes on top of its own, so floods of tiny messages count too).

docs.title: By the host's address
docs.text:
Without a relay, players anywhere can still join the host's public address (Network.join("203.0.113.7")) if the host's router forwards the game's port (7777, TCP) to the host's machine.

A host reached directly, whether it is a player or a dedicated server, lets go of a machine that sends far more than a game does: more than 256 KB a second over time (and a burst of 2 MB), or more than 8192 messages a second (and a burst of 16384), however short they are.

docs.title: On a dedicated server
docs.text:
A dedicated server runs the game itself, with no player, and everyone joins it (see Dedicated server):

Network.join("play.example.com")                  # any room with a free place
Network.join("play.example.com", room: "K7QM3P")  # the room a friend is in (their Network.room)

The server runs the same scripts with Network.server? true. It hosts the game (Network.host?, id 1) but plays nobody, so skip "my player" there, and use Network.players (everyone else without the server) where a game shows the other players:

Network.on_connect do
  spawn_my_hero unless Network.server?
  Network.players.each { |peer| show_hero_of(peer) }
end

To let in only players who logged in, the join carries their token and the server's game decides (Network.join(address, auth: { token: token }), Network.authenticate): see Online services.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Machines talk in named messages:

Network.on(:hit) { |data, from| @health -= data[:damage] }

Network.emit(:hit, { damage: 3, at: transform.position })   # to everyone else
Network.emit(:hit, { damage: 3 }, to: 2)                    # to one machine
Network.emit(:score, 120, to: :host)

A message carries nil, true/false, numbers, texts, Vector3, and arrays and hashes of those (hash keys arrive as symbols; a key no script of the receiving game uses anywhere arrives as a text instead, so data[:damage] works as written and only keys nobody asked for stay texts). An array or a hash holds at most 4096 things (in a message: Save keeps any number). Messages arrive whole and in the order they were sent. Handlers last until the next level is loaded, so register them in a behaviour's start or a scene script's setup. Names starting with $ are the engine's own.

docs.title: Objects in the same place everywhere
docs.text:
A NetworkSync keeps an object where its owner has it: the owner's machine moves it as usual and the others see it follow. Only the owner should read input or decide where it goes (with no game on, everything is this machine's, so the same script works in single player):

class Player < Behaviour
  def update(dt)
    return unless get_component(NetworkSync).mine?
    # ... read the keyboard and move, as in a single-player game
  end
end

For objects that are in the level on every machine (a moving platform, a ball), add a NetworkSync to them; the host owns them unless you say otherwise:

find!("Lift").add_component(NetworkSync)
find!("Ball").add_component(NetworkSync, owner: 2, key: "ball")   # key: its name on the network

A key is one object's: a second NetworkSync under a key another object goes by already raises an error (the behaviour is disabled, the first object keeps the key), and so does assign to it. A key is at most 128 bytes long.

The owner sends where its object is 20 times a second, in a few bytes: only what changed since the last time (an object standing still sends little more than its key). The other machines show it a moment behind, blended between the last two places they heard of, so it moves smoothly however unevenly those arrive. The delay follows the network: about 75 milliseconds when places arrive steadily, longer (up to 350) when they come in bursts. When the next place is late, the object goes on the way it was going for a fifth of a second, then waits; moved far at once (more than 6 meters), it jumps there instead of sliding across. Your own objects are never delayed: they are moved on your machine. Each watcher can tune it per object:

add_component(NetworkSync, delay: 0.2)            # always this many seconds behind
add_component(NetworkSync, interpolate: false)    # no delay: chases the newest place, less smoothly

What the object's own animation does goes along with its place: play an attack on the owner's machine (animation.play(:Attack, loop: false, fade: 0.1)) and the others see the same clip, from the same moment of it, as far behind as they show the object, fading in as it does there. So do its speed, a pause, a clip mixed over it (animation.mix) and going back to the level's clips (animation.follow_scene). Only changes are sent, as part of the object's place, and the whole of it now and then, so a machine that joins in the middle of a fight sees it too. Clips are known by name: every machine needs the same ones, and a name is at most 64 bytes long. To leave a character's animation to each machine's own scripts:

add_component(NetworkSync, animation: false)

For objects created while playing, Network.spawn makes the copy on every machine, including the ones that join later, and removes it when its owner leaves:

Network.on_connect { Network.spawn("Hero", position: spawn_point) }   # one hero per player

The owner's copy has its physics; the others' copies are only shown, so what a spawned object touches is decided on its owner's machine and told to the others in a message.

A machine only creates for others what the game itself spawns: templates it has passed to Network.spawn, prefab = true objects, and the ones named with Network.allow_spawn("Hero", "Bullet") (worth saying in a scene script's setup). And each machine can only spawn objects of its own: 64 at a time, 512 in the whole game. Past that Network.spawn makes nothing and returns nil.

Loading a level happens on one machine: its spawned objects go away everywhere, and it is shown the others' again. To change level together, send a message and load it on every machine.

docs.title: Deciding things once
docs.text:
Two machines must not both decide the same thing. The simple rule: each machine decides for the objects it owns and tells the others. A coin picked up by a player is announced by that player's machine:

def on_trigger_enter(other)
  return unless other.get_component(NetworkSync)&.mine?

  Network.emit(:coin, name)
  collect
end

# in a manager's start
Network.on(:coin) { |coin_name, _from| Scene.find(coin_name)&.get_component(Coin)&.collect }

The platformer demo plays together this way: Esc > Multiplayer hosts or joins a game, and games/platformer/scripts/co_op.rb is the whole of its networking.

docs.title: Testing it
docs.text: The engine's own multiplayer test runs two copies of the game at once, each with its own test script (tests/system_pairs/), and two copies against the game on a dedicated server (tests/system_servers/). For a quick try on one machine, open the game twice, host in one and join 127.0.0.1 in the other.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text: There is no matchmaking or public list of games: players are on the same network, share a room code, or know the host's or the server's address. No relay or server is run for you: each game runs its own. Every message passes through the host (or the relay), over TCP: a packet lost on the way holds up the ones after it. Nothing rewinds time to judge a shot where its shooter saw the target (lag compensation), so the shooter's machine should decide its own hits, as in "Deciding things once": fine for co-op and casual games, not for competitive shooters. Messages are not encrypted. Players are not authenticated unless the game hosting asks for it (Online services), in a room on a relay too.

docs.title: Online services
docs.text:
What a game played online needs besides the game itself: talking to web services (HTTP), letting in only the players who logged in (connection approval) and keeping their progress (Save on a dedicated server, or a database behind a web service). No service is built into the engine and none is required: below are two ways to do it, a hosted service (Supabase) and a backend of your own.

A game that makes web requests says "network": true in its game.json (a build of one that says nothing guesses it from its scripts, and warns; "network": false keeps its Android app off the network; see Building and sharing).

The player's password only ever goes from their device to the service, over HTTPS. The game connection carries the token the service gave, then gameplay.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
HTTP.get("https://api.example.com/news") { |response| @news = response.json if response.ok? }

HTTP.post("https://api.example.com/scores", json: { player: id, points: 120 },
          headers: { "Authorization" => "Bearer #{token}" }) do |response|
  next Debug.warn("scores: #{response.error || response.status}") unless response.ok?

  show_ranking(response.json[:top])
end
  • HTTP.get, post, put, patch, delete(url, json:, body:, headers:, timeout:). json: sends a hash or an array as JSON (with its Content-Type); body: sends a text as it is.
  • The block gets the response a moment later, on the game's own thread: the frame never waits. ok? (a 2xx status), status (0 when no answer came), headers (names in lower case), body, json (nil when the body is not JSON) and error (why no answer came).
  • response.json gives hash keys as symbols when your scripts use that symbol, as strings otherwise (as messages do).
  • Addresses are https://, checked against the certificates the system trusts, or http:// to this machine or the local network only (a backend you run beside the game): 127.x, 10.x, 172.16.x to 172.31.x, 192.168.x and 169.254.x. No request goes to a cloud's metadata address (169.254.169.254, 100.100.100.200), over http:// or https://. Over https://, an answer whose end only the connection's end marks must end with the server's TLS goodbye (close_notify), or it is taken as cut short.
  • An answer is at most 8 MB; 16 requests may be on their way at once; each gives up after 15 seconds unless timeout: says otherwise (at most 120). Redirects are not followed.
  • When a level is loaded, the blocks of requests still on their way are not called (the requests still go out). When the game ends (or Play is stopped in the editor) they are given up.

docs.title: Letting players in
docs.text:
The joining machine sends a hash with its join, usually the token it got when logging in. The game that hosts (on a dedicated server, the server's game) decides:

# on the device, after logging in
Network.join("play.example.com", auth: { token: session_token })

# on the server
Network.authenticate do |peer, auth, decide|
  HTTP.get("https://auth.example.com/user",
           headers: { "Authorization" => "Bearer #{auth[:token]}" }) do |response|
    next decide.deny("not logged in") unless response.ok?

    decide.accept(identity: response.json[:id], name: response.json[:name])
  end
end

Network.on_join { |peer| greet(Network.identity(peer), Network.player_name(peer)) }
  • The block gets the newcomer's id, what its join carried (a hash, empty when nothing) and the decision to make: decide.accept(identity:, name:) or decide.deny(reason), now or later.
  • Until then the newcomer waits: on_join fires once it is accepted. One not decided on within 10 seconds is turned away. A player turned away gets on_fail { |reason| } with the reason.
  • Network.identity(peer) and Network.player_name(peer) say who a player is, on the machine that accepted it, until after its on_leave.
  • Without authenticate everyone is let in, as before. Network.authenticate with no block turns it off. The handler stays when a level is loaded.
  • What a join carries is at most 4 KB once written as JSON. It is untrusted: check it with the service that issued it.
  • It works with a player hosting too, and in a room on a relay, where the game of whoever opened the room decides: the relay decides nothing, it passes each join on and the decision back.

docs.title: Saving on a server
docs.text:
Save on a dedicated server is written to the server's data folder (--data, see Dedicated server), shared by all its rooms, and survives restarts. Save keeps numbers, texts, true/false, Vector3, and arrays and hashes of those (hashes come back with string keys), so each player's data can be kept under their identity:

Network.on_leave do |peer|
  Save.update("players", {}) do |players|
    players.merge(Network.identity(peer) => { "level" => @level, "coins" => @coins })
  end
end

The server's rooms run at the same time, each on a thread of its own, and share its Save. Reading a value and writing it back (players = Save["players"]; ...; Save["players"] = players) can lose what another room wrote in between: change a value that more than one room may change with Save.update, whose block gets the value as it is and returns the new one, with no other room reading or writing the save meanwhile (keep the block short: the other rooms' saves wait for it).

The server keeps its saves in a database, one row per key, each written as soon as it changes: a hash of every player is rewritten whole when one player changes, so with many players keep a key per player instead (Save["player:#{Network.identity(peer)}"]). For queries such as a ranking, send the data to a backend with HTTP.

Secrets of the server (the key a backend lets only the server write with) go in the server's own save, written with the sqlite3 tool while the server is stopped (each value is stored as JSON, so a text is in double quotes):

sqlite3 /srv/platformer-data/save.sqlite3 \
  "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS saves (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL, value TEXT NOT NULL) WITHOUT ROWID;
   INSERT OR REPLACE INTO saves VALUES ('backend_key', '\"some-long-secret\"');"

The server's game reads them with Save["backend_key"]; players' machines never see a server's saves.

docs.title: With a hosted service: Supabase
docs.text:
Supabase has a free tier with accounts and a database reached over HTTPS.

  1. Create a project. Its settings give the project's address (https://<ref>.supabase.co), the public anon key (for the game) and the secret service_role key (for the server only).
  2. In the SQL editor, create a table for each player's progress that anyone may read:
create table progress (player_id uuid primary key references auth.users, name text, coins int not null default 0);
alter table progress enable row level security;
create policy "anyone reads the ranking" on progress for select using (true);

On the device (SUPABASE is the project's address, ANON_KEY its anon key):

# Sign up once (Supabase may ask the player to confirm their email first)
HTTP.post("#{SUPABASE}/auth/v1/signup", json: { email: email, password: password },
          headers: { "apikey" => ANON_KEY }) { |response| ... }

# Log in: the answer holds the session token
HTTP.post("#{SUPABASE}/auth/v1/token?grant_type=password", json: { email: email, password: password },
          headers: { "apikey" => ANON_KEY }) do |response|
  next show_error("could not log in (#{response.error || response.status})") unless response.ok?

  Network.join(SERVER, auth: { token: response.json[:access_token] })
end

# The ranking
HTTP.get("#{SUPABASE}/rest/v1/progress?select=name,coins&order=coins.desc&limit=10",
         headers: { "apikey" => ANON_KEY }) { |response| @ranking = response.json if response.ok? }

On the server, the token is checked with Supabase, and each player's coins (kept in the server's save, as above) are written with the service_role key, kept in the server's save too:

Network.authenticate do |_peer, auth, decide|
  HTTP.get("#{SUPABASE}/auth/v1/user",
           headers: { "apikey" => ANON_KEY, "Authorization" => "Bearer #{auth[:token]}" }) do |response|
    next decide.deny("not logged in") unless response.ok?

    decide.accept(identity: response.json[:id], name: response.json[:email])
  end
end

Network.on_leave do |peer|
  key = Save["supabase_service_key"]
  coins = Save["players"][Network.identity(peer)]["coins"]
  HTTP.post("#{SUPABASE}/rest/v1/progress",
            json: { player_id: Network.identity(peer), name: Network.player_name(peer), coins: coins },
            headers: { "apikey" => key, "Authorization" => "Bearer #{key}",
                       "Prefer" => "resolution=merge-duplicates" }) { |response| ... }
end

docs.title: With a backend of your own
docs.text:
A backend of your own needs only a few calls. The essentials, in Ruby with Sinatra and SQLite (a players table with id, name, salt, digest and coins, and a sessions table that ties tokens to players; signing up inserts a player with a random salt and the digest of its password):

DB = SQLite3::Database.new("accounts.sqlite3", results_as_hash: true)

def digest(password, salt) = OpenSSL::KDF.pbkdf2_hmac(password, salt: salt, iterations: 100_000,
                                                                 length: 32, hash: "sha256").unpack1("H*")

post "/login" do
  name, password = JSON.parse(request.body.read).values_at("name", "password")
  player = DB.get_first_row("SELECT * FROM players WHERE name = ?", [name.to_s])
  correct = player && Rack::Utils.secure_compare(player["digest"], digest(password.to_s, player["salt"]))
  halt 401, { error: "wrong name or password" }.to_json unless correct
  token = SecureRandom.hex(32)
  DB.execute("INSERT INTO sessions (token, player_id) VALUES (?, ?)", [token, player["id"]])
  { token: token, id: player["id"], name: player["name"] }.to_json
end

get "/me" do   # who a token is: what the game server asks
  token = request.env["HTTP_AUTHORIZATION"].to_s.delete_prefix("Bearer ").dup.force_encoding("UTF-8")
  player = DB.get_first_row("SELECT players.* FROM sessions JOIN players ON players.id = player_id " \
                            "WHERE token = ?", [token])
  halt 401, { error: "not logged in" }.to_json unless player
  { id: player["id"], name: player["name"] }.to_json
end

post "/progress" do   # only the game server, which holds the key
  halt 403 unless Rack::Utils.secure_compare(request.env["HTTP_X_SERVER_KEY"].to_s, ENV.fetch("SERVER_KEY"))
  player, coins = JSON.parse(request.body.read).values_at("player", "coins")
  DB.execute("UPDATE players SET coins = coins + ? WHERE id = ?", [coins.to_i, player.to_i])
  halt 204
end
Call Sends Answers POST /login {name, password} 200 {token, id, name}, 401 {error} GET /me Authorization: Bearer <token> 200 {id, name}, 401 POST /progress {player, coins} and X-Server-Key 204, 403 without the key

Sinatra listens on this machine only (-o 0.0.0.0 lets the local network in). On the internet, put it behind HTTPS (a reverse proxy in front of it): games reach other machines over https:// only.

docs.title: The platformer with it
docs.text:
The platformer demo logs in when its ACCOUNTS constant is set (scripts/main_scene.rb), next to SERVER:

SERVER = "127.0.0.1".freeze
ACCOUNTS = "http://127.0.0.1:4567".freeze

The multiplayer menu then offers Log in (a name, then a password) before Play online, which joins with the token. The server checks it with GET /me, lets the player in as user-<id>, and when the player leaves keeps their coins in its save and, given the backend's key, in the backend too:

mkdir -p /srv/platformer-data      # once: the backend's key, in the server's own save (see above)
redgem-server games/platformer --data /srv/platformer-data

With ACCOUNTS empty (as it ships), players join as guests, each under an id their machine keeps, and the server keeps their coins all the same. See scripts/accounts.rb and scripts/server_gate.rb.
